HASH MAP PATTERN

Mapping Relationships

Use a mapping to enforce a consistent one-to-one relationship between elements of two sequences. The values themselves may differ; what matters is whether their relationship remains consistent.

🧠 Pattern Overview

This pattern is about checking whether elements from two sequences follow the same one-to-one relationship. The central question is: “Does every element on one side always map to the same element on the other side, and is the mapping one-to-one?”

Core idea: Establish a mapping → verify that every future occurrence respects it → make sure two different source elements do not map to the same target.

🧩 Mental Model

Imagine two sequences being compared position by position. Every element on the first side points to an element on the second side. Once that relationship is established, it cannot change.

↔️

Source → Target

A source element must always map to the same target element.

🔒

Consistency

Once a relationship is established, every future occurrence must obey it.

1️⃣

One-to-One

Two different source elements cannot map to the same target when the relationship must be bijective.

🔗 What Does One-to-One Mean?

Suppose we have:

A → X    B → Y    C → Z

This is valid because every source has a consistent and unique target.

But:

A → X    B → X

This is invalid if the relationship must be one-to-one because two different source elements are trying to use the same target.

Two rules must always hold:
1. Same source → same target.
2. Different source → different target.

🔎 When Should You Think of This Pattern?

  • The problem uses words such as isomorphic or same pattern.
  • You need to check whether two sequences have the same structure.
  • The problem describes a one-to-one mapping or bijection.
  • Each character or element must be replaced consistently.
  • You need to compare corresponding characters or elements.
  • Two strings or sequences should follow the same pattern of occurrence.

🚨 Recognition Clues

isomorphic
same pattern
same structure
one-to-one mapping
bijection
corresponding characters
consistent replacement
same occurrence pattern

⚙️ How the Mapping Works

Consider the two strings:

egg→add

Compare them position by position:

Position-wise Relationship
e → a
g → d
g → d

The first g maps to d. When g appears again, it must still map to d.

e → a    g → d
Invariant: Once a relationship is established, every future occurrence must respect that relationship.

💡 Two Ways to Enforce the Mapping

↔️

Two HashMaps

Store both source → target and target → source. This directly checks both directions.

🗺️

HashMap + HashSet

Store source → target in a HashMap and keep already-assigned target values in a HashSet.

Both approaches enforce the same invariant: every source has one consistent target, and every target is assigned to at most one source.

💡 Practical Problem: Isomorphic Strings

Question: Given two strings, determine whether they are isomorphic. Characters in one string must be replaceable to obtain the other string while preserving the one-to-one relationship.

Step 1 — Read the question carefully

We are not simply checking whether both strings contain the same characters. We need to know whether corresponding positions follow a consistent mapping.

Step 2 — Identify the information we need

We need to remember the relationship between corresponding characters and ensure that the same relationship is never contradicted.

State: either two maps for both directions, or one map plus a set of already-used target values.

Step 3 — Apply the pattern

Suppose the strings are paper and title.

  • p → t
  • a → i
  • p → t again, which is consistent.
  • e → l
  • r → e

The repeated p continues to map to t, so the relationship remains consistent.

Why this pattern fits

The problem is about a position-wise relationship, not frequency counting. Once a mapping is established, every future occurrence must obey it.

🧱 Pattern Template — Two HashMaps

This is the most explicit version because both directions of the relationship are stored.

Two HashMaps — Java
HashMap<Character, Character> sourceToTarget = new HashMap<>();
HashMap<Character, Character> targetToSource = new HashMap<>();

for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
    char source = s.charAt(i);
    char target = t.charAt(i);

    if (sourceToTarget.containsKey(source)
            && sourceToTarget.get(source) != target) {
        return false;
    }

    if (targetToSource.containsKey(target)
            && targetToSource.get(target) != source) {
        return false;
    }

    sourceToTarget.put(source, target);
    targetToSource.put(target, source);
}

return true;
Two HashMaps — C++
unordered_map<char, char> sourceToTarget;
unordered_map<char, char> targetToSource;

for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
    char source = s[i];
    char target = t[i];

    if (sourceToTarget.count(source)
            && sourceToTarget[source] != target) {
        return false;
    }

    if (targetToSource.count(target)
            && targetToSource[target] != source) {
        return false;
    }

    sourceToTarget[source] = target;
    targetToSource[target] = source;
}

return true;
Two HashMaps — Python
source_to_target = {}
target_to_source = {}

for source, target in zip(s, t):
    if source in source_to_target and source_to_target[source] != target:
        return False

    if target in target_to_source and target_to_source[target] != source:
        return False

    source_to_target[source] = target
    target_to_source[target] = source

return True

🧱 Pattern Template — HashMap + HashSet

This version stores the source-to-target mapping and separately tracks which target values have already been assigned.

HashMap + HashSet — Java
HashMap<Character, Character> sourceToTarget = new HashMap<>();
HashSet<Character> usedTargets = new HashSet<>();

for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
    char source = s.charAt(i);
    char target = t.charAt(i);

    if (sourceToTarget.containsKey(source)) {
        if (sourceToTarget.get(source) != target) {
            return false;
        }
    } else {
        if (usedTargets.contains(target)) {
            return false;
        }

        sourceToTarget.put(source, target);
        usedTargets.add(target);
    }
}

return true;
HashMap + HashSet — C++
unordered_map<char, char> sourceToTarget;
unordered_set<char> usedTargets;

for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
    char source = s[i];
    char target = t[i];

    if (sourceToTarget.count(source)) {
        if (sourceToTarget[source] != target) {
            return false;
        }
    } else {
        if (usedTargets.count(target)) {
            return false;
        }

        sourceToTarget[source] = target;
        usedTargets.insert(target);
    }
}

return true;
HashMap + HashSet — Python
source_to_target = {}
used_targets = set()

for source, target in zip(s, t):
    if source in source_to_target:
        if source_to_target[source] != target:
            return False
    else:
        if target in used_targets:
            return False

        source_to_target[source] = target
        used_targets.add(target)

return True

💻 Problem Solution

Now apply the mapping relationship pattern to the Isomorphic Strings problem using the two-HashMap approach.

Isomorphic Strings — Java
class Solution {
    public boolean isIsomorphic(String s, String t) {
        if (s.length() != t.length()) {
            return false;
        }

        HashMap<Character, Character> sourceToTarget = new HashMap<>();
        HashMap<Character, Character> targetToSource = new HashMap<>();

        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
            char source = s.charAt(i);
            char target = t.charAt(i);

            if (sourceToTarget.containsKey(source)
                    && sourceToTarget.get(source) != target) {
                return false;
            }

            if (targetToSource.containsKey(target)
                    && targetToSource.get(target) != source) {
                return false;
            }

            sourceToTarget.put(source, target);
            targetToSource.put(target, source);
        }

        return true;
    }
}
Isomorphic Strings — C++
class Solution {
public:
    bool isIsomorphic(string s, string t) {
        if (s.length() != t.length()) {
            return false;
        }

        unordered_map<char, char> sourceToTarget;
        unordered_map<char, char> targetToSource;

        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
            char source = s[i];
            char target = t[i];

            if (sourceToTarget.count(source)
                    && sourceToTarget[source] != target) {
                return false;
            }

            if (targetToSource.count(target)
                    && targetToSource[target] != source) {
                return false;
            }

            sourceToTarget[source] = target;
            targetToSource[target] = source;
        }

        return true;
    }
};
Isomorphic Strings — Python
class Solution:
    def isIsomorphic(self, s, t):
        if len(s) != len(t):
            return False

        source_to_target = {}
        target_to_source = {}

        for source, target in zip(s, t):
            if source in source_to_target and source_to_target[source] != target:
                return False

            if target in target_to_source and target_to_source[target] != source:
                return False

            source_to_target[source] = target
            target_to_source[target] = source

        return True
Pattern → Invariant → Decision:
Mapping Relationship → every source-target relationship stays consistent and one-to-one → accept only if both directions remain valid.

📚 How the Three Problems Build the Pattern

1️⃣

LC 205 — Isomorphic Strings

Learn the basic one-to-one character mapping invariant.

2️⃣

LC 290 — Word Pattern

Apply the same mapping idea between characters and words.

3️⃣

LC 890 — Find and Replace Pattern

Apply the same mapping test repeatedly to multiple strings.

Progression: Understand bijective mapping → apply it to different data types → reuse the same invariant across multiple candidates.

⚠️ Common Mistakes

1. Checking only source → target

Checking A → X is not enough for a bijection. You must also make sure another source does not map to X.

2. Confusing mapping with frequency counting

Frequency tells you how many times values occur. Mapping checks the position-wise relationship between two sequences.

3. Allowing a source to change its target

If A → X was established, a later A → Y violates the mapping immediately.

4. Using only a HashSet

A HashSet can tell you whether a target has already been used, but it cannot remember which target belongs to each source. You still need the mapping.

5. Forgetting length compatibility

For position-wise comparison, the two sequences must have compatible lengths before comparing corresponding elements.

📊 Complexity

TimeO(n)

We scan the two sequences once and perform constant-average-time HashMap or HashSet operations for each position.

Extra SpaceO(n)

In the general case, the maps and set can store relationships for up to n distinct elements.

🎯 Mental Trigger

“Do these two sequences follow the same one-to-one relationship?”

Think Mapping → Consistency → One-to-One → Two-Way Check.

HASH SET PATTERN

Set Membership & Seen-State Tracking

Use a HashSet to track values or states that have already been seen, then use fast membership checks to detect sequence starts, cycles, duplicates, or constraint violations.

🧠 Pattern Overview

The key idea is not simply “use a HashSet.” It is to put relevant values or states into a Set and use membership checking to avoid repeated traversal or repeated processing.

Core idea: Store relevant values or states → perform an expected O(1) membership check → decide whether the value should be processed, skipped, or rejected.

🧩 Mental Model

Imagine keeping a record of everything important that you have already encountered. Before processing something, ask: “Have I seen this before?”

👀

Seen State

The HashSet stores values or states that have already appeared.

🔎

Membership Check

contains() tells us whether the value or state has already been seen.

➕

Record Once

add() records a new value or state so future checks can detect it.

🔧 Fundamental Operations

The basic state is:

HashSet State — Java
HashSet<Integer> set = new HashSet<>();

set.add(x);
set.contains(x);

The type of the Set depends on what you need to track.

HashSet<Integer> → numbers
HashSet<Character> → characters
HashSet<String> → strings or states
Expected complexity: add() and contains() are O(1) on average.

🔎 When Should You Think of This Pattern?

  • The problem asks whether something has been seen before.
  • You need to detect duplicates.
  • You need to determine whether a value or state already exists.
  • You need to detect a cycle in a repeated state process.
  • You need to process each state only once.
  • You need to detect the start of a consecutive sequence.
  • You need to validate whether a value violates a uniqueness constraint.

🚨 Recognition Clues

already seen
visited
duplicate
consecutive sequence
cycle
check whether something exists
visit each state once
validate uniqueness

🧱 Type 1 — Starting-Point Detection

This is the important idea behind LC 128 — Longest Consecutive Sequence.

Suppose the Set contains:

1234100101

Instead of starting a sequence from every number, ask whether the previous number exists.

Finding a Sequence Start
if (!set.contains(x - 1)) {
    // x is a starting point
}

For 2, the previous number 1 exists, so 2 is not a starting point.

For 1, the previous number 0 does not exist, so 1 is the beginning of the sequence.

Recognition trick: Previous element exists? → YES: skip this value as a starting point. NO: start the sequence here.

This prevents repeatedly traversing the same consecutive sequence.

🔄 Type 2 — Visited-State Detection

This is the idea behind LC 202 — Happy Number.

A process repeatedly generates a new state:

current state → next state → next state → ...

The danger is that the process may eventually return to a state that has already appeared, creating a cycle.

Visited-State Pattern
HashSet<Integer> visited = new HashSet<>();

if (visited.contains(state)) {
    // state was seen before → cycle detected
}

visited.add(state);
Key insight: A HashSet turns “Have I reached this state before?” into an expected O(1) membership lookup.

🧩 Type 3 — Constraint Validation

This is the idea behind LC 36 — Valid Sudoku.

Here the HashSet is not being used to find a sequence or detect a cycle. Instead, it answers:

“Has this value already appeared in this constraint?”

There are three types of constraints:

↔️

Row

Each row must contain unique values.

↕️

Column

Each column must contain unique values.

▦

3 × 3 Box

Each box must contain unique values.

When processing a value, check whether it has already appeared in the relevant row, column, or box.

Check: Already present? → YES: invalid. NO: record it and continue.

💡 The Common Pattern Behind All Three

These problems look different:

LC 128 → consecutive sequence
LC 202 → cycle detection
LC 36 → constraint validation

But underneath, they use the same fundamental operation:

HashSet → Fast Membership Test → “Have I seen this?”
Same tool, different meaning:
Consecutive values → visited states → duplicate constraints.

💡 Practical Problem: Longest Consecutive Sequence

Question: Given an unsorted array of integers, find the length of the longest consecutive elements sequence.

Step 1 — Read the question carefully

The array is unsorted, so simply scanning adjacent elements cannot reliably find consecutive values. We need to know whether neighboring values exist.

Step 2 — Identify the information we need

For every value, we need to quickly answer whether x - 1 or x + 1 exists.

State: A HashSet containing all values from the array.

Step 3 — Find only sequence starts

If x - 1 exists, then x is inside an existing sequence and should not start another traversal.

If x - 1 does not exist, x is a sequence start. From there, keep checking x + 1, x + 2, and so on.

Why this pattern fits

The Set gives fast membership checks, while the starting-point condition prevents us from repeatedly scanning the same sequence.

🧱 Pattern Template — Membership Tracking

This is the reusable HashSet pattern for tracking values or states that have already been seen.

HashSet Membership — Java
HashSet<Integer> seen = new HashSet<>();

for (int value : arr) {
    if (seen.contains(value)) {
        // Already seen
    } else {
        seen.add(value);
    }
}
HashSet Membership — C++
unordered_set<int> seen;

for (int value : arr) {
    if (seen.count(value)) {
        // Already seen
    } else {
        seen.insert(value);
    }
}
HashSet Membership — Python
seen = set()

for value in arr:
    if value in seen:
        # Already seen
        pass
    else:
        seen.add(value)

🧱 Pattern Template — Starting-Point Detection

Use this form when the problem involves consecutive values and you want to avoid starting a traversal from the middle of a sequence.

Starting-Point Detection — Java
HashSet<Integer> set = new HashSet<>();

for (int value : nums) {
    set.add(value);
}

for (int value : nums) {
    if (!set.contains(value - 1)) {
        // value is a sequence start

        int current = value;

        while (set.contains(current)) {
            current++;
        }
    }
}
Starting-Point Detection — C++
unordered_set<int> set;

for (int value : nums) {
    set.insert(value);
}

for (int value : nums) {
    if (!set.count(value - 1)) {
        // value is a sequence start

        int current = value;

        while (set.count(current)) {
            current++;
        }
    }
}
Starting-Point Detection — Python
seen = set(nums)

for value in nums:
    if value - 1 not in seen:
        # value is a sequence start

        current = value

        while current in seen:
            current += 1

🧱 Pattern Template — Visited-State Detection

Use this form when repeatedly generated states may eventually repeat and form a cycle.

Visited-State Detection — Java
HashSet<Integer> visited = new HashSet<>();

while (true) {
    if (visited.contains(state)) {
        // Cycle detected
        break;
    }

    visited.add(state);
    state = getNextState(state);
}
Visited-State Detection — C++
unordered_set<int> visited;

while (true) {
    if (visited.count(state)) {
        // Cycle detected
        break;
    }

    visited.insert(state);
    state = getNextState(state);
}
Visited-State Detection — Python
visited = set()

while True:
    if state in visited:
        # Cycle detected
        break

    visited.add(state)
    state = get_next_state(state)

💻 Problem Solution

Now apply the starting-point version of the HashSet pattern to Longest Consecutive Sequence.

Longest Consecutive Sequence — Java
class Solution {
    public int longestConsecutive(int[] nums) {
        HashSet<Integer> set = new HashSet<>();

        for (int num : nums) {
            set.add(num);
        }

        int longest = 0;

        for (int num : set) {
            if (!set.contains(num - 1)) {
                int current = num;
                int length = 1;

                while (set.contains(current + 1)) {
                    current++;
                    length++;
                }

                longest = Math.max(longest, length);
            }
        }

        return longest;
    }
}
Longest Consecutive Sequence — C++
class Solution {
public:
    int longestConsecutive(vector<int>& nums) {
        unordered_set<int> set;

        for (int num : nums) {
            set.insert(num);
        }

        int longest = 0;

        for (int num : set) {
            if (!set.count(num - 1)) {
                int current = num;
                int length = 1;

                while (set.count(current + 1)) {
                    current++;
                    length++;
                }

                longest = max(longest, length);
            }
        }

        return longest;
    }
};
Longest Consecutive Sequence — Python
class Solution:
    def longestConsecutive(self, nums):
        seen = set(nums)
        longest = 0

        for num in seen:
            if num - 1 not in seen:
                current = num
                length = 1

                while current + 1 in seen:
                    current += 1
                    length += 1

                longest = max(longest, length)

        return longest
Pattern → Invariant → Decision:
HashSet → fast membership check → identify the correct starting point and traverse each consecutive sequence only once.

📚 How the Three Problems Build the Pattern

1️⃣

LC 128 — Longest Consecutive Sequence

Use membership checking to identify sequence starts and avoid repeated traversal.

2️⃣

LC 202 — Happy Number

Use a Set to remember visited states and detect when a process enters a cycle.

3️⃣

LC 36 — Valid Sudoku

Use Sets to enforce uniqueness constraints across rows, columns, and boxes.

Progression: Membership for values → membership for generated states → membership for structured constraints.

⚠️ Common Mistakes

1. Thinking “HashSet” is the pattern

The real pattern is fast membership testing. First identify what value or state needs to be remembered and why.

2. Starting a sequence from every value

For consecutive-sequence problems, check whether the previous value exists. Only sequence starts should begin a traversal.

3. Forgetting to record a visited state

In cycle-detection problems, check membership and then add the new state before generating the next state.

4. Using one global Set for separate constraints

Problems such as Sudoku require membership to be tracked separately for different rows, columns, and boxes.

5. Using a HashMap when only membership matters

If you only need to know whether something exists, a HashSet is usually the simpler state representation.

📊 Complexity

TimeO(n) average

HashSet membership and insertion are O(1) on average. In the starting-point approach, each consecutive value is processed only as part of its sequence traversal.

Extra SpaceO(n)

The HashSet may store up to n distinct values or states.

🎯 Mental Trigger

“Do I repeatedly need to ask: Have I seen this value or state before?”

Think HashSet → Membership Check → Process Once / Detect / Reject.

TWO POINTERS PATTERN

Opposite Direction Two Pointers

Use two pointers starting from opposite ends of an array and move them toward each other based on the relationship between the current pair of elements. The key idea is not simply using two pointers—it is using the sorted or ordered property of the data to determine which pointer can safely move.

🧠 Pattern Overview

TP1 maintains a left pointer at the beginning and a right pointer at the end. At every step, evaluate the relationship between the two endpoints and move the pointer that can safely eliminate impossible candidates.

left →[ ... ... ... ... ... ... ]← right
Core idea: Use the sorted/order property of the data to determine which pointer can safely move.

🧩 When to Think of This Pattern

Sorted arrayOrdering makes pointer movement predictable.
Pair conditionYou need a pair satisfying some relationship.
Target sumCompare the current pair's sum with a target.
Maximize / minimizeEndpoint movement can eliminate impossible candidates.
3Sum or combinationsFix one element, then apply two pointers.
Many pair checksOpposite pointers may reduce the search significantly.
Strongest recognition signal: Sorted array + pair relationship + need to find or optimize something → consider opposite-direction two pointers.

📌 State to Maintain

L

Left

Starts at the first element.

left = 0
R

Right

Starts at the last element.

right = nums.length - 1
↔

Relationship

Evaluate the current pair to decide which pointer moves.

nums[left] ↔ nums[right]

🎯 Target-Sum Decision Rule

sum < target→left++
sum > target→right--
sum == target→found

Because the array is sorted, moving left to the right increases the left value, while moving right to the left decreases the right value.

  • Need a larger sum → move left.
  • Need a smaller sum → move right.
  • Required relationship found → process the result.

💡 Why Pointer Movement Works

Do not memorize the condition. Understand why the movement is safe.

[ 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 ]L = 1R = 9

Suppose 1 + 9 = 10 and the target is 12. We need a larger sum. Moving right would replace 9 with 7 and make the sum smaller, so it cannot help. Therefore, move left.

[ 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 ]L = 3R = 93 + 9 = 12
The real pattern: Pointer movement should eliminate a region of impossible candidates.

🧱 Template — Opposite Direction

Generic TP1 Template
int left = 0;
int right = nums.length - 1;

while (left < right) {
    // Evaluate nums[left] and nums[right]

    if (/* need a larger value */) {
        left++;
    } else if (/* need a smaller value */) {
        right--;
    } else {
        // Required relationship found
        break;
    }
}
int left = 0;
int right = nums.size() - 1;

while (left < right) {
    // Evaluate nums[left] and nums[right]

    if (/* need a larger value */) {
        left++;
    } else if (/* need a smaller value */) {
        right--;
    } else {
        // Required relationship found
        break;
    }
}
left = 0
right = len(nums) - 1

while left < right:
    # Evaluate nums[left] and nums[right]

    if ...:  # need a larger value
        left += 1
    elif ...:  # need a smaller value
        right -= 1
    else:
        # Required relationship found
        break

🧱 Template — Target Sum

Sorted Array + Target Sum
int left = 0;
int right = nums.length - 1;

while (left < right) {
    int sum = nums[left] + nums[right];

    if (sum < target) {
        left++;
    } else if (sum > target) {
        right--;
    } else {
        // Found the pair
        break;
    }
}
int left = 0;
int right = nums.size() - 1;

while (left < right) {
    int sum = nums[left] + nums[right];

    if (sum < target) {
        left++;
    } else if (sum > target) {
        right--;
    } else {
        // Found the pair
        break;
    }
}
left = 0
right = len(nums) - 1

while left < right:
    current_sum = nums[left] + nums[right]

    if current_sum < target:
        left += 1
    elif current_sum > target:
        right -= 1
    else:
        # Found the pair
        break

🧪 Practical Example — LC 167: Two Sum II

Question: Given a sorted array of integers and a target, find the two numbers whose sum equals the target.

How to read it: The array is sorted, the problem asks for a pair, and the pair is defined by a sum. These are strong TP1 signals.

Pattern reasoning: Start with the smallest and largest values. If the sum is too small, increase the left value. If the sum is too large, decrease the right value. Each movement removes candidates that cannot produce the target.
LC 167 Solution
public int[] twoSum(int[] numbers, int target) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = numbers.length - 1;

    while (left < right) {
        int sum = numbers[left] + numbers[right];

        if (sum < target) {
            left++;
        } else if (sum > target) {
            right--;
        } else {
            return new int[]{left + 1, right + 1};
        }
    }

    return new int[]{-1, -1};
}
vector<int> twoSum(vector<int>& numbers, int target) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = numbers.size() - 1;

    while (left < right) {
        int sum = numbers[left] + numbers[right];

        if (sum < target) {
            left++;
        } else if (sum > target) {
            right--;
        } else {
            return {left + 1, right + 1};
        }
    }

    return {-1, -1};
}
def twoSum(self, numbers, target):
    left = 0
    right = len(numbers) - 1

    while left < right:
        current_sum = numbers[left] + numbers[right]

        if current_sum < target:
            left += 1
        elif current_sum > target:
            right -= 1
        else:
            return [left + 1, right + 1]

    return [-1, -1]

🔄 How the Pattern Extends

167

Two Sum II

Compare the endpoint sum with the target and move the appropriate pointer.

11

Container With Most Water

Use the endpoint heights and width to decide which side can potentially improve the result.

15

3Sum

Fix one element, then apply opposite-direction two pointers to the remaining range.

⚠️ Common Mistakes

  • Using two pointers without understanding why each movement is safe.
  • Moving the wrong pointer because the sorted-order relationship was ignored.
  • Thinking TP1 is only a target-sum technique.
  • Forgetting that 3Sum first fixes one element before applying two pointers.
  • Applying the pattern when the required ordering property is not available.

⏱️ Complexity

Two-Pointer Scan

O(n) because each pointer moves only toward the other and does not move backward.

Auxiliary Space

O(1) for the basic opposite-direction scan.

Remember: If sorting is required first, include the sorting cost separately. The two-pointer scan itself is linear.

🎯 Mental Trigger

“Sorted/order matters + pair or endpoint relationship + I can safely eliminate candidates → opposite-direction two pointers.”

TWO POINTERS PATTERN

Same Direction — Read / Write Pointers

TP2 uses two pointers moving in the same direction. One pointer reads the input, while the other writes or places the next valid element. This is the same core idea as the Read / Write Pointer pattern from A4: In-place Array Manipulation, included here as a short reinforcement topic within Two Pointers.

🧠 Pattern Overview

The two pointers move in the same direction, but they have different jobs.

Read →[ ... ... ... ... ... ... ]Write →
Core idea: The read pointer explores the array. The write pointer records where the next useful element should go.

🔍 When to Think of This Pattern

In-place modificationModify the array without creating another full array.
Filter elementsKeep valid elements and move them toward the front.
Remove duplicatesRead every value while writing only the values you want to keep.
Move valid elementsSeparate useful elements from elements that should be ignored.
Compact the arrayWrite selected elements into the earliest available positions.
Extra array not neededThe write pointer lets you reuse the existing array.
Recognition signal: “Read through the array + keep/process selected elements + modify in place” → think Read / Write Two Pointers.

📌 State to Maintain

R

Read Pointer

Scans every element and decides whether it should be kept or processed.

read = 0
W

Write Pointer

Marks where the next valid element should be written.

write = 0
↔

Relationship

Read moves through the input; write moves only when an element is accepted.

write ≤ read

💡 How It Works

Think of the array as having two regions:

[ processed / written ]|[ not processed yet ]

The read pointer explores the unprocessed region. When the current element is valid, write it at the write position and advance write.

Important: Read and write move in the same direction, but they do not necessarily move together. The write pointer advances only when something should be kept or written.

🧱 Template — Read / Write

Generic TP2 Template
int write = 0;

for (int read = 0; read < nums.length; read++) {
    if (/* keep nums[read] */) {
        nums[write] = nums[read];
        write++;
    }
}

return write;
int write = 0;

for (int read = 0; read < nums.size(); read++) {
    if (/* keep nums[read] */) {
        nums[write] = nums[read];
        write++;
    }
}

return write;
write = 0

for read in range(len(nums)):
    if ...:  # keep nums[read]
        nums[write] = nums[read]
        write += 1

return write

🧪 Mini Example — Remove Unwanted Elements

Question: Read through an array and keep only the elements that satisfy a condition, modifying the array in place.

How to read it: We do not need to move every element immediately. The read pointer finds the next useful element, while write places it at the next available position.

Input: [ 2, 5, 3, 8, 1 ]Keep values > 3Output prefix: [ 5, 8, ... ]
Pattern reasoning: Read everything once. When an element is valid, write it at the current write position and advance write. The prefix [0 ... write-1] contains the processed result.

⚠️ Common Mistakes

  • Moving the write pointer for every read, even when the current element should be skipped.
  • Confusing the read pointer with the position where the answer should be written.
  • Creating another array when the problem specifically asks for in-place modification.
  • Forgetting that the useful result is often only the prefix before the write pointer.

⏱️ Complexity

Time

O(n) because the read pointer scans the array once.

Auxiliary Space

O(1) because the transformation happens inside the existing array.

🎯 Mental Trigger

“Read everything → keep what matters → write it forward in place.”

TP2 is essentially the Read / Write Pointer pattern from A4, reinforced here as a Two Pointers technique.

TWO POINTERS PATTERN

Merge Two Sequences

Process two sequences together using two pointers. Compare the current element from each sequence, decide which pointer can safely move, and continue until one sequence is exhausted.

🧠 Pattern Overview

TP3 is used when two sequences need to be processed together, usually by comparing their current elements. The most important requirement is that the sequences have an order that makes pointer movement safe.

A → [ 1, 3, 5, 7 ]B → [ 2, 3, 6, 8 ]
Core idea: Two sequences → compare their current elements → move the pointer belonging to the smaller or inappropriate element.

🔍 When to Think of This Pattern

Merge sorted arraysProcess two ordered sequences without repeatedly searching.
IntersectionFind elements that appear in both sorted sequences.
Common elementsCompare both sequences while advancing only the pointer that can no longer match.
Compare sequencesProcess two strings or ordered sequences together.
Ordered eventsWalk through two ordered streams and process the next event.
O(n + m) processingEach pointer moves forward instead of repeatedly searching the other sequence.
Recognition signal: “Two ordered sequences + compare their current elements + process them together” → think Merge Two Sequences.

📌 State to Maintain

A

Pointer i

Tracks the current element in the first sequence.

i = 0
B

Pointer j

Tracks the current element in the second sequence.

j = 0
↔

Comparison

Compare the two current elements to decide which pointer moves.

A[i] ↔ B[j]

⚖️ The Three Cases

A[i] < B[j]→move i
A[i] > B[j]→move j
A[i] == B[j]→usually move both

The exact action after equality depends on the problem, but for common sorted-array intersection or merge problems, both pointers usually advance.

💡 Why Can We Safely Move a Pointer?

Suppose:

A[i] = 3B[j] = 5

If both sequences are sorted, every element after B[j] is ≥ 5. Therefore, the current A[i] = 3 cannot match any later element of B. Keeping it would not help.

Reasoning: Because the sequences are ordered, a smaller current element can safely be discarded or processed before moving its pointer forward.

🧱 Template — Merge Two Sequences

Generic TP3 Template
int i = 0;
int j = 0;

while (i < A.length && j < B.length) {
    if (A[i] < B[j]) {
        // Process A[i]
        i++;
    } else if (A[i] > B[j]) {
        // Process B[j]
        j++;
    } else {
        // Process equal elements
        i++;
        j++;
    }
}
int i = 0;
int j = 0;

while (i < A.size() && j < B.size()) {
    if (A[i] < B[j]) {
        // Process A[i]
        i++;
    } else if (A[i] > B[j]) {
        // Process B[j]
        j++;
    } else {
        // Process equal elements
        i++;
        j++;
    }
}
i = 0
j = 0

while i < len(A) and j < len(B):
    if A[i] < B[j]:
        # Process A[i]
        i += 1
    elif A[i] > B[j]:
        # Process B[j]
        j += 1
    else:
        # Process equal elements
        i += 1
        j += 1

🧪 Practical Example — Intersection of Two Sorted Arrays

Question: Given two sorted arrays, find their common elements.

How to read it: We have two ordered sequences and need to find values that appear in both. Instead of searching for every element of one array inside the other, compare the two current elements.

A = [ 1, 2, 3, 4, 7 ]B = [ 2, 3, 5, 7 ]
Walk through: 1 vs 2 → move i. 2 vs 2 → common, record 2 and move both. 3 vs 3 → record 3 and move both. 4 vs 5 → move i. 7 vs 5 → move j. 7 vs 7 → record 7 and move both.

Result: [2, 3, 7]

Intersection Solution
public List<Integer> intersection(int[] A, int[] B) {
    List<Integer> result = new ArrayList<>();
    int i = 0;
    int j = 0;

    while (i < A.length && j < B.length) {
        if (A[i] < B[j]) {
            i++;
        } else if (A[i] > B[j]) {
            j++;
        } else {
            result.add(A[i]);
            i++;
            j++;
        }
    }

    return result;
}
vector<int> intersection(vector<int>& A, vector<int>& B) {
    vector<int> result;
    int i = 0;
    int j = 0;

    while (i < A.size() && j < B.size()) {
        if (A[i] < B[j]) {
            i++;
        } else if (A[i] > B[j]) {
            j++;
        } else {
            result.push_back(A[i]);
            i++;
            j++;
        }
    }

    return result;
}
def intersection(A, B):
    result = []
    i = 0
    j = 0

    while i < len(A) and j < len(B):
        if A[i] < B[j]:
            i += 1
        elif A[i] > B[j]:
            j += 1
        else:
            result.append(A[i])
            i += 1
            j += 1

    return result

🔄 Where This Pattern Appears

↔

Merge

Compare the front elements and take the smaller one.

∩

Intersection

Record equal elements and advance both pointers.

⇄

Sequence Comparison

Compare two ordered sequences while advancing the pointer that can no longer help.

⚠️ Common Mistakes

  • Moving both pointers when one current element is smaller than the other.
  • Moving the larger element's pointer instead of the smaller one.
  • Ignoring the fact that the ordering property is what makes the movement safe.
  • Continuing after one sequence is exhausted when no comparison is possible.
  • Assuming equality always means the same action for every problem—the required action depends on the problem.

⏱️ Complexity

Time

O(n + m) because pointer i moves through A at most once and pointer j moves through B at most once.

Space

O(1) auxiliary space for the pointer traversal itself. Output storage, if required, is separate.

🎯 Mental Trigger

“Two ordered sequences → compare current elements → safely advance one pointer → finish in O(n + m).”

learning.html:
TWO POINTERS PATTERN

Cycle Detection — Fast & Slow Pointers

Use two pointers moving at different speeds to detect whether a sequence eventually enters a cycle. The slow pointer moves one step at a time, while the fast pointer moves two steps.

🧠 Pattern Overview

The core idea is to let slow move 1 step and fast move 2 steps. If the sequence contains a cycle, fast continuously gains one position on slow and eventually catches it.

slow → 1 stepfast → 2 stepscycle → eventually meet
Core idea: If two pointers move at different speeds inside a cycle, the faster pointer must eventually catch the slower pointer.

🔍 When to Think of This Pattern

Detect a cycleDetermine whether a sequence contains a loop.
Find cycle startLocate the node or state where the cycle begins.
Repeated transformationsA state repeatedly leads to another state.
Linked structureEach node or state points to another node or state.
O(1) extra spaceCycle detection is required without storing visited states.
Constrained duplicate problemAn array can sometimes be interpreted as a linked structure.
Strongest recognition signal: A sequence repeatedly points to another state + possible cycle/repetition + O(1) extra space → consider Fast & Slow Pointers.

📌 State to Maintain

S

Slow

Moves one step at a time.

slow = slow.next
F

Fast

Moves two steps at a time.

fast = fast.next.next
↻

Invariant

Inside a cycle, fast gains one position on slow every iteration.

fast → +2, slow → +1

🔄 Type 1 — Detect Whether a Cycle Exists

Start both pointers at the beginning. Continue while fast can safely move two steps. If slow == fast, a cycle exists.

Reasoning: Without a cycle, fast eventually reaches the end. Inside a cycle, fast keeps moving around the loop and eventually catches slow.
Cycle Detection Template
public boolean hasCycle(ListNode head) {
    ListNode slow = head;
    ListNode fast = head;

    while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
        slow = slow.next;
        fast = fast.next.next;

        if (slow == fast) {
            return true;
        }
    }

    return false;
}
bool hasCycle(ListNode* head) {
    ListNode* slow = head;
    ListNode* fast = head;

    while (fast != nullptr && fast->next != nullptr) {
        slow = slow->next;
        fast = fast->next->next;

        if (slow == fast) {
            return true;
        }
    }

    return false;
}
def hasCycle(self, head):
    slow = head
    fast = head

    while fast is not None and fast.next is not None:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next

        if slow is fast:
            return True

    return False

🎯 Type 2 — Find the Beginning of the Cycle

This is the important Floyd's Cycle Detection Algorithm variant. It has two phases.

1

Find Meeting Point

Move slow by 1 and fast by 2 until they meet.

2

Reset One Pointer

Move slow back to the head.

→

Find Entrance

Move both one step at a time. Their meeting point is the cycle start.

Important: The first meeting point is not necessarily the beginning of the cycle.
Find Cycle Entrance
public ListNode detectCycle(ListNode head) {
    ListNode slow = head;
    ListNode fast = head;

    // Phase 1: Detect cycle
    while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
        slow = slow.next;
        fast = fast.next.next;

        if (slow == fast) {
            // Phase 2: Find cycle start
            slow = head;

            while (slow != fast) {
                slow = slow.next;
                fast = fast.next;
            }

            return slow;
        }
    }

    return null;
}
ListNode* detectCycle(ListNode* head) {
    ListNode* slow = head;
    ListNode* fast = head;

    // Phase 1: Detect cycle
    while (fast != nullptr && fast->next != nullptr) {
        slow = slow->next;
        fast = fast->next->next;

        if (slow == fast) {
            // Phase 2: Find cycle start
            slow = head;

            while (slow != fast) {
                slow = slow->next;
                fast = fast->next;
            }

            return slow;
        }
    }

    return nullptr;
}
def detectCycle(self, head):
    slow = head
    fast = head

    # Phase 1: Detect cycle
    while fast is not None and fast.next is not None:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next

        if slow is fast:
            # Phase 2: Find cycle start
            slow = head

            while slow is not fast:
                slow = slow.next
                fast = fast.next

            return slow

    return None

💡 Why Does Resetting Work?

Do not memorize “reset slow to head because it works.” The movement is based on the distance relationship created when fast travels twice as quickly.

2 × slow distance=fast distance

If a is the distance from the head to the cycle entrance, b is the distance from the entrance to the meeting point, and L is the cycle length, the meeting relationship implies that the remaining distance from the meeting point back to the entrance matches the distance from the head to the entrance modulo the cycle length.

Practical understanding: After the first meeting, reset one pointer to the head and move both one step at a time. They meet exactly at the cycle entrance.

🧪 Important Variant — LC 287: Find the Duplicate Number

Question: Given the constrained array from LC 287, find the duplicate number using constant extra space.

How to read it: Interpret the array as a linked structure where index → nums[index]. The duplicate creates a cycle, so the same Floyd two-phase technique can be applied.

0 → 1 → 3 → 2 → 4↑ ↓└─────────┘
LC 287 Solution
public int findDuplicate(int[] nums) {
    int slow = nums[0];
    int fast = nums[0];

    // Phase 1: Find meeting point
    do {
        slow = nums[slow];
        fast = nums[nums[fast]];
    } while (slow != fast);

    // Phase 2: Find cycle entrance
    slow = nums[0];

    while (slow != fast) {
        slow = nums[slow];
        fast = nums[fast];
    }

    return slow;
}
int findDuplicate(vector<int>& nums) {
    int slow = nums[0];
    int fast = nums[0];

    // Phase 1: Find meeting point
    do {
        slow = nums[slow];
        fast = nums[nums[fast]];
    } while (slow != fast);

    // Phase 2: Find cycle entrance
    slow = nums[0];

    while (slow != fast) {
        slow = nums[slow];
        fast = nums[fast];
    }

    return slow;
}
def findDuplicate(self, nums):
    slow = nums[0]
    fast = nums[0]

    # Phase 1: Find meeting point
    while True:
        slow = nums[slow]
        fast = nums[nums[fast]]

        if slow == fast:
            break

    # Phase 2: Find cycle entrance
    slow = nums[0]

    while slow != fast:
        slow = nums[slow]
        fast = nums[fast]

    return slow
Key insight: The duplicate value is the cycle entrance in the array-as-linked-list interpretation.

⚠️ Common Mistakes

  • Thinking the first slow/fast meeting point is always the cycle entrance.
  • Forgetting to check fast != null and fast.next != null before moving fast two steps.
  • Resetting a pointer without understanding the distance relationship.
  • Using a HashSet automatically when the problem is specifically testing O(1) extra-space cycle detection.
  • Applying the pattern without first establishing that the sequence behaves like a chain of states.

⏱️ Complexity

Time

O(n) because the pointers traverse the sequence a bounded number of times.

Auxiliary Space

O(1) because only a constant number of pointers are maintained.

🎯 Mental Trigger

“Sequence of states + possible repetition/cycle + O(1) space → slow = 1 step, fast = 2 steps.”

If they meet → cycle exists. If the cycle entrance is required → reset one pointer to the start and move both one step at a time.

SLIDING WINDOW PATTERN

Fixed-Size Sliding Window

Maintain a window of exactly k consecutive elements and slide it one position at a time by adding the new element and removing the old one. The key idea is to reuse the previous window's information instead of recalculating every window from scratch.

🧠 Pattern Overview

Suppose nums = [2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2] and k = 3. Each window contains exactly three consecutive elements.

[ 2, 1, 5 ] → 8[ 1, 5, 1 ] → 7[ 5, 1, 3 ] → 9[ 1, 3, 2 ] → 6
Core idea: When the window moves one position, remove the outgoing element and add the incoming element instead of recalculating all k elements.

🔍 When to Think of This Pattern

Subarray of size kFind something among every contiguous subarray of exactly size k.
Substring of length kProcess every consecutive substring with a fixed length.
Maximum / minimum sumCompare the sum of every fixed-size window.
Average of every kMaintain the current window sum efficiently.
Count in every windowUpdate a count when elements enter and leave.
Maximum elementFixed window plus a suitable structure such as a monotonic deque.
Strongest recognition signal: “Find something among every contiguous subarray or substring of exactly size k.”

📌 State to Maintain

L

Left

Beginning of the current window.

left
R

Right

End or incoming position of the current window.

right
Σ

Window State

Depends on the problem: sum, count, frequency, or another structure.

windowState

For a sum problem, maintain windowSum. For counting, maintain a count. For frequency-based problems, use a frequency map or array. For window maximum/minimum, a deque is commonly used.

🔄 Fundamental Movement

Suppose the current window is:

OLD: [ 2, 1, 5 ]→NEW: [ 1, 5, 1 ]

Only two elements changed their role: 2 leaves the window and 1 enters the window.

newState=oldState − outgoing + incoming
For a sum: windowSum -= outgoing and windowSum += incoming. This is the heart of fixed-size sliding window.

🧱 Template — Build First Window, Then Slide

Recommended SW1 Template
int windowSum = 0;

// Build first window
for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) {
    windowSum += nums[i];
}

int answer = windowSum;

// Slide the window
for (int i = k; i < nums.length; i++) {
    windowSum += nums[i];       // incoming
    windowSum -= nums[i - k];   // outgoing

    answer = Math.max(answer, windowSum);
}
int windowSum = 0;

// Build first window
for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) {
    windowSum += nums[i];
}

int answer = windowSum;

// Slide the window
for (int i = k; i < nums.size(); i++) {
    windowSum += nums[i];       // incoming
    windowSum -= nums[i - k];   // outgoing

    answer = max(answer, windowSum);
}
window_sum = 0

# Build first window
for i in range(k):
    window_sum += nums[i]

answer = window_sum

# Slide the window
for i in range(k, len(nums)):
    window_sum += nums[i]       # incoming
    window_sum -= nums[i - k]   # outgoing

    answer = max(answer, window_sum)

🧱 Template — Generic Left / Right

Useful General Form
int left = 0;

for (int right = 0; right < nums.length; right++) {
    // Add nums[right] to the window state

    if (right - left + 1 == k) {
        // Process current window

        // Remove nums[left] from the state
        left++;
    }
}
int left = 0;

for (int right = 0; right < nums.size(); right++) {
    // Add nums[right] to the window state

    if (right - left + 1 == k) {
        // Process current window

        // Remove nums[left] from the state
        left++;
    }
}
left = 0

for right in range(len(nums)):
    # Add nums[right] to the window state

    if right - left + 1 == k:
        # Process current window

        # Remove nums[left] from the state
        left += 1
For SW1: learn Template A first. Template B becomes more useful when you study variable-size sliding windows.

🧪 Practical Example — Maximum Sum of Size K

Question: Given nums = [2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2] and k = 3, find the maximum sum of any contiguous subarray of size 3.

How to read it: The window size is fixed at exactly k = 3. Therefore, instead of calculating every three-element sum from scratch, maintain the current window sum and slide it.

[ 2, 1, 5 ] = 88 − 2 + 1 = 77 − 1 + 3 = 99 − 5 + 2 = 6
Answer: The maximum window sum is 9, from the window [5, 1, 3].
Maximum Sum of Size K — Solution
public int maxSum(int[] nums, int k) {
    int windowSum = 0;

    for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) {
        windowSum += nums[i];
    }

    int answer = windowSum;

    for (int i = k; i < nums.length; i++) {
        windowSum += nums[i];
        windowSum -= nums[i - k];

        answer = Math.max(answer, windowSum);
    }

    return answer;
}
int maxSum(vector<int>& nums, int k) {
    int windowSum = 0;

    for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) {
        windowSum += nums[i];
    }

    int answer = windowSum;

    for (int i = k; i < nums.size(); i++) {
        windowSum += nums[i];
        windowSum -= nums[i - k];

        answer = max(answer, windowSum);
    }

    return answer;
}
def max_sum(nums, k):
    window_sum = sum(nums[:k])
    answer = window_sum

    for i in range(k, len(nums)):
        window_sum += nums[i]
        window_sum -= nums[i - k]

        answer = max(answer, window_sum)

    return answer

📈 Why Is This Better Than Brute Force?

Brute force calculates all k elements for every window. There are n - k + 1 windows, so the total work is approximately O(nk).

With sliding window, every element enters the window once and leaves once. The current state is updated in constant time.

Brute Force

O((n-k+1) × k) ≈ O(nk)

Sliding Window

O(n) because each element is added and removed at most once.

🔄 Common Variations

Σ

Sum

Add incoming and subtract outgoing.

sum += in; sum -= out;
#

Count

Update the count as elements enter and leave.

count += in; count -= out;
ƒ

Frequency

Update a frequency map or frequency array.

freq[in]++; freq[out]--;
Maximum / Minimum: Maintaining only a sum or count is not enough for problems such as maximum element in every window. That extension commonly uses a monotonic deque.

⚠️ Important Distinction

K

Fixed Size

Window always contains exactly k elements.

[xxx] [xxx] [xxx]
↔

Variable Size

Window size changes according to a condition.

[xx] [xxx] [xxxx]
?

Recognition

Fixed k → SW1. Longest or smallest satisfying a condition → usually variable window.

size changes

⚠️ Common Mistakes

  • Recalculating all k elements for every window.
  • Forgetting to remove the outgoing element when the window slides.
  • Adding the incoming element but forgetting to update the answer.
  • Confusing fixed-size sliding window with variable-size sliding window.
  • Using a complicated data structure when the window state only requires a sum or count.

⏱️ Complexity

Time

O(n) because every element enters and leaves the window at most once.

Auxiliary Space

O(1) for the basic sum/count fixed-window pattern.

🎯 Mental Trigger

“Window size is exactly k → build the first window → remove outgoing → add incoming → process.”

Think: OLD [A B C] → NEW [B C D] → remove A + add D.

learning.html:
SLIDING WINDOW PATTERN

Variable-Size Sliding Window

Maintain a contiguous window whose size changes according to a condition. Unlike a fixed-size sliding window, there is no fixed k controlling the window.

🧠 Pattern Overview

The right pointer expands the window, while the left pointer shrinks it when the current window no longer satisfies the required condition—or when a valid window can be made smaller.

right → expands[ ... current window ... ]left → shrinks
Core idea: SW2 is controlled by a condition, not by a fixed window size.

🔍 When to Think of This Pattern

Longest subarrayFind the longest contiguous window satisfying a condition.
Shortest subarrayFind the smallest contiguous window satisfying a condition.
Longest substringWindow size changes while maintaining a validity rule.
At most K distinctA frequency structure controls whether the window is valid.
Condition-controlled sizeThe window grows or shrinks depending on its current state.
Not fixed at kIf the required window size changes, consider variable-size sliding window.
Key recognition question: Is the window size controlled by a condition rather than a fixed k?

📌 State to Maintain

L

Left

Beginning of the current window. Moves forward when the window needs to shrink.

left
R

Right

Expands the window by adding the next element.

right
Σ

Window State

Depends on the condition: sum, frequency, count, or another structure.

windowState

Common state choices include sum, HashMap / frequency array, HashSet, and count.

📈 Type A — Longest Valid Window

Goal: Find the longest window that satisfies a condition.

Expand→Invalid?→Shrink until valid→Record maximum
Rule: Add the new element, shrink while invalid, then update the maximum length.
Longest Valid Window Template
int left = 0;
int answer = 0;

for (int right = 0; right < n; right++) {
    // Add nums[right] to state

    while (/* window is invalid */) {
        // Remove nums[left] from state
        left++;
    }

    answer = Math.max(answer, right - left + 1);
}
int left = 0;
int answer = 0;

for (int right = 0; right < n; right++) {
    // Add nums[right] to state

    while (/* window is invalid */) {
        // Remove nums[left] from state
        left++;
    }

    answer = max(answer, right - left + 1);
}
left = 0
answer = 0

for right in range(n):
    # Add nums[right] to state

    while ...:  # window is invalid
        # Remove nums[left] from state
        left += 1

    answer = max(answer, right - left + 1)

📉 Type B — Shortest Valid Window

Goal: Find the shortest window that satisfies a condition.

Expand→Valid?→Record minimum→Shrink while valid
Rule: Add the new element, then shrink while valid, recording the answer before each removal.
Shortest Valid Window Template
int left = 0;
int answer = Integer.MAX_VALUE;

for (int right = 0; right < n; right++) {
    // Add nums[right] to state

    while (/* window is valid */) {
        answer = Math.min(answer, right - left + 1);

        // Remove nums[left] from state
        left++;
    }
}
int left = 0;
int answer = INT_MAX;

for (int right = 0; right < n; right++) {
    // Add nums[right] to state

    while (/* window is valid */) {
        answer = min(answer, right - left + 1);

        // Remove nums[left] from state
        left++;
    }
}
left = 0
answer = float('inf')

for right in range(n):
    # Add nums[right] to state

    while ...:  # window is valid
        answer = min(answer, right - left + 1)

        # Remove nums[left] from state
        left += 1

⭐ The Most Important Rule — Use While

Longest→while invalid → shrink → record max
Shortest→while valid → record min → shrink

Do not automatically replace the while with if. The window may need to shrink by multiple elements before reaching the required state.

Think: The left pointer keeps moving until the window reaches the correct state.

🧪 Practical Example — Minimum Size Subarray Sum

Question: Given target = 7 and nums = [2,3,1,2,4,3], find the minimum length of a contiguous subarray whose sum is at least 7.

How to read it: There is no fixed k. We want the shortest window satisfying sum >= target, so this is a shortest-valid-window problem.

[ 2, 3, 1, 2 ]sum = 8 ✓→ remove 2[ 3, 1, 2 ]sum = 6 ✗
Reasoning: Once the window becomes valid, record its length and keep shrinking. Stop shrinking when the condition becomes invalid. The minimum valid length is 2, from [4,3].
Minimum Size Subarray Sum — Solution
public int minSubArrayLen(int target, int[] nums) {
    int left = 0;
    int windowSum = 0;
    int answer = Integer.MAX_VALUE;

    for (int right = 0; right < nums.length; right++) {
        windowSum += nums[right];

        while (windowSum >= target) {
            answer = Math.min(answer, right - left + 1);
            windowSum -= nums[left];
            left++;
        }
    }

    return answer == Integer.MAX_VALUE ? 0 : answer;
}
int minSubArrayLen(int target, vector<int>& nums) {
    int left = 0;
    int windowSum = 0;
    int answer = INT_MAX;

    for (int right = 0; right < nums.size(); right++) {
        windowSum += nums[right];

        while (windowSum >= target) {
            answer = min(answer, right - left + 1);
            windowSum -= nums[left];
            left++;
        }
    }

    return answer == INT_MAX ? 0 : answer;
}
def minSubArrayLen(self, target, nums):
    left = 0
    window_sum = 0
    answer = float('inf')

    for right in range(len(nums)):
        window_sum += nums[right]

        while window_sum >= target:
            answer = min(answer, right - left + 1)
            window_sum -= nums[left]
            left += 1

    return 0 if answer == float('inf') else answer

🔄 The Window Movement

→

Expand

Move right forward and add the incoming element.

←

Shrink

Move left forward and remove the outgoing element.

↕

Control

The current condition determines when shrinking should happen.

⚠️ Important Limitation

For sum-based variable-size sliding window, the standard technique generally relies on non-negative numbers. With negative numbers, adding and removing elements does not preserve the monotonic behavior needed by the standard expand/shrink logic, so this approach may fail.

Do not blindly apply SW2 to arbitrary sum problems. Check whether the condition behaves monotonically as the window expands and shrinks.

⚠️ Fixed vs Variable Window

K

SW1 — Fixed

The window size is controlled by k.

size == k
↔

SW2 — Variable

The window size is controlled by a condition.

condition → shrink / expand
?

Recognition

Exactly k → SW1. Longest/shortest satisfying a condition → usually SW2.

condition controls size

⚠️ Common Mistakes

  • Using a fixed-size template when the window size is controlled by a condition.
  • Using if instead of while when multiple shrink operations may be required.
  • Updating the answer at the wrong point in the shrink process.
  • Forgetting to remove the outgoing element from the window state.
  • Applying the standard sum-based technique to problems with negative numbers without checking whether the required monotonic behavior exists.

⏱️ Complexity

Time

O(n) for normal sliding-window problems. Although there is a nested while, both pointers only move forward, so the total movement is linear.

Auxiliary Space

O(1) when only scalar state is required. With a HashMap or HashSet, space depends on the number of tracked values.

🎯 Mental Trigger

“No fixed k → condition controls the window → expand right → shrink left when required.”

Longest: expand → invalid → shrink until valid → record max.
Shortest: expand → valid → record min → shrink while valid.

SLIDING WINDOW PATTERN

Sliding Window + Frequency Map

Combine a sliding window with a frequency map to track what is currently inside the window. The frequency map becomes part of the window state and helps determine whether the current window satisfies the required condition.

🧠 Pattern Overview

The right pointer expands the window and adds the incoming element to the frequency map. When the current window violates the required condition, the left pointer moves forward and removes elements from the frequency map until the window becomes valid again.

right → expands[ ... current window ... ]left → shrinksfrequency map → tracks window
Core idea: SW3 = Sliding Window + a frequency structure that tells us what is currently inside the window.

🔍 When to Think of This Pattern

Frequency mattersThe number of occurrences of a character or element affects validity.
Longest substringFind the longest contiguous substring satisfying a frequency condition.
At most K distinctThe number of distinct values inside the window is restricted.
Duplicate conditionThe window must avoid or control repeated values.
Anagram / permutationCompare character frequencies inside a fixed-size window.
Window + countsThe problem needs both two pointers and frequency information.
Key recognition question: Do I need to know the frequency of values currently inside a contiguous window?

📌 State to Maintain

L

Left

Beginning of the current window. Moves forward when the window needs to shrink.

left
R

Right

Expands the window by adding the next element.

right
F

Frequency Map

Stores how many times each relevant value currently appears inside the window.

freq

The frequency map must always represent the current window. When an element enters, increase its frequency. When an element leaves, decrease its frequency and remove it when the count reaches zero.

📈 Type A — Longest Valid Window

Goal: Find the longest window satisfying a frequency-based condition.

Expand→Update frequency→Invalid?→Shrink→Record maximum
Rule: Add the new element, update the frequency map, shrink while invalid, then update the maximum length.
Longest Valid Window + Frequency Map
Map<Character, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
int left = 0;
int answer = 0;

for (int right = 0; right < s.length(); right++) {
    char current = s.charAt(right);
    freq.put(current, freq.getOrDefault(current, 0) + 1);

    while (/* window is invalid */) {
        char remove = s.charAt(left);
        freq.put(remove, freq.get(remove) - 1);

        if (freq.get(remove) == 0) {
            freq.remove(remove);
        }

        left++;
    }

    answer = Math.max(answer, right - left + 1);
}
unordered_map<char, int> freq;
int left = 0;
int answer = 0;

for (int right = 0; right < s.size(); right++) {
    char current = s[right];
    freq[current]++;

    while (/* window is invalid */) {
        char remove = s[left];
        freq[remove]--;

        if (freq[remove] == 0) {
            freq.erase(remove);
        }

        left++;
    }

    answer = max(answer, right - left + 1);
}
freq = {}
left = 0
answer = 0

for right in range(len(s)):
    current = s[right]
    freq[current] = freq.get(current, 0) + 1

    while window_is_invalid:
        remove = s[left]
        freq[remove] -= 1

        if freq[remove] == 0:
            del freq[remove]

        left += 1

    answer = max(answer, right - left + 1)

📉 Type B — Shortest Valid Window

Goal: Find the shortest window satisfying a frequency-based condition.

Expand→Update frequency→Valid?→Record minimum→Shrink
Rule: Add the new element, then shrink while valid, recording the answer before each removal.
Shortest Valid Window + Frequency Map
Map<Character, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
int left = 0;
int answer = Integer.MAX_VALUE;

for (int right = 0; right < s.length(); right++) {
    char current = s.charAt(right);
    freq.put(current, freq.getOrDefault(current, 0) + 1);

    while (/* window is valid */) {
        answer = Math.min(answer, right - left + 1);

        char remove = s.charAt(left);
        freq.put(remove, freq.get(remove) - 1);

        if (freq.get(remove) == 0) {
            freq.remove(remove);
        }

        left++;
    }
}
unordered_map<char, int> freq;
int left = 0;
int answer = INT_MAX;

for (int right = 0; right < s.size(); right++) {
    char current = s[right];
    freq[current]++;

    while (/* window is valid */) {
        answer = min(answer, right - left + 1);

        char remove = s[left];
        freq[remove]--;

        if (freq[remove] == 0) {
            freq.erase(remove);
        }

        left++;
    }
}
freq = {}
left = 0
answer = float('inf')

for right in range(len(s)):
    current = s[right]
    freq[current] = freq.get(current, 0) + 1

    while window_is_valid:
        answer = min(answer, right - left + 1)

        remove = s[left]
        freq[remove] -= 1

        if freq[remove] == 0:
            del freq[remove]

        left += 1

⭐ The Most Important Rule — Keep the Map Accurate

Element enters→frequency + 1
Element leaves→frequency − 1

The frequency map is not separate from the window. It represents the current window. If left moves, the outgoing element must also be removed from the frequency structure.

Think: The window and the frequency map must always describe the same elements.

🧪 Practical Example — Longest Substring with At Most K Distinct Characters

Question: Given a string and an integer k, find the length of the longest substring containing at most k distinct characters.

How to read it: “Substring” means contiguous. “At most K distinct” means we need to know how many distinct characters are currently inside the window. A frequency map gives us that information.

s = ecebak = 2ece ✓eceb ✗ceb ✓
Reasoning: Expand until the window contains more than k distinct characters. Then shrink from the left until the frequency map contains at most k distinct characters again. Record the maximum valid length.
Longest Substring with At Most K Distinct Characters — Solution
public int lengthOfLongestSubstringKDistinct(String s, int k) {
    Map<Character, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
    int left = 0;
    int answer = 0;

    for (int right = 0; right < s.length(); right++) {
        char current = s.charAt(right);
        freq.put(current, freq.getOrDefault(current, 0) + 1);

        while (freq.size() > k) {
            char remove = s.charAt(left);
            freq.put(remove, freq.get(remove) - 1);

            if (freq.get(remove) == 0) {
                freq.remove(remove);
            }

            left++;
        }

        answer = Math.max(answer, right - left + 1);
    }

    return answer;
}
int lengthOfLongestSubstringKDistinct(string s, int k) {
    unordered_map<char, int> freq;
    int left = 0;
    int answer = 0;

    for (int right = 0; right < s.size(); right++) {
        char current = s[right];
        freq[current]++;

        while (freq.size() > k) {
            char remove = s[left];
            freq[remove]--;

            if (freq[remove] == 0) {
                freq.erase(remove);
            }

            left++;
        }

        answer = max(answer, right - left + 1);
    }

    return answer;
}
def lengthOfLongestSubstringKDistinct(self, s: str, k: int) -> int:
    freq = {}
    left = 0
    answer = 0

    for right in range(len(s)):
        current = s[right]
        freq[current] = freq.get(current, 0) + 1

        while len(freq) > k:
            remove = s[left]
            freq[remove] -= 1

            if freq[remove] == 0:
                del freq[remove]

            left += 1

        answer = max(answer, right - left + 1)

    return answer

🔄 The Window + Frequency Map Movement

→

Expand

Move right forward and add the incoming element to the frequency map.

F

Update Frequency

Increase or decrease the count of the element currently entering or leaving the window.

←

Shrink

Move left forward when the frequency-based condition is violated.

⚠️ Fixed vs Frequency-Map Window

K

SW1 — Fixed

The window size is controlled directly by k.

size == k
↔

SW2 — Variable

The window size is controlled by a condition.

condition → shrink / expand
F

SW3 — Frequency

The window condition depends on frequencies or distinct values inside the window.

window + freq map

⚠️ Common Mistakes

  • Moving left without decreasing the frequency of the outgoing element.
  • Forgetting to remove an element when its frequency becomes zero.
  • Using if instead of while when multiple shrink operations may be required.
  • Confusing frequency with distinct count. A character appearing five times is still only one distinct character.
  • Updating the answer before restoring the required window condition.
  • Trying to memorize the frequency-map code without first defining what makes the window valid.

⏱️ Complexity

Time

O(n) for normal sliding-window problems. Both pointers move only forward, so each element is added and removed at most once.

Auxiliary Space

O(k) when the map stores up to k distinct values. With a fixed-size alphabet, this can be treated as O(1).

🎯 Mental Trigger

“Contiguous window + frequency/count condition → Sliding Window + Frequency Map.”

Expand right → update frequency → check validity → shrink left while required → update answer.

Longest: invalid → shrink → record max.
Shortest: valid → record min → shrink.
Fixed-size frequency: maintain exactly k → process window.

SLIDING WINDOW PATTERN

Advanced Variable Window

Use a variable-size sliding window when the problem asks for a longest or shortest contiguous range whose validity depends on a more advanced condition such as covering required frequencies, limiting distinct values, or allowing a limited number of modifications.

🧠 Pattern Overview

SW4 builds on variable-size sliding window. The right pointer expands the window, while the left pointer moves forward according to a carefully maintained validity condition. The main challenge is identifying exactly what makes the current window valid.

right → expands[ ... current window ... ]window state → determines validityleft → shrinks
Core idea: Expand the window, maintain the required state, determine whether the window is valid, then move left as required by the problem.

🔍 When to Think of This Pattern

Minimum WindowFind the smallest substring containing all required characters or frequencies.
At Most K DistinctMaintain a window containing no more than K distinct values.
Limited ModificationsAllow at most K changes while maximizing the window.
Contains / CoversThe current window must contain everything required by another string or condition.
Longest After ChangesFind the longest valid window after allowing a limited number of modifications.
Complex Window StateThe validity condition requires more than simply checking the window size.
Key recognition question: Is this a contiguous variable-size window where validity requires carefully maintained state?

📌 State to Maintain

L

Left

Beginning of the current window. Moves forward when the current window must shrink.

left
R

Right

Expands the window by adding the next element.

right
S

Window State

Stores the information needed to determine whether the current window is valid.

windowState

Depending on the problem, the state may include a frequency map, required frequencies, distinct count, number of changes, or another derived quantity.

📈 Type A — Cover / Minimum Window

Goal: Find the shortest window that contains everything required.

Expand→Window becomes valid→Record minimum→Shrink while valid
Rule: Expand until the window covers the requirement. Once valid, record the answer and keep shrinking until the window becomes invalid.
Minimum Cover Window Template
Map<Character, Integer> need = new HashMap<>();
Map<Character, Integer> have = new HashMap<>();

int left = 0;
int formed = 0;
int required = need.size();
int answer = Integer.MAX_VALUE;

for (int right = 0; right < s.length(); right++) {
    char current = s.charAt(right);

    // Add current to the window
    // Update formed when a required frequency is satisfied

    while (formed == required) {
        answer = Math.min(answer, right - left + 1);

        char remove = s.charAt(left);
        // Remove from window
        // Update formed if a requirement becomes unsatisfied

        left++;
    }
}

unordered_map<char, int> have;

        char remove = s[left];
        // Remove from window

        left++;
    }
}

📊 Type B — At Most K Distinct

Goal: Find the longest window containing at most K distinct values.

Expand→Track frequencies→Distinct > K?→Shrink→Record maximum
Rule: Add the new value, update its frequency, and shrink while the number of distinct values is greater than K.
At Most K Distinct Template

🔄 Type C — Limited Modifications

Goal: Find the longest window where at most K elements need to be modified.

Expand→Count changes needed→changes > K?→Shrink
Rule: Instead of requiring every element to already satisfy the desired condition, count how many changes are needed. If that number exceeds K, shrink the window.
changes needed=number of elements that violate the desired condition

}
