🧪 Practical Example — LC 76: Minimum Window Substring

Question: Given strings s and t, find the smallest substring of s that contains every character of t with the required frequency. If no such substring exists, return an empty string.

How to read it: “Substring” means contiguous, so sliding window is a candidate. We must cover every character of t, including repeated characters, so we need frequency information. Because we want the minimum valid window, we shrink while the window remains valid.

s = ADOBECODEBANCt = ABCvalid → shrinkbest = BANC
Reasoning: Expand right until all required frequencies are satisfied. Then record the window and move left forward while the window remains valid. The moment a required frequency becomes insufficient, stop shrinking and continue expanding.
Minimum Window Substring — Solution
public String minWindow(String s, String t) {
    if (t.length() > s.length()) {
        return "";
    }

    Map<Character, Integer> need = new HashMap<>();
    Map<Character, Integer> have = new HashMap<>();

    for (char c : t.toCharArray()) {
        need.put(c, need.getOrDefault(c, 0) + 1);
    }

    int left = 0;
    int formed = 0;
    int required = need.size();
    int minLength = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
    int bestStart = 0;

    for (int right = 0; right < s.length(); right++) {
        char current = s.charAt(right);
        have.put(current, have.getOrDefault(current, 0) + 1);

        if (need.containsKey(current) && have.get(current).intValue() == need.get(current).intValue()) {
            formed++;
        }

        while (formed == required) {
            int currentLength = right - left + 1;

            if (currentLength < minLength) {
                minLength = currentLength;
                bestStart = left;
            }

            char remove = s.charAt(left);
            have.put(remove, have.get(remove) - 1);

            if (need.containsKey(remove) && have.get(remove) < need.get(remove)) {
                formed--;
            }

            left++;
        }
    }

    return minLength == Integer.MAX_VALUE ? "" : s.substring(bestStart, bestStart + minLength);
}
string minWindow(string s, string t) {
    if (t.size() > s.size()) {
        return "";
    }

    unordered_map<char, int> need;
    unordered_map<char, int> have;

    for (char c : t) {
        need[c]++;
    }

    int left = 0;
    int formed = 0;
    int required = need.size();
    int minLength = INT_MAX;
    int bestStart = 0;

    for (int right = 0; right < s.size(); right++) {
        char current = s[right];
        have[current]++;

        if (need.count(current) && have[current] == need[current]) {
            formed++;
        }

        while (formed == required) {
            int currentLength = right - left + 1;

            if (currentLength < minLength) {
                minLength = currentLength;
                bestStart = left;
            }

            char remove = s[left];
            have[remove]--;

            if (need.count(remove) && have[remove] < need[remove]) {
                formed--;
            }

            left++;
        }
    }

    return minLength == INT_MAX ? "" : s.substr(bestStart, minLength);
}
def minWindow(self, s: str, t: str) -> str:
    if len(t) > len(s):
        return ""

    need = {}
    have = {}

    for char in t:
        need[char] = need.get(char, 0) + 1

    left = 0
    formed = 0
    required = len(need)
    min_length = float('inf')
    best_start = 0

    for right in range(len(s)):
        current = s[right]
        have[current] = have.get(current, 0) + 1

        if current in need and have[current] == need[current]:
            formed += 1

        while formed == required:
            current_length = right - left + 1

            if current_length < min_length:
                min_length = current_length
                best_start = left

            remove = s[left]
            have[remove] -= 1

            if remove in need and have[remove] < need[remove]:
                formed -= 1

            left += 1

    if min_length == float('inf'):
        return ""

    return s[best_start:best_start + min_length]

⭐ Why LC 76 Is Advanced

LC 76 combines several sliding-window ideas at once. The window must contain required frequencies, validity must be tracked efficiently, and the left pointer must shrink aggressively to find the minimum valid window.

1

Need

Stores the required frequency of every relevant character.

2

Have

Stores the frequency currently present inside the window.

3

Formed

Tracks how many required character frequencies are currently satisfied.

🔄 The Advanced Window Movement

→

Expand

Move right forward and add the incoming element to the window state.

✓

Validate

Check the maintained state to determine whether the current window is valid.

←

Shrink

Move left forward while the problem's condition allows or requires it.

⚠️ Common Mistakes

  • Checking only whether a required character exists instead of checking its required frequency.
  • Forgetting that the frequency map must be updated when elements leave the window.
  • Updating the validity counter at the wrong frequency threshold.
  • Stopping after finding the first valid window when the problem asks for the minimum.
  • Confusing “at most K distinct” with “exactly K distinct”.
  • For limited-modification problems, forgetting that the window is valid as long as the number of required changes is at most K.
  • Memorizing LC 76 without understanding what makes the window valid.

⏱️ Complexity

Time

O(n) for standard sliding-window implementations. The right pointer moves forward once and the left pointer also moves forward at most n times.

Auxiliary Space

O(k) when the frequency structures track up to k distinct values or required characters. With a fixed alphabet, this can be treated as O(1).

📚 Problem Progression

1

LC 76

Minimum Window Substring

Learn cover-window logic and minimum valid windows.

2

LC 904

Fruit Into Baskets

Reinforce longest window with at most two distinct values.

3

LC 1004

Max Consecutive Ones III

Learn how a limited number of modifications can define validity.

Recommended order: LC 76 → LC 904 → LC 1004. Focus on identifying the validity condition before writing the pointer logic.

🎯 The Real Pattern

Do not memorize three separate solutions.

All three follow the same high-level process:

Expand right → update window state → determine validity → move left as required → update answer.

The important difference is what defines validity.

🎯 Mental Trigger

“Contiguous + variable window + advanced validity condition?”

Think Advanced Variable Sliding Window.

Cover: required frequencies → valid → shrink while valid → minimum.
At Most K: frequency map → distinct > K → shrink → maximum.
Limited Modification: changes needed > K → shrink → maximum.

BINARY SEARCH PATTERN

Classic Binary Search

Binary Search is a divide-and-conquer pattern for searching a target inside a sorted search space. Instead of checking every element, repeatedly eliminate half of the remaining range.

Pattern Overview

When the search space is sorted and the question is whether a target exists, Binary Search lets us discard half of the candidates after every comparison.

Core idea: Maintain a search range using left and right, inspect the middle element, and decide which half can still contain the answer.

Mental Model

L

Left

Start of the current search range.

left = 0
M

Middle

Candidate used to decide which half survives.

mid = left + (right - left) / 2
R

Right

End of the current search range.

right = n - 1
[ 2 ][ 5 ][ 8 ][ 12 ][ 16 ][ 23 ][ 38 ]

Compare the target with the middle value → keep only the half that can still contain the target.

Recognition Clues

SortedThe array or search space is sorted.
SearchFind whether a target exists or where it belongs.
Eliminate HalfOne comparison can discard half of the candidates.

Fundamental Operations

  • Initialize left and right to define the search range.
  • Calculate the middle index safely.
  • If the middle value equals the target, return the answer.
  • If the middle value is smaller than the target, search the right half.
  • If the middle value is larger than the target, search the left half.
  • Stop when the search range becomes empty.

Template — Standard Binary Search

Binary Search Template
int binarySearch(int[] nums, int target) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = nums.length - 1;

    while (left <= right) {
        int mid = left + (right - left) / 2;

        if (nums[mid] == target) {
            return mid;
        } else if (nums[mid] < target) {
            left = mid + 1;
        } else {
            right = mid - 1;
        }
    }

    return -1;
}
int binarySearch(vector<int>& nums, int target) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = nums.size() - 1;

    while (left <= right) {
        int mid = left + (right - left) / 2;

        if (nums[mid] == target) {
            return mid;
        } else if (nums[mid] < target) {
            left = mid + 1;
        } else {
            right = mid - 1;
        }
    }

    return -1;
}
def binary_search(nums, target):
    left = 0
    right = len(nums) - 1

    while left <= right:
        mid = left + (right - left) // 2

        if nums[mid] == target:
            return mid
        elif nums[mid] < target:
            left = mid + 1
        else:
            right = mid - 1

    return -1

Practical Example — LC 704: Binary Search

Question: Given a sorted array of distinct integers and a target value, return the index of the target if it exists. Otherwise, return -1.

How to read it: The key clue is that the array is sorted. Because the values are ordered, comparing the target with the middle value tells us which half can be discarded.

Why Binary Search fits: If nums[mid] < target, every value at or before mid is too small, so we can discard that entire half. If nums[mid] > target, we discard the right half.
LC 704 — Binary Search Solution
class Solution {
    public int search(int[] nums, int target) {
        int left = 0;
        int right = nums.length - 1;

        while (left <= right) {
            int mid = left + (right - left) / 2;

            if (nums[mid] == target) {
                return mid;
            } else if (nums[mid] < target) {
                left = mid + 1;
            } else {
                right = mid - 1;
            }
        }

        return -1;
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    int search(vector<int>& nums, int target) {
        int left = 0;
        int right = nums.size() - 1;

        while (left <= right) {
            int mid = left + (right - left) / 2;

            if (nums[mid] == target) {
                return mid;
            } else if (nums[mid] < target) {
                left = mid + 1;
            } else {
                right = mid - 1;
            }
        }

        return -1;
    }
};
class Solution:
    def search(self, nums, target):
        left = 0
        right = len(nums) - 1

        while left <= right:
            mid = left + (right - left) // 2

            if nums[mid] == target:
                return mid
            elif nums[mid] < target:
                left = mid + 1
            else:
                right = mid - 1

        return -1
Why this works: Every iteration removes half of the remaining search space. The loop therefore needs only logarithmically many iterations.

Common Mistakes

  • Using Binary Search when the search space does not provide a valid ordering.
  • Updating the wrong boundary after comparing with nums[mid].
  • Using mid = (left + right) / 2 when a safer midpoint calculation is preferred.
  • Using inconsistent boundary rules, causing an infinite loop or skipping a candidate.
  • Forgetting that the standard exact-match version returns -1 when the target is absent.

Complexity

Time

O(log n)

Each comparison eliminates roughly half of the remaining search space.

Space

O(1)

The iterative implementation uses only a constant number of variables.

Pattern Progression

LC 704 — Binary Search → Learn the classic sorted-array search.
LC 35 — Search Insert Position → Reinforce binary-search boundary and insertion logic.
LC 278 — First Bad Version → Extend the idea toward finding the first valid answer in a search space.

Mental Trigger

“Is the search space ordered, and can one comparison eliminate half of it?”
If yes, think Binary Search.

BINARY SEARCH PATTERN

Binary Search on Boundaries

Boundary Binary Search is used when the goal is not simply to find whether a target exists, but to locate a specific boundary such as the first occurrence, last occurrence, lower bound, or upper bound.

Pattern Overview

Instead of stopping when nums[mid] == target, boundary search continues searching after finding a valid candidate. The key question becomes: Can there be a better answer further to the left or right?

Core idea: Use Binary Search to find the boundary where a condition changes from false to true, or to locate the first or last position satisfying a condition.

Mental Model

F

First

When a valid answer is found, continue searching left for an earlier valid position.

right = mid - 1
L

Last

When a valid answer is found, continue searching right for a later valid position.

left = mid + 1
B

Boundary

Find the exact point where the search condition changes.

first valid position

Recognition Clues

First / LastFind the first or last occurrence of a value.
Lower / Upper BoundFind the first position satisfying a comparison condition.
BoundaryThe answer lies at the point where a condition changes.

Boundary Thinking

  • First occurrence: when the target is found, save the position and continue searching left.
  • Last occurrence: when the target is found, save the position and continue searching right.
  • Lower bound: find the first position where nums[mid] >= target.
  • Upper bound: find the first position where nums[mid] > target.
  • The important difference from Classic Binary Search is that finding a valid candidate does not necessarily mean the search is finished.

Templates — Boundary Search

First Occurrence Template
int firstOccurrence(int[] nums, int target) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = nums.length - 1;
    int answer = -1;

    while (left <= right) {
        int mid = left + (right - left) / 2;

        if (nums[mid] == target) {
            answer = mid;
            right = mid - 1;
        } else if (nums[mid] < target) {
            left = mid + 1;
        } else {
            right = mid - 1;
        }
    }

    return answer;
}
int firstOccurrence(vector<int>& nums, int target) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = nums.size() - 1;
    int answer = -1;

    while (left <= right) {
        int mid = left + (right - left) / 2;

        if (nums[mid] == target) {
            answer = mid;
            right = mid - 1;
        } else if (nums[mid] < target) {
            left = mid + 1;
        } else {
            right = mid - 1;
        }
    }

    return answer;
}
def first_occurrence(nums, target):
    left = 0
    right = len(nums) - 1
    answer = -1

    while left <= right:
        mid = left + (right - left) // 2

        if nums[mid] == target:
            answer = mid
            right = mid - 1
        elif nums[mid] < target:
            left = mid + 1
        else:
            right = mid - 1

    return answer

Practical Example — LC 34: Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array

Question: Given a sorted array of integers and a target value, return the starting and ending position of the target's range. If the target is not present, return [-1, -1].

How to read it: The array is sorted and the target may appear multiple times. We do not just need to know whether the target exists. We need the first and last positions, so a normal Binary Search is not enough.

Why Boundary Search fits: Run Binary Search twice. The first search keeps moving left after finding the target to locate its first occurrence. The second keeps moving right to locate its last occurrence.
[5][7][7][8][8][8][10]

Target = 8 → first boundary = index 3 → last boundary = index 5

LC 34 — Boundary Search Solution
class Solution {
    public int[] searchRange(int[] nums, int target) {
        return new int[]{firstOccurrence(nums, target), lastOccurrence(nums, target)};
    }

    private int firstOccurrence(int[] nums, int target) {
        int left = 0;
        int right = nums.length - 1;
        int answer = -1;

        while (left <= right) {
            int mid = left + (right - left) / 2;

            if (nums[mid] == target) {
                answer = mid;
                right = mid - 1;
            } else if (nums[mid] < target) {
                left = mid + 1;
            } else {
                right = mid - 1;
            }
        }

        return answer;
    }

    private int lastOccurrence(int[] nums, int target) {
        int left = 0;
        int right = nums.length - 1;
        int answer = -1;

        while (left <= right) {
            int mid = left + (right - left) / 2;

            if (nums[mid] == target) {
                answer = mid;
                left = mid + 1;
            } else if (nums[mid] < target) {
                left = mid + 1;
            } else {
                right = mid - 1;
            }
        }

        return answer;
    }
}

public:
    int firstOccurrence(vector<int>& nums, int target) {
        int left = 0, right = nums.size() - 1;
        int answer = -1;

        while (left <= right) {
            int mid = left + (right - left) / 2;

            if (nums[mid] == target) {
                answer = mid;
                right = mid - 1;
            } else if (nums[mid] < target) {
                left = mid + 1;
            } else {
                right = mid - 1;
            }
        }

        return answer;
    }

    int lastOccurrence(vector<int>& nums, int target) {
        int left = 0, right = nums.size() - 1;
        int answer = -1;

        while (left <= right) {
            int mid = left + (right - left) / 2;

            if (nums[mid] == target) {
                answer = mid;
                left = mid + 1;
            } else if (nums[mid] < target) {
                left = mid + 1;
            } else {
                right = mid - 1;
            }
        }

        return answer;
    }

    vector<int> searchRange(vector<int>& nums, int target) {
        return {firstOccurrence(nums, target), lastOccurrence(nums, target)};
    }
};
class Solution:
    def searchRange(self, nums, target):
        return [self.first_occurrence(nums, target), self.last_occurrence(nums, target)]

    def first_occurrence(self, nums, target):
        left = 0
        right = len(nums) - 1
        answer = -1

        while left <= right:
            mid = left + (right - left) // 2

            if nums[mid] == target:
                answer = mid
                right = mid - 1
            elif nums[mid] < target:
                left = mid + 1
            else:
                right = mid - 1

        return answer

    def last_occurrence(self, nums, target):
        left = 0
        right = len(nums) - 1
        answer = -1

        while left <= right:
            mid = left + (right - left) // 2

            if nums[mid] == target:
                answer = mid
                left = mid + 1
            elif nums[mid] < target:
                left = mid + 1
            else:
                right = mid - 1

        return answer
Key observation: The two searches use the same Binary Search structure. The only change is what happens after finding the target: first occurrence moves right left, while last occurrence moves left right.

Common Mistakes

  • Stopping immediately when nums[mid] == target.
  • Forgetting to save the current valid position before continuing the search.
  • Moving the boundary in the wrong direction after finding a valid candidate.
  • Confusing lower bound with exact target search.
  • Using different boundary conventions inconsistently.

Complexity

Time

O(log n)

Each boundary search eliminates roughly half of the remaining search space. For LC 34, two Binary Searches still give O(log n) overall.

Space

O(1)

The iterative boundary search uses only a constant number of variables.

Pattern Progression

LC 34 — Find First and Last Position → Learn first/last boundary searching.
LC 744 — Find Smallest Letter Greater Than Target → Reinforce upper-bound logic.
LC 540 — Single Element in a Sorted Array → Extend Binary Search with parity-based boundary reasoning.

Mental Trigger

“I found a valid answer — but can there be a better one further left or right?”
If yes, do not stop. Continue Binary Search toward the required boundary.

BINARY SEARCH PATTERN

Binary Search on Rotated Arrays

Rotated Array Binary Search applies Binary Search to a sorted array that has been rotated around a pivot. The key is to determine which half is still sorted, then decide whether the target belongs inside that sorted half.

Pattern Overview

A rotated sorted array is not globally sorted, but at every Binary Search step, at least one half of the current search range remains sorted. Use that information to determine which half can contain the target.

Core idea: Compare the boundary value with nums[mid] to identify the sorted half. Then check whether the target lies inside that half. If it does, search there; otherwise, search the other half.

Mental Model

S

Sorted Half

One side of the current range is guaranteed to remain sorted.

nums[left] <= nums[mid]
T

Target Range

Check whether the target falls inside the sorted half.

nums[left] <= target < nums[mid]
P

Pivot

The rotation point separates the two sorted portions.

... 7, 8, 1, 2, 3 ...
[4][5][6][7][0][1][2]

The array was sorted, then rotated. At each step, identify the sorted half before deciding where to search.

Recognition Clues

RotatedThe sorted array has been rotated around a pivot.
PivotA rotation point divides the array into sorted portions.
CircularThe ordering wraps around from the end back toward the beginning.

How the Search Works

  • Calculate mid as in normal Binary Search.
  • Determine which half is sorted.
  • If the left half is sorted, check whether the target lies between nums[left] and nums[mid].
  • If the target belongs to that sorted half, move right left. Otherwise, search the other half.
  • If the right half is sorted, perform the symmetric check.
  • Repeat until the target is found or the search range becomes empty.

Template — Rotated Array Search

Search in Rotated Sorted Array
int searchRotated(int[] nums, int target) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = nums.length - 1;

    while (left <= right) {
        int mid = left + (right - left) / 2;

        if (nums[mid] == target) {
            return mid;
        }

        if (nums[left] <= nums[mid]) {
            if (nums[left] <= target && target < nums[mid]) {
                right = mid - 1;
            } else {
                left = mid + 1;
            }
        } else {
            if (nums[mid] < target && target <= nums[right]) {
                left = mid + 1;
            } else {
                right = mid - 1;
            }
        }
    }

    return -1;
}
int searchRotated(vector<int>& nums, int target) {
    int left = 0;
    int right = nums.size() - 1;

    while (left <= right) {
        int mid = left + (right - left) / 2;

        if (nums[mid] == target) {
            return mid;
        }

        if (nums[left] <= nums[mid]) {
            if (nums[left] <= target && target < nums[mid]) {
                right = mid - 1;
            } else {
                left = mid + 1;
            }
        } else {
            if (nums[mid] < target && target <= nums[right]) {
                left = mid + 1;
            } else {
                right = mid - 1;
            }
        }
    }

    return -1;
}
def search_rotated(nums, target):
    left = 0
    right = len(nums) - 1

    while left <= right:
        mid = left + (right - left) // 2

        if nums[mid] == target:
            return mid

        if nums[left] <= nums[mid]:
            if nums[left] <= target < nums[mid]:
                right = mid - 1
            else:
                left = mid + 1
        else:
            if nums[mid] < target <= nums[right]:
                left = mid + 1
            else:
                right = mid - 1

    return -1

Practical Example — LC 33: Search in Rotated Sorted Array

Question: Given an array of distinct integers that was originally sorted in ascending order and then rotated, return the index of the target if it exists. Otherwise, return -1.

How to read it: The important clues are sorted and rotated. A normal Binary Search cannot directly use the global ordering, but one of the two halves around mid is always sorted.

Why this pattern fits: First identify the sorted half. Then ask whether the target lies inside that half. If it does, discard the other half. If it does not, discard the sorted half and search the remaining half.
[4][5][6][7][0][1][2]

Target = 0 → left half [4, 5, 6, 7] is sorted → target is not there → search the right half.

LC 33 — Rotated Array Binary Search Solution
class Solution {
    public int search(int[] nums, int target) {
        int left = 0;
        int right = nums.length - 1;

        while (left <= right) {
            int mid = left + (right - left) / 2;

            if (nums[mid] == target) {
                return mid;
            }

            if (nums[left] <= nums[mid]) {
                if (nums[left] <= target && target < nums[mid]) {
                    right = mid - 1;
                } else {
                    left = mid + 1;
                }
            } else {
                if (nums[mid] < target && target <= nums[right]) {
                    left = mid + 1;
                } else {
                    right = mid - 1;
                }
            }
        }

        return -1;
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    int search(vector<int>& nums, int target) {
        int left = 0;
        int right = nums.size() - 1;

        while (left <= right) {
            int mid = left + (right - left) / 2;

            if (nums[mid] == target) {
                return mid;
            }

            if (nums[left] <= nums[mid]) {
                if (nums[left] <= target && target < nums[mid]) {
                    right = mid - 1;
                } else {
                    left = mid + 1;
                }
            } else {
                if (nums[mid] < target && target <= nums[right]) {
                    left = mid + 1;
                } else {
                    right = mid - 1;
                }
            }
        }

        return -1;
    }
};
class Solution:
    def search(self, nums, target):
        left = 0
        right = len(nums) - 1

        while left <= right:
            mid = left + (right - left) // 2

            if nums[mid] == target:
                return mid

            if nums[left] <= nums[mid]:
                if nums[left] <= target < nums[mid]:
                    right = mid - 1
                else:
                    left = mid + 1
            else:
                if nums[mid] < target <= nums[right]:
                    left = mid + 1
                else:
                    right = mid - 1

        return -1
Key observation: You do not need to explicitly find the pivot first. At every step, identifying the sorted half is enough to decide which half can be discarded.

Handling Duplicates

When duplicates are allowed, as in LC 81, the usual sorted-half test can become ambiguous because nums[left] == nums[mid] == nums[right]. In that case, the boundary values do not reveal which half is sorted.

Extension: When the ordering is ambiguous, shrink the boundaries and continue the search. This handles the additional difficulty introduced by duplicate values.

Finding the Minimum / Pivot

LC 153 changes the goal from finding a target to locating the smallest value. The same rotated-array structure is used, but the comparison with the right boundary tells us whether the minimum lies to the left or right of mid.

Common Mistakes

  • Trying to apply normal Binary Search without accounting for the rotation.
  • Forgetting to identify which half is sorted before deciding where to search.
  • Using incorrect inclusive/exclusive conditions when checking whether the target lies inside the sorted half.
  • Assuming the same logic works unchanged when duplicates are present.
  • Thinking the pivot must always be found explicitly before searching. LC 33 can locate the target without a separate pivot-search step.

Complexity

Time

O(log n)

For distinct values, each iteration discards roughly half of the remaining search space.

Space

O(1)

The iterative implementation uses only a constant number of variables.

Pattern Progression

LC 33 — Search in Rotated Sorted Array → Learn how to search when a sorted array has been rotated.
LC 81 — Search in Rotated Sorted Array II → Extend the pattern to handle duplicates.

Mental Trigger

“The array is sorted but rotated — which half is sorted right now, and can the target belong to it?”
Identify the sorted half, test the target range, then discard the impossible half.

BINARY SEARCH PATTERN

Binary Search on Answer

Binary Search on Answer is used when the answer is not directly present in an array, but lies inside a range of possible values. Instead of searching for an element, binary search is performed over the answer space using a feasibility condition.

Pattern Overview

The key idea is to turn an optimization problem into a decision problem. Instead of asking directly for the minimum or maximum answer, ask: “Is this candidate answer feasible?”

Core idea: Define the possible answer range, test the middle candidate, and use the result of the feasibility check to eliminate half of the answer space.

Mental Model

A

Answer Space

Define the smallest and largest possible answers.

low = minimum possible
M

Candidate

Test the middle value as a possible answer.

mid = low + (high - low) / 2
F

Feasibility

Check whether the candidate can satisfy the problem constraints.

isFeasible(mid)

Recognition Clues

Minimize / MaximizeFind the smallest or largest value satisfying a condition.
Capacity / SpeedChoose a numeric capacity, rate, speed, or limit.
FeasibleA candidate answer can be tested as valid or invalid.

How the Pattern Works

  • Identify the complete range of possible answers.
  • Choose the middle candidate from that answer space.
  • Build a feasibility check that answers whether the candidate works.
  • If the candidate is feasible and you want to minimize, search the smaller answers.
  • If the candidate is not feasible, search larger answers.
  • Continue until the search space contains the optimal feasible answer.
Important: The array does not need to be sorted. What must be monotonic is the feasibility condition across the answer space.

Template — Search on Answer

Minimize a Feasible Answer
int searchAnswer(int low, int high) {
    int answer = high;

    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;

        if (isFeasible(mid)) {
            answer = mid;
            high = mid - 1;
        } else {
            low = mid + 1;
        }
    }

    return answer;
}
int searchAnswer(int low, int high) {
    int answer = high;

    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;

        if (isFeasible(mid)) {
            answer = mid;
            high = mid - 1;
        } else {
            low = mid + 1;
        }
    }

    return answer;
}
def search_answer(low, high):
    answer = high

    while low <= high:
        mid = low + (high - low) // 2

        if is_feasible(mid):
            answer = mid
            high = mid - 1
        else:
            low = mid + 1

    return answer

Practical Example — LC 875: Koko Eating Bananas

Question: Koko has several piles of bananas and must eat all bananas within h hours. If she eats at speed k bananas per hour, determine the minimum integer value of k that allows her to finish on time.

How to read it: The answer is not an index or an element in the array. The answer is an eating speed. The possible speeds form a numeric range from 1 to the largest pile.

Why Search on Answer fits: For a candidate speed k, we can calculate how many hours are required. If Koko can finish within h hours, that speed is feasible. If she cannot, the speed is too small. This creates a monotonic feasibility condition.
piles = [3][6][7][11]h = 8

Answer space: speed 1 → 11. Test the middle speed and eliminate the impossible half.

LC 875 — Binary Search on Answer Solution
class Solution {
    public int minEatingSpeed(int[] piles, int h) {
        int low = 1;
        int high = 0;

        for (int pile : piles) {
            high = Math.max(high, pile);
        }

        int answer = high;

        while (low <= high) {
            int speed = low + (high - low) / 2;
            long hours = 0;

            for (int pile : piles) {
                hours += (pile + speed - 1) / speed;
            }

            if (hours <= h) {
                answer = speed;
                high = speed - 1;
            } else {
                low = speed + 1;
            }
        }

        return answer;
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    int minEatingSpeed(vector<int>& piles, int h) {
        int low = 1;
        int high = *max_element(piles.begin(), piles.end());
        int answer = high;

        while (low <= high) {
            int speed = low + (high - low) / 2;
            long long hours = 0;

            for (int pile : piles) {
                hours += (pile + speed - 1) / speed;
            }

            if (hours <= h) {
                answer = speed;
                high = speed - 1;
            } else {
                low = speed + 1;
            }
        }

        return answer;
    }
};
class Solution:
    def minEatingSpeed(self, piles, h):
        low = 1
        high = max(piles)
        answer = high

        while low <= high:
            speed = low + (high - low) // 2
            hours = 0

            for pile in piles:
                hours += (pile + speed - 1) // speed

            if hours <= h:
                answer = speed
                high = speed - 1
            else:
                low = speed + 1

        return answer
Key observation: If speed k is feasible, every speed greater than k is also feasible. If speed k is not feasible, every smaller speed is also not feasible. That monotonic property is what makes Binary Search possible.

Feasibility Check

For each pile, the number of hours required at speed k is the ceiling of pile / k. The total hours determine whether the candidate speed is feasible.

hours = Σ ceil(pile / speed)→hours <= h → feasible

Common Mistakes

  • Binary searching the input array instead of the answer space.
  • Failing to identify the minimum and maximum possible answers.
  • Writing a feasibility check that is not monotonic.
  • Searching in the wrong direction after a candidate is feasible.
  • Using an integer calculation that incorrectly rounds down instead of computing the required ceiling.
  • Forgetting that the goal may be to minimize or maximize a feasible answer rather than simply find any feasible value.

Complexity

Time

O(n log M)

There are O(log M) candidate answers, where M is the answer-space range, and each feasibility check scans the n input values.

Space

O(1)

The binary search and feasibility calculation use constant extra space.

Pattern Progression

LC 875 — Koko Eating Bananas → Learn to search over a speed answer space.
LC 1011 — Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days → Reinforce feasibility checking with capacity as the answer.
LC 1283 — Find the Smallest Divisor Given a Threshold → Extend the same minimum-feasible-answer pattern.

Mental Trigger

“I need the minimum or maximum value, and I can check whether a candidate value is feasible.”
Do not search for the answer directly. Search the answer space and use feasibility to eliminate half.

learning.html:
STACK PATTERN

Balanced Parentheses

Balanced Parentheses is a stack pattern used to validate nested brackets and parentheses. The key idea is to remember the most recent opening bracket and match it with the next closing bracket.

Pattern Overview

Whenever an opening bracket appears, push it onto the stack. Whenever a closing bracket appears, it must match the most recently opened bracket. This naturally follows the Last In, First Out behavior of a stack.

Core idea: Opening brackets go into the stack. A closing bracket must match the stack's top element. If it does not, the sequence is invalid. At the end, the stack must be empty.

Mental Model

+

Opening

Store every opening bracket because it still needs a matching closing bracket.

push(opening)
↔

Matching

A closing bracket must match the most recently opened bracket.

top == matching(opening)
✓

Balanced

After processing the complete string, no unmatched opening brackets may remain.

stack.empty()

Recognition Clues

ParenthesesQuestions involving (), {}, or [] matching.
NestedOpening and closing structures can be nested inside each other.
MatchingThe latest unmatched opening symbol must be closed first.

How the Pattern Works

  • Scan the string from left to right.
  • When an opening bracket is found, push it onto the stack.
  • When a closing bracket is found, first check whether the stack is empty.
  • Compare the closing bracket with the top opening bracket.
  • If they match, pop the opening bracket.
  • If they do not match, the sequence is invalid.
  • After the scan, the stack must be empty for the sequence to be balanced.

Template — Balanced Parentheses

Stack Matching Template
boolean isBalanced(String s) {
    Stack<Character> stack = new Stack<>();

    for (char bracket : s.toCharArray()) {
        if (bracket == '(' || bracket == '[' || bracket == '{') {
            stack.push(bracket);
        } else {
            if (stack.isEmpty()) {
                return false;
            }

            char opening = stack.pop();

            if ((bracket == ')' && opening != '(') ||
                (bracket == ']' && opening != '[') ||
                (bracket == '}' && opening != '{')) {
                return false;
            }
        }
    }

    return stack.isEmpty();
}
bool isBalanced(string s) {
    stack<char> st;

    for (char bracket : s) {
        if (bracket == '(' || bracket == '[' || bracket == '{') {
            st.push(bracket);
        } else {
            if (st.empty()) {
                return false;
            }

            char opening = st.top();
            st.pop();

            if ((bracket == ')' && opening != '(') ||
                (bracket == ']' && opening != '[') ||
                (bracket == '}' && opening != '{')) {
                return false;
            }
        }
    }

    return st.empty();
}
def is_balanced(s):
    stack = []

    matching = {')': '(', ']': '[', '}': '{'}

    for bracket in s:
        if bracket in '([{':
            stack.append(bracket)
        else:
            if not stack or stack[-1] != matching[bracket]:
                return False
            stack.pop()

    return not stack

Practical Example — LC 20: Valid Parentheses

Question: Given a string containing only (), {}, and [], determine whether the input string is valid. Every opening bracket must have the correct closing bracket, and brackets must close in the correct order.

How to read it: The important clues are matching and nested. If we see ([, the [ must be closed before the (. Therefore, the most recently opened bracket must be handled first — exactly what a stack provides.

Why Stack fits: For ({[]}), the opening brackets are pushed in the order ( → { → [. When ] appears, it must match [. Then } matches {, and finally ) matches (.
({[]})→Valid
LC 20 — Valid Parentheses Solution
class Solution {
    public boolean isValid(String s) {
        Stack<Character> stack = new Stack<>();

        for (char bracket : s.toCharArray()) {
            if (bracket == '(' || bracket == '[' || bracket == '{') {
                stack.push(bracket);
            } else {
                if (stack.isEmpty()) {
                    return false;
                }

                char opening = stack.pop();

                if ((bracket == ')' && opening != '(') ||
                    (bracket == ']' && opening != '[') ||
                    (bracket == '}' && opening != '{')) {
                    return false;
                }
            }
        }

        return stack.isEmpty();
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    bool isValid(string s) {
        stack<char> st;

        for (char bracket : s) {
            if (bracket == '(' || bracket == '[' || bracket == '{') {
                st.push(bracket);
            } else {
                if (st.empty()) {
                    return false;
                }

                char opening = st.top();
                st.pop();

                if ((bracket == ')' && opening != '(') ||
                    (bracket == ']' && opening != '[') ||
                    (bracket == '}' && opening != '{')) {
                    return false;
                }
            }
        }

        return st.empty();
    }
};
class Solution:
    def isValid(self, s):
        stack = []
        matching = {')': '(', ']': '[', '}': '{'}

        for bracket in s:
            if bracket in '([{':
                stack.append(bracket)
            else:
                if not stack or stack[-1] != matching[bracket]:
                    return False
                stack.pop()

        return not stack
Key observation: The stack stores exactly the opening brackets that have not been matched yet. Because the newest opening bracket must be closed first, LIFO ordering gives the correct matching behavior.

Nested Traversal

The same stack idea appears when the problem asks about nesting depth. LC 1614 tracks how deeply nested the parentheses become by increasing the current depth when an opening parenthesis appears and decreasing it when a closing parenthesis appears.

Balanced Group Manipulation

LC 1021 extends the concept by working with balanced groups. Instead of only validating the structure, the nesting level can be used to identify outermost parentheses and manipulate balanced groups.

Common Mistakes

  • Checking only whether the counts of opening and closing brackets are equal.
  • Forgetting that the order of brackets matters.
  • Trying to match a closing bracket with the oldest opening bracket instead of the most recent one.
  • Forgetting to check whether the stack is empty before accessing its top element.
  • Returning true without checking that all opening brackets have been matched.

Complexity

Time

O(n)

Each bracket is processed once and each stack operation takes constant time.

Space

O(n)

In the worst case, all opening brackets can be stored in the stack.

Pattern Progression

LC 20 — Valid Parentheses → Learn stack-based bracket matching.
LC 1614 — Maximum Nesting Depth → Reinforce nested traversal using the same structure.
LC 1021 — Remove Outermost Parentheses → Extend the concept to manipulate balanced groups.

Mental Trigger

“The most recently opened thing must be handled first.”
When nested structures require matching, think Stack.

learning.html:
STACK PATTERN

Monotonic Stack

A Monotonic Stack maintains elements in increasing or decreasing order while scanning through the input. It is useful when the problem asks for the next or previous greater or smaller value.

Pattern Overview

Instead of comparing every element with every future or previous element, a monotonic stack keeps only the elements that are still waiting for a useful answer. When a new value makes some stack elements resolvable, those elements are removed and their answers are determined.

Core idea: Keep the stack monotonic. When the current value breaks that order, pop elements until the required increasing or decreasing property is restored. Each element is pushed and popped at most once.

Mental Model

→

Next Greater

Pop smaller values when the current value is greater.

nums[stack.top()] < current
←

Next Smaller

Pop larger values when the current value is smaller.

nums[stack.top()] > current
S

Waiting States

The stack contains elements that have not yet found their answer.

stack = unresolved

Recognition Clues

Next GreaterFind the next larger value to the right.
Next SmallerFind the next smaller value to the right.
PreviousFind the nearest greater or smaller value on the left.

How the Pattern Works

  • Scan the elements from left to right.
  • Keep unresolved elements in a stack.
  • When the current element satisfies the required greater/smaller relationship, resolve the elements it can answer by popping them.
  • Push the current element after restoring the monotonic order.
  • Elements remaining in the stack have not found their required answer.
  • Because an element is pushed once and popped at most once, the total work remains linear.

Template — Next Greater Element

Decreasing Stack for Next Greater
int[] nextGreater(int[] nums) {
    int[] answer = new int[nums.length];
    Arrays.fill(answer, -1);
    Stack<Integer> stack = new Stack<>();

    for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        while (!stack.isEmpty() && nums[stack.peek()] < nums[i]) {
            int index = stack.pop();
            answer[index] = nums[i];
        }

        stack.push(i);
    }

    return answer;
}
vector<int> nextGreater(vector<int>& nums) {
    vector<int> answer(nums.size(), -1);
    stack<int> stack;

    for (int i = 0; i < nums.size(); i++) {
        while (!stack.empty() && nums[stack.top()] < nums[i]) {
            int index = stack.top();
            stack.pop();
            answer[index] = nums[i];
        }

        stack.push(i);
    }

    return answer;
}
def next_greater(nums):
    answer = [-1] * len(nums)
    stack = []

    for i in range(len(nums)):
        while stack and nums[stack[-1]] < nums[i]:
            index = stack.pop()
            answer[index] = nums[i]

        stack.append(i)

    return answer

Practical Example — LC 496: Next Greater Element I

Question: Given two arrays where nums1 is a subset of nums2, find the next greater element for every value in nums1. The next greater element is the first value to its right in nums2 that is greater than it.

How to read it: The important clue is next greater. For every element, we are looking toward the right for the first larger value. Instead of repeatedly scanning forward, keep elements that are still waiting for a greater value in a monotonic stack.

Why Monotonic Stack fits: For [2, 1, 2, 4, 3], when we reach 2, it resolves 1. When we reach 4, it resolves both remaining smaller values. Each unresolved element waits in the stack until the first greater value appears.
21243→-1
LC 496 — Next Greater Element I Solution
class Solution {
    public int[] nextGreaterElement(int[] nums1, int[] nums2) {
        Map<Integer, Integer> nextGreater = new HashMap<>();
        Stack<Integer> stack = new Stack<>();

        for (int value : nums2) {
            while (!stack.isEmpty() && stack.peek() < value) {
                nextGreater.put(stack.pop(), value);
            }
            stack.push(value);
        }

        int[] answer = new int[nums1.length];

        for (int i = 0; i < nums1.length; i++) {
            answer[i] = nextGreater.getOrDefault(nums1[i], -1);
        }

        return answer;
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    vector<int> nextGreaterElement(vector<int>& nums1, vector<int>& nums2) {
        unordered_map<int, int> nextGreater;
        stack<int> stack;

        for (int value : nums2) {
            while (!stack.empty() && stack.top() < value) {
                nextGreater[stack.top()] = value;
                stack.pop();
            }
            stack.push(value);
        }

        vector<int> answer;

        for (int value : nums1) {
            if (nextGreater.count(value)) {
                answer.push_back(nextGreater[value]);
            } else {
                answer.push_back(-1);
            }
        }

        return answer;
    }
};
class Solution:
    def nextGreaterElement(self, nums1, nums2):
        next_greater = {}
        stack = []

        for value in nums2:
            while stack and stack[-1] < value:
                next_greater[stack.pop()] = value
            stack.append(value)

        return [next_greater.get(value, -1) for value in nums1]
Key observation: The stack stores values whose next greater element has not been found. When a larger value arrives, it resolves every smaller value on top of the stack until the monotonic order is restored.

Increasing vs Decreasing Stack

Next Greater: Maintain a decreasing stack so that a larger current value can pop smaller waiting values.
Next Smaller: Maintain an increasing stack so that a smaller current value can pop larger waiting values.

Circular Arrays

LC 503 extends the same next-greater idea to a circular array. The array is conceptually traversed twice so that elements near the beginning can find greater values near the end.

Common Mistakes

  • Using a nested loop and losing the O(n) advantage of the monotonic stack.
  • Choosing the wrong stack direction for greater versus smaller queries.
  • Storing values when indices are needed to update answers at specific positions.
  • Forgetting to resolve all possible stack elements before pushing the current value.
  • Assuming every remaining stack element has an answer; unresolved elements should keep the default value.

Complexity

Time

O(n)

Every element is pushed once and popped at most once, so the total number of stack operations is linear.

Space

O(n)

In the worst case, the stack can contain every element.

Pattern Progression

LC 496 — Next Greater Element I → Learn the basic monotonic stack.
LC 739 — Daily Temperatures → Reinforce waiting for the next greater value.
LC 503 — Next Greater Element II → Extend the pattern to circular arrays.

Mental Trigger

“For each element, I need the nearest greater or smaller element.”
If repeated forward/backward scanning is involved, think Monotonic Stack.

STACK PATTERN

Stack for Expression Evaluation

Stack-based Expression Evaluation is used when an expression must be processed while respecting operands, operators, parentheses, and evaluation order. A stack provides a natural way to store values and resolve operations when the required operands are available.

Pattern Overview

Expressions contain two main kinds of information: operands such as numbers and operators such as +, -, *, and /. A stack can temporarily store operands until an operator is ready to combine them.

Core idea: Read the expression according to its format. Push operands onto the stack. When an operator is encountered, pop the required operands, apply the operator in the correct order, and push the result back.

Mental Model

N

Operand

Numbers are stored until an operator needs them.

stack.push(number)
O

Operator

An operator consumes operands from the stack.

b = pop(), a = pop()
R

Result

The calculated result is pushed back for later operations.

stack.push(a op b)

Recognition Clues

ExpressionThe input represents a mathematical expression.
CalculatorNumbers and operators must be evaluated according to rules.
Reverse PolishOperators appear after their operands and can be evaluated directly with a stack.

How the Pattern Works

  • Read the expression in its required order.
  • When an operand is encountered, push it onto the operand stack.
  • When an operator is encountered, pop the required operands.
  • Apply the operator carefully, preserving operand order for subtraction and division.
  • Push the calculated result back onto the stack.
  • After the expression is completely processed, the remaining value is the final result.

Template — Operand & Operator Stack

Expression Evaluation Template
Stack<Integer> operands = new Stack<>();

for (String token : tokens) {
    if (isNumber(token)) {
        operands.push(Integer.parseInt(token));
    } else {
        int right = operands.pop();
        int left = operands.pop();
        int result = apply(left, right, token);
        operands.push(result);
    }
}

int answer = operands.pop();
stack<int> operands;

for (string token : tokens) {
    if (isNumber(token)) {
        operands.push(stoi(token));
    } else {
        int right = operands.top();
        operands.pop();
        int left = operands.top();
        operands.pop();

        int result = apply(left, right, token);
        operands.push(result);
    }
}

int answer = operands.top();
operands = []

for token in tokens:
    if is_number(token):
        operands.append(int(token))
    else:
        right = operands.pop()
        left = operands.pop()
        result = apply(left, right, token)
        operands.append(result)

answer = operands.pop()

Practical Example — LC 150: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation

Question: Given an array of tokens representing an arithmetic expression in Reverse Polish Notation, evaluate the expression and return the integer result.

How to read it: In Reverse Polish Notation, an operator appears after the operands it needs. For example, ["2", "1", "+", "3", "*"] represents (2 + 1) * 3. This makes stack evaluation natural because every operator can immediately consume the most recent operands.

Why Stack fits: Read 2 and 1 → push both. Read + → pop 1 and 2, calculate 2 + 1 = 3, then push 3. Read 3 → push it. Read * → calculate 3 * 3 = 9.
21+3*→9
LC 150 — Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation Solution
class Solution {
    public int evalRPN(String[] tokens) {
        Stack<Integer> stack = new Stack<>();

        for (String token : tokens) {
            if (token.equals("+") || token.equals("-") ||
                token.equals("*") || token.equals("/")) {

                int right = stack.pop();
                int left = stack.pop();
                int result;

                if (token.equals("+")) {
                    result = left + right;
                } else if (token.equals("-")) {
                    result = left - right;
                } else if (token.equals("*")) {
                    result = left * right;
                } else {
                    result = left / right;
                }

                stack.push(result);
            } else {
                stack.push(Integer.parseInt(token));
            }
        }

        return stack.pop();
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    int evalRPN(vector<string>& tokens) {
        stack<int> stack;

        for (string token : tokens) {
            if (token == "+" || token == "-" ||
                token == "*" || token == "/") {

                int right = stack.top();
                stack.pop();
                int left = stack.top();
                stack.pop();

                if (token == "+") {
                    stack.push(left + right);
                } else if (token == "-") {
                    stack.push(left - right);
                } else if (token == "*") {
                    stack.push(left * right);
                } else {
                    stack.push(left / right);
                }
            } else {
                stack.push(stoi(token));
            }
        }

        return stack.top();
    }
};
class Solution:
    def evalRPN(self, tokens):
        stack = []

        for token in tokens:
            if token in '+-*/':
                right = stack.pop()
                left = stack.pop()

                if token == '+':
                    result = left + right
                elif token == '-':
                    result = left - right
                elif token == '*':
                    result = left * right
                else:
                    result = int(left / right)

                stack.append(result)
            else:
                stack.append(int(token))

        return stack.pop()
Key observation: For an operator, the first value popped is the right operand and the second value popped is the left operand. This matters for subtraction and division.

Parentheses and Parsing

LC 224 extends expression evaluation to infix expressions containing parentheses. The stack can be used to preserve intermediate values and signs while parsing the expression from left to right.

Operator Precedence

LC 227 adds multiplication and division precedence over addition and subtraction. The same stack-based idea is extended so that higher-precedence operations are resolved before lower-precedence ones.

Common Mistakes

  • Reversing the left and right operands after popping them from the stack.
  • Applying operators in the wrong order.
  • Ignoring operator precedence when evaluating infix expressions.
  • Forgetting to convert numeric tokens from strings into numbers.
  • Trying to evaluate the entire expression without maintaining intermediate results.

Complexity

Time

O(n)

Each token is processed once, with constant-time stack operations.

Space

O(n)

In the worst case, the operand stack can contain a linear number of values.

Pattern Progression

LC 150 — Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation → Learn basic stack-based expression evaluation.
LC 224 — Basic Calculator → Reinforce parsing with parentheses.
LC 227 — Basic Calculator II → Extend the pattern to operator precedence.

Mental Trigger

“Operators need operands, and the most recently available operands should be combined first.”
When expression evaluation requires temporary values and controlled evaluation order, think Stack.

STACK PATTERN

Stack + Simulation

Stack + Simulation is a pattern where a stack is used to process a sequence while simulating actions such as removal, undo, collision, or string transformation. The stack represents the current state after processing everything seen so far.

Pattern Overview

Instead of solving the entire sequence at once, process elements from left to right and let the stack represent the current result. When the current element causes an action such as removal or collision, modify the stack before continuing.

Core idea: Treat the stack as the current state of the simulation. Push when an element survives, and pop when the current element causes the previous element to be removed or changed.

Mental Model

+

Push

Add the current element when it survives the simulation.

stack.push(current)
−

Remove

Pop the previous element when the current element cancels or removes it.

stack.pop()
S

State

The stack always represents the processed result so far.

stack = current state

Recognition Clues

UndoA recent action needs to be reversed.
RemoveProcessing one element can eliminate a previous element.
SimulationThe problem asks you to repeatedly apply rules to a sequence.

How the Pattern Works

  • Process the input from left to right.
  • Use the stack to represent the current state of the processed elements.
  • Check whether the current element interacts with the stack top.
  • If the simulation rule removes the top element, pop it.
  • If the current element survives, push it onto the stack.
  • After processing the entire input, the stack contains the final simulated result.

Template — Stack Simulation

Process and Modify Current State
Stack<Character> stack = new Stack<>();

for (char current : input.toCharArray()) {
    if (!stack.isEmpty() && shouldRemove(stack.peek(), current)) {
        stack.pop();
    } else {
        stack.push(current);
    }
}
stack<char> stack;

for (char current : input) {
    if (!stack.empty() && shouldRemove(stack.top(), current)) {
        stack.pop();
    } else {
        stack.push(current);
    }
}
stack = []

for current in input:
    if stack and should_remove(stack[-1], current):
        stack.pop()
    else:
        stack.append(current)

Practical Example — LC 1047: Remove All Adjacent Duplicates In String

Question: Given a string, repeatedly remove adjacent equal characters until no adjacent duplicates remain. Return the final string.

How to read it: The important clues are remove and adjacent duplicates. When the current character is equal to the most recently kept character, those two characters cancel each other. A stack naturally stores the current result.

Why Stack fits: For abbaca, process each character. Push a, then b. The next b matches the stack top, so both are removed. Continue with a, then c, then a. The final result is ca.
abbaca→ca
LC 1047 — Remove All Adjacent Duplicates Solution
class Solution {
    public String removeDuplicates(String s) {
        Stack<Character> stack = new Stack<>();

        for (char current : s.toCharArray()) {
            if (!stack.isEmpty() && stack.peek() == current) {
                stack.pop();
            } else {
                stack.push(current);
            }
        }

        StringBuilder result = new StringBuilder();

        for (char current : stack) {
            result.append(current);
        }

        return result.toString();
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    string removeDuplicates(string s) {
        string stack;

        for (char current : s) {
            if (!stack.empty() && stack.back() == current) {
                stack.pop_back();
            } else {
                stack.push_back(current);
            }
        }

        return stack;
    }
};
class Solution:
    def removeDuplicates(self, s):
        stack = []

        for current in s:
            if stack and stack[-1] == current:
                stack.pop()
            else:
                stack.append(current)

        return ''.join(stack)
Key observation: The stack is not just storing elements. It is the simulated final string after processing the prefix seen so far. A duplicate with the stack top cancels both characters immediately.

Backspace Simulation

LC 844 applies the same idea to backspaces. A normal character is pushed into the current state, while a backspace removes the most recently stored character when one exists. Two strings can then be compared after applying the same simulation.

Collision Simulation

LC 735 extends the pattern to interacting objects. The current asteroid can repeatedly collide with the stack top while the collision rules allow it. This is the same stack-state idea, but the simulation may require multiple pops before the current object can be pushed.

Common Mistakes

  • Modifying the input directly when a stack can represent the evolving state more clearly.
  • Forgetting to check whether the stack is empty before accessing its top element.
  • Only checking one previous element when the simulation rule can cause repeated removals.
  • Confusing the stack with the original input; the stack represents the processed state.
  • Forgetting that a removal can expose a new interaction with the next element.

Complexity

Time

O(n)

Each element is pushed and can be popped at most once for the basic stack-simulation pattern.

Space

O(n)

In the worst case, the stack can contain every processed element.

Pattern Progression

LC 1047 — Remove All Adjacent Duplicates → Learn basic stack-based simulation.
LC 844 — Backspace String Compare → Reinforce character deletion and state reconstruction.
LC 735 — Asteroid Collision → Extend the pattern to repeated collision simulation.

Mental Trigger

“Can processing the current element undo, remove, or interact with the most recent surviving element?”
If yes, think Stack + Simulation.

QUEUE PATTERN

Queue Simulation

Queue Simulation is a pattern for processing elements in First In, First Out order. It is useful when requests, people, tickets, or tasks must be handled in the same order they arrive.

Pattern Overview

A queue always processes the element that has been waiting the longest. New elements are added at the back, while processing happens from the front. This makes a queue a natural model for real-world waiting lines and cyclic processing.

Core idea: Enqueue new elements at the back and dequeue elements from the front. The order of processing follows FIFO — First In, First Out.

Mental Model

+

Enqueue

Add a new element to the back of the queue.

queue.offer(current)
→

Dequeue

Process and remove the element at the front.

queue.poll()
F

FIFO

The earliest element added is the first one processed.

front → oldest

Recognition Clues

QueueThe problem explicitly describes a waiting line or queue.
Recent RequestItems arrive over time and only recent items may remain relevant.
Ticket / RotationPeople or tasks are processed in arrival order, sometimes repeatedly.

How the Pattern Works

  • Create a queue to store elements in arrival order.
  • Add new elements to the back of the queue.
  • Process elements from the front of the queue.
  • Remove an element after it has been processed when the simulation requires it.
  • For cyclic simulations, process the front element and place it back at the rear when it still needs more processing.
  • Continue until the required condition is reached.

Template — Queue Simulation

FIFO Queue Template
ArrayDeque<Integer> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();

for (int value : values) {
    queue.offer(value);
}

while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
    int current = queue.poll();

    if (needsMoreProcessing(current)) {
        queue.offer(current);
    } else {
        process(current);
    }
}
queue<int> queue;

for (int value : values) {
    queue.push(value);
}

while (!queue.empty()) {
    int current = queue.front();
    queue.pop();

    if (needsMoreProcessing(current)) {
        queue.push(current);
    } else {
        process(current);
    }
}
from collections import deque

queue = deque(values)

while queue:
    current = queue.popleft()

    if needs_more_processing(current):
        queue.append(current)
    else:
        process(current)

Practical Example — LC 933: Number of Recent Calls

Question: Given a sequence of ping requests arriving at different times, return the number of requests that have happened during the most recent 3000 milliseconds, including the current request.

How to read it: Requests arrive in increasing time order. For every new request, older requests may become too old to count. Because requests leave the valid time range from the oldest side first, a FIFO queue naturally fits.

Why Queue fits: Store every request time in arrival order. When a new request arrives at time t, add it to the back. Then remove times from the front while they are older than t - 3000. The remaining queue contains exactly the recent requests.
t = 3001→[1][100][3001]→2 recent requests
LC 933 — Number of Recent Calls Solution
class RecentCounter {
    private ArrayDeque<Integer> queue;

    public RecentCounter() {
        queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
    }

    public int ping(int t) {
        queue.offer(t);

        while (queue.peek() < t - 3000) {
            queue.poll();
        }

        return queue.size();
    }
}
class RecentCounter {
private:
    queue<int> queue;

public:
    RecentCounter() {}

    int ping(int t) {
        queue.push(t);

        while (queue.front() < t - 3000) {
            queue.pop();
        }

        return queue.size();
    }
};
from collections import deque

class RecentCounter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.queue = deque()

    def ping(self, t):
        self.queue.append(t)

        while self.queue[0] < t - 3000:
            self.queue.popleft()

        return len(self.queue)
Key observation: The request times are already ordered. Once the oldest request is outside the valid window, it can never become valid again. Therefore, removing outdated requests from the front is enough.

Cyclic Queue Processing

LC 1700 and LC 2073 extend the queue idea beyond simple FIFO removal. In cyclic simulations, the front element may be processed and then moved back to the rear if it still has work remaining. The queue therefore represents the current order of participants.

Common Mistakes

  • Using a stack when the problem requires First In, First Out ordering.
  • Removing elements from the wrong end of the queue.
  • Forgetting to reinsert an element at the back during cyclic processing when it still needs work.
  • Checking only the newest element when outdated elements must be removed from the front.
  • Using an inefficient structure where removing from the front costs O(n).

Complexity

Time

O(n)

Each request is added once and removed from the queue at most once in the recent-request pattern.

Space

O(n)

The queue can contain all currently relevant requests or participants.

Pattern Progression

LC 933 — Number of Recent Calls → Learn basic FIFO queue operations and removing outdated requests.
LC 1700 — Number of Students Unable to Eat Lunch → Reinforce queue simulation.
LC 2073 — Time Needed to Buy Tickets → Extend the pattern to cyclic queue processing.

Mental Trigger

“The oldest waiting item must be processed first.”
If the problem describes a waiting line, recent requests, tickets, or repeated rotation in arrival order, think Queue.

MONOTONIC DEQUE PATTERN

Monotonic Deque

A Monotonic Deque keeps useful candidates ordered so that the maximum or minimum of a sliding window can be found efficiently without repeatedly scanning the entire window.

Pattern Overview

The key idea is to maintain a deque of indices whose values are kept in monotonic order. Elements that can no longer become the answer are removed immediately, so the front of the deque always represents the current maximum or minimum candidate.

Core idea: Maintain candidates in a deque → remove expired indices → remove dominated values → the front gives the window answer.

Mental Model

01

Store Indices

Keep indices rather than only values so we can detect when an element leaves the window.

02

Remove Expired

If the front index is outside the current window, remove it.

03

Remove Dominated

For a maximum, remove smaller values from the back because they can never become useful while the larger value remains.

Recognition Clues

Sliding Window MaximumFind the largest value in every fixed-size window.
Sliding Window MinimumFind the smallest value in every fixed-size window.
Window OptimizationA repeated max/min scan makes the solution too slow.

How the Pattern Works

  • For a maximum, maintain values in decreasing order from front to back.
  • For a minimum, maintain values in increasing order from front to back.
  • Store indices so expired elements can be removed.
  • Before adding the current index, remove expired indices from the front.
  • Remove dominated candidates from the back.
  • The front of the deque is the answer for the current window.

Practical Example — LC 239: Sliding Window Maximum

Question: Given an array and a window size k, return the maximum value in every contiguous window of size k.

How to read the problem: We need the maximum of every sliding window. A normal scan of all k elements for every window can take O(nk). The window moves one position at a time, so we should preserve only the candidates that can still become the maximum.

Why Monotonic Deque fits: When a larger value enters the window, smaller values behind it can never become the maximum before the larger value leaves. Therefore, we can remove those smaller candidates immediately.
nums = [1,3,-1,-3,5,3,6,7], k = 3 → output = [3,3,5,5,6,7]

Step-by-step idea: For each index, first remove indices outside the current window. Then remove smaller values from the back because they are dominated by the current value. After that, the front index points to the largest value in the current window.

Solution — Java
class Solution {
    public int[] maxSlidingWindow(int[] nums, int k) {
        int n = nums.length;
        int[] result = new int[n - k + 1];
        Deque<Integer> deque = new ArrayDeque<>();
        int resultIndex = 0;

        for (int currentIndex = 0; currentIndex < n; currentIndex++) {
            while (!deque.isEmpty() && deque.peekFirst() <= currentIndex - k) {
                deque.pollFirst();
            }

            while (!deque.isEmpty() && nums[deque.peekLast()] <= nums[currentIndex]) {
                deque.pollLast();
            }

            deque.offerLast(currentIndex);

            if (currentIndex >= k - 1) {
                result[resultIndex++] = nums[deque.peekFirst()];
            }
        }

        return result;
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    vector<int> maxSlidingWindow(vector<int>& nums, int k) {
        deque<int> deque;
        vector<int> result;

        for (int currentIndex = 0; currentIndex < nums.size(); currentIndex++) {
            while (!deque.empty() && deque.front() <= currentIndex - k) {
                deque.pop_front();
            }

            while (!deque.empty() && nums[deque.back()] <= nums[currentIndex]) {
                deque.pop_back();
            }

            deque.push_back(currentIndex);

            if (currentIndex >= k - 1) {
                result.push_back(nums[deque.front()]);
            }
        }

        return result;
    }
};
from collections import deque

class Solution:
    def maxSlidingWindow(self, nums, k):
        candidate_indices = deque()
        result = []

        for current_index in range(len(nums)):
            while candidate_indices and candidate_indices[0] <= current_index - k:
                candidate_indices.popleft()

            while candidate_indices and nums[candidate_indices[-1]] <= nums[current_index]:
                candidate_indices.pop()

            candidate_indices.append(current_index)

            if current_index >= k - 1:
                result.append(nums[candidate_indices[0]])

        return result

Why this is O(n): Every index enters the deque once and can leave the deque at most once from the front or back. Therefore, although there are nested while-loops, the total number of deque operations across the entire array is linear.

Common Mistakes

  • Storing values instead of indices, making expiration difficult to detect.
  • Forgetting to remove indices that are outside the current window.
  • Keeping dominated values that can never become the answer.
  • Using increasing order when solving a maximum problem, or decreasing order when solving a minimum problem.

Complexity

Time

O(n) — every index is added and removed at most once.

Space

O(k) — the deque contains candidates from the current window.

Pattern Progression

LC 239 → LC 862 → LC 1438
Start with Sliding Window Maximum to learn the monotonic deque, then extend the idea to prefix sums and finally to maintaining both maximum and minimum efficiently.

Mental Trigger

When you see sliding window + repeated maximum/minimum + need better than O(nk), think: Monotonic Deque.
