QUEUE DESIGN PATTERN

Circular Queue / Deque Design

A Circular Queue reuses freed positions by wrapping the rear and front indices around the underlying array. The same circular indexing idea can be extended to support insertion and deletion from both ends in a Circular Deque.

Pattern Overview

The key idea is to treat a fixed-size array as circular. When an index reaches the end of the array, it wraps back to index 0 instead of stopping.

Core idea: Use modular indexing to wrap front and rear around the array so previously freed positions can be reused.

Mental Model

01

Fixed Capacity

The queue has a fixed number of available positions.

02

Wrap Around

When an index reaches the last position, it moves back to the beginning.

03

Track State

Maintain enough state to distinguish an empty queue from a full queue.

Recognition Clues

CircularThe structure should reuse positions by wrapping around.
Fixed BufferA fixed-size array stores elements while old positions become available again.
Queue / Deque DesignYou are asked to implement queue operations rather than solve a traversal problem.

How the Pattern Works

  • Maintain a fixed-size array as the underlying storage.
  • Track the front position and the number of stored elements.
  • Calculate the next position using modulo capacity.
  • For enqueue, insert at the rear position and advance it circularly.
  • For dequeue, remove from the front position and advance it circularly.
  • The same indexing principle can be extended to insert and delete from both ends for a deque.
front → [ A ][ B ][ C ][ _ ][ _ ] ← rear
After wrap-around → [ F ][ _ ][ C ][ D ][ E ]

Practical Example — LC 622: Design Circular Queue

Question: Design a circular queue with a fixed capacity that supports enqueue, dequeue, checking the front and rear values, and determining whether the queue is empty or full.

How to read the problem: The important clue is circular. A normal array queue can waste positions after elements are removed from the front. Instead of shifting elements, we move the rear and front positions circularly and reuse those freed positions.

Why Circular Queue fits: We only need to move two logical positions. The expression (index + 1) % capacity makes the array behave like a circle.

Example: With capacity 3, enqueue 10, 20, 30. After removing 10, the front moves forward. The next enqueue can wrap around and reuse the freed position instead of requiring the existing elements to be shifted.

Solution — Java
class MyCircularQueue {
    private int[] queue;
    private int front;
    private int rear;
    private int size;
    private int capacity;

    public MyCircularQueue(int k) {
        queue = new int[k];
        capacity = k;
        front = 0;
        rear = 0;
        size = 0;
    }

    public boolean enQueue(int value) {
        if (isFull()) return false;

        queue[rear] = value;
        rear = (rear + 1) % capacity;
        size++;
        return true;
    }

    public boolean deQueue() {
        if (isEmpty()) return false;

        front = (front + 1) % capacity;
        size--;
        return true;
    }

    public int Front() {
        return isEmpty() ? -1 : queue[front];
    }

    public int Rear() {
        if (isEmpty()) return -1;
        return queue[(rear - 1 + capacity) % capacity];
    }

    public boolean isEmpty() {
        return size == 0;
    }

    public boolean isFull() {
        return size == capacity;
    }
}
class MyCircularQueue {
private:
    vector<int> queue;
    int front;
    int rear;
    int size;
    int capacity;

public:
    MyCircularQueue(int k) {
        queue.resize(k);
        capacity = k;
        front = 0;
        rear = 0;
        size = 0;
    }

    bool enQueue(int value) {
        if (isFull()) return false;

        queue[rear] = value;
        rear = (rear + 1) % capacity;
        size++;
        return true;
    }

    bool deQueue() {
        if (isEmpty()) return false;

        front = (front + 1) % capacity;
        size--;
        return true;
    }

    int Front() {
        return isEmpty() ? -1 : queue[front];
    }

    int Rear() {
        if (isEmpty()) return -1;
        return queue[(rear - 1 + capacity) % capacity];
    }

    bool isEmpty() {
        return size == 0;
    }

    bool isFull() {
        return size == capacity;
    }
};
class MyCircularQueue:
    def __init__(self, k):
        self.queue = [0] * k
        self.capacity = k
        self.front = 0
        self.rear = 0
        self.size = 0

    def enQueue(self, value):
        if self.isFull():
            return False

        self.queue[self.rear] = value
        self.rear = (self.rear + 1) % self.capacity
        self.size += 1
        return True

    def deQueue(self):
        if self.isEmpty():
            return False

        self.front = (self.front + 1) % self.capacity
        self.size -= 1
        return True

    def Front(self):
        return -1 if self.isEmpty() else self.queue[self.front]

    def Rear(self):
        if self.isEmpty():
            return -1
        return self.queue[(self.rear - 1 + self.capacity) % self.capacity]

    def isEmpty(self):
        return self.size == 0

    def isFull(self):
        return self.size == self.capacity

Why this works: rear always points to the next insertion position, while front points to the current first element. The size variable tells us whether the queue is empty or full. Modulo arithmetic makes both positions wrap around without shifting elements.

Extension — Circular Deque

LC 641: Once circular indexing is understood, the same idea can support insertion and deletion at both the front and rear. The core concept does not change — only the number of operations and boundary cases increase.

Common Mistakes

  • Shifting all elements after every dequeue, which defeats the purpose of the circular structure.
  • Forgetting to wrap an index using modulo capacity.
  • Confusing the rear element with the next insertion position.
  • Failing to distinguish the full and empty states.
  • Using negative modulo incorrectly when calculating the previous circular position.

Complexity

Time

O(1) per queue operation because front and rear are moved directly.

Space

O(k) for the fixed-size underlying array.

Pattern Progression

LC 622 → LC 641
Start with Circular Queue to understand circular indexing, then extend the same design to a Circular Deque with operations at both ends.

Mental Trigger

When you see fixed-size queue + reuse freed positions + circular/wrap-around behavior, think: Circular Queue / Deque Design.

learning.html:
LINKED LIST PATTERN

Linked List Traversal & Dummy Node

Linked List problems are mainly about controlled pointer movement. A dummy node gives us a stable node before the real head, making insertion, deletion, and traversal easier to handle without special-casing the first node.

Pattern Overview

The core skill is moving a pointer through the list while keeping track of the node or nodes needed to modify links safely. A dummy node is especially useful when the head itself may be deleted or changed.

Core idea: Use a pointer to traverse the list, preserve the links you still need, and use a dummy node when the operation can affect the original head.

Mental Model

01

Traverse

Move a pointer from one node to the next until the required condition is reached.

02

Dummy Node

Place a temporary node before the head so the first real node can be handled like every other node.

03

Relink

Change next pointers carefully while preserving access to the remaining list.

Recognition Clues

Delete NodesRemove elements from a linked list, especially when the head may also be removed.
Insert NodesInsert a node before or after another node while maintaining the chain.
Pointer ManipulationThe problem requires changing or reconnecting next pointers.

How the Pattern Works

  • Create a dummy node pointing to the original head when the head may change.
  • Use a traversal pointer to inspect the current node or the next node.
  • For deletion, bypass the unwanted node by changing the previous node's next pointer.
  • For insertion, connect the new node between the appropriate neighboring nodes.
  • Always preserve the remaining list before changing pointers.
  • Return dummy.next when a dummy node is used.

Coding Template

Basic Linked List Traversal + Dummy Node
ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0);
dummy.next = head;
ListNode current = dummy;

while (current.next != null) {
    // inspect current.next
    // modify current.next when needed
    current = current.next;
}

return dummy.next;
ListNode dummy(0);
dummy.next = head;
ListNode* current = &dummy;

while (current->next != nullptr) {
    // inspect current->next
    // modify current->next when needed
    current = current->next;
}

return dummy.next;
dummy = ListNode(0)
dummy.next = head
current = dummy

while current.next:
    # inspect current.next
    # modify current.next when needed
    current = current.next

return dummy.next

Practical Example — LC 203: Remove Linked List Elements

Question: Given the head of a linked list and an integer val, remove every node whose value equals val and return the resulting list.

How to read the problem: We need to traverse the list and delete nodes. The important edge case is that the head itself may contain val. A dummy node removes that special case because every real node now has a previous node.

Why this pattern fits: We inspect current.next. If it should be removed, we bypass it with current.next = current.next.next. Otherwise, we advance current.
dummy → 1 → 2 → 6 → 3 → 6 → 4 → 5 → 6
remove 6 → dummy → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5
Solution — Java
class Solution {
    public ListNode removeElements(ListNode head, int val) {
        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0);
        dummy.next = head;
        ListNode current = dummy;

        while (current.next != null) {
            if (current.next.val == val) {
                current.next = current.next.next;
            } else {
                current = current.next;
            }
        }

        return dummy.next;
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    ListNode* removeElements(ListNode* head, int val) {
        ListNode dummy(0);
        dummy.next = head;
        ListNode* current = &dummy;

        while (current->next != nullptr) {
            if (current->next->val == val) {
                current->next = current->next->next;
            } else {
                current = current->next;
            }
        }

        return dummy.next;
    }
};
class Solution:
    def removeElements(self, head, val):
        dummy = ListNode(0)
        dummy.next = head
        current = dummy

        while current.next:
            if current.next.val == val:
                current.next = current.next.next
            else:
                current = current.next

        return dummy.next

Why this works: When current.next matches the target, we skip that node. We do not advance current after deletion because the new current.next must also be checked. If the value does not match, we move forward. The dummy node guarantees that deleting the original head follows exactly the same logic.

Important Pointer Rule

Before changing a link, make sure you still have access to the rest of the list. In linked-list problems, losing the reference to the next node can disconnect the remaining list.

Extensions

203

Remove Elements

Traversal + dummy node + deletion.

206

Reverse List

Pointer manipulation using previous, current, and next references.

21

Merge Lists

Dummy node + pointer manipulation while combining two sorted lists.

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting that the original head itself may need to be changed or deleted.
  • Advancing the pointer immediately after deleting a node and therefore skipping consecutive matches.
  • Changing a next pointer without preserving the remaining list.
  • Returning head instead of dummy.next when the head can change.

Complexity

Time

O(n) — each node is visited at most a constant number of times.

Space

O(1) extra space — only a constant number of pointers are used.

Pattern Progression

LC 203 → LC 206 → LC 21
Start with traversal and dummy-node deletion, then strengthen pointer manipulation with reversal, and finally apply the same ideas to merge two sorted lists.

Mental Trigger

When you see linked list + traversal + insertion/deletion + possible head change, think: Pointer Traversal + Dummy Node.

learning.html:
LINKED LIST PATTERN

Fast & Slow Pointer

Fast and slow pointers move through a linked list at different speeds. This lets us find the middle, detect cycles, split a list into halves, and support more advanced linked-list transformations without extra space.

Pattern Overview

The slow pointer moves one step while the fast pointer moves two steps. Their relative movement gives us information about the structure of the list.

Core idea: Slow moves 1 step → fast moves 2 steps → when fast reaches the end, slow reveals the middle or useful split point.

Mental Model

01

Slow Pointer

Moves one node at a time and tracks the middle or meeting position.

02

Fast Pointer

Moves two nodes at a time and reaches the end earlier.

03

Relative Speed

The difference in movement speed reveals structural information about the list.

Recognition Clues

MiddleFind the middle node without knowing the list length first.
CycleDetermine whether two traversal speeds eventually meet.
Half / SplitSplit a linked list into two parts using the middle position.

How the Pattern Works

  • Initialize both pointers at the head when appropriate.
  • Move slow one step at a time.
  • Move fast two steps at a time.
  • When fast reaches the end, slow is around the middle.
  • For cycle detection, if the list contains a cycle, the two pointers eventually meet.
  • The middle position can then be used to split, reverse, compare, or merge list sections.

Coding Template

Fast & Slow Pointer
ListNode slow = head;
ListNode fast = head;

while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
    slow = slow.next;
    fast = fast.next.next;
}

// slow is at the middle / split position
ListNode* slow = head;
ListNode* fast = head;

while (fast != nullptr && fast->next != nullptr) {
    slow = slow->next;
    fast = fast->next->next;
}

// slow is at the middle / split position
slow = head
fast = head

while fast and fast.next:
    slow = slow.next
    fast = fast.next.next

# slow is at the middle / split position

Practical Example — LC 876: Middle of the Linked List

Question: Given the head of a singly linked list, return the middle node. If there are two middle nodes, return the second middle node.

How to read the problem: We need the middle of a linked list, but we are not given its length. Counting the nodes first and then traversing again works, but fast and slow pointers find the middle in one traversal.

Why this pattern fits: Slow advances by one node while fast advances by two. When fast reaches the end, slow has covered roughly half the distance, so it points to the middle.
1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6
slow: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4
fast: 1 → 3 → 5 → end
Answer: 4
Solution — Java
class Solution {
    public ListNode middleNode(ListNode head) {
        ListNode slow = head;
        ListNode fast = head;

        while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
            slow = slow.next;
            fast = fast.next.next;
        }

        return slow;
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    ListNode* middleNode(ListNode* head) {
        ListNode* slow = head;
        ListNode* fast = head;

        while (fast != nullptr && fast->next != nullptr) {
            slow = slow->next;
            fast = fast->next->next;
        }

        return slow;
    }
};
class Solution:
    def middleNode(self, head):
        slow = head
        fast = head

        while fast and fast.next:
            slow = slow.next
            fast = fast.next.next

        return slow

Why this works: Every time slow moves one node, fast moves two. Therefore fast covers twice the distance of slow. When fast can no longer make another two-step move, slow has reached the required middle. Starting both at the head naturally returns the second middle for even-length lists.

Extensions

876

Find Middle

Use the relative speed difference to locate the middle node.

234

Palindrome List

Find the middle, reverse the second half, then compare both halves.

143

Reorder List

Find the middle, reverse the second half, then merge the two halves alternately.

Common Mistakes

  • Using the wrong loop condition and accessing fast.next.next when fast.next is null.
  • Choosing the wrong starting positions when a specific middle or split position is required.
  • Forgetting that even-length lists have two middle nodes and the required one depends on the problem.
  • Assuming fast and slow pointers are only for cycle detection; they are also useful for finding positions and splitting lists.

Complexity

Time

O(n) — the fast pointer traverses the list at most once.

Space

O(1) extra space — only a constant number of pointers are used.

Pattern Progression

LC 876 → LC 234 → LC 143
Start by finding the middle, then combine middle finding with reversing the second half, and finally combine middle finding, reversing, and merging.

Mental Trigger

When you see linked list + middle + cycle + half/split, think: Fast & Slow Pointer.

learning.html:
LINKED LIST PATTERN

Reverse in Groups

Reverse in Groups means reversing a connected segment of a linked list while carefully reconnecting that segment with the nodes before and after it. The same pointer-rewiring idea scales from a single sublist to groups of k nodes.

Pattern Overview

The core skill is reversing next pointers inside a selected segment while preserving the connections outside that segment. The boundaries of the segment must be identified before the reversal begins.

Core idea: Identify the segment → preserve its boundaries → reverse its pointers → reconnect the reversed segment to the rest of the list.

Mental Model

01

Find Boundaries

Identify the node before the segment and the node after the segment.

02

Reverse Segment

Reverse only the selected nodes by changing their next pointers.

03

Reconnect

Connect the previous part and remaining part back to the reversed segment.

Recognition Clues

Reverse BetweenReverse only a portion of a linked list between two positions.
Groups of KReverse nodes repeatedly in fixed-size groups.
Pointer RewiringThe main challenge is changing links while preserving the remaining list.

How the Pattern Works

  • Use a dummy node when the segment can begin at the original head.
  • Move a pointer to the node immediately before the segment.
  • Identify the first node and the node after the segment.
  • Reverse the selected segment using pointer manipulation.
  • Reconnect the node before the segment to the new segment head.
  • Reconnect the original segment head, which becomes the segment tail, to the remaining list.

Coding Template

Reverse a Linked List Segment
ListNode previous = null;
ListNode current = segmentStart;

while (current != segmentEnd) {
    ListNode next = current.next;
    current.next = previous;
    previous = current;
    current = next;
}

// previous = new segment head
// segmentStart = new segment tail
ListNode* previous = nullptr;
ListNode* current = segmentStart;

while (current != segmentEnd) {
    ListNode* next = current->next;
    current->next = previous;
    previous = current;
    current = next;
}

// previous = new segment head
// segmentStart = new segment tail
previous = None
current = segment_start

while current != segment_end:
    next_node = current.next
    current.next = previous
    previous = current
    current = next_node

# previous = new segment head
# segment_start = new segment tail

Practical Example — LC 92: Reverse Linked List II

Question: Given the head of a linked list and two positions left and right, reverse the nodes from position left to position right and return the modified list.

How to read the problem: We are not reversing the entire list. Only one continuous segment must be reversed. The important part is preserving the node before the segment and reconnecting it to the newly reversed segment.

Why this pattern fits: The problem gives an exact segment boundary. We can isolate that segment, reverse its pointers, and then reconnect both sides without changing the order of nodes outside the segment.
1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5
left = 2, right = 4
1 → 4 → 3 → 2 → 5
Solution — Java
class Solution {
    public ListNode reverseBetween(ListNode head, int left, int right) {
        if (head == null || left == right) return head;

        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0);
        dummy.next = head;
        ListNode segmentPrevious = dummy;

        for (int position = 1; position < left; position++) {
            segmentPrevious = segmentPrevious.next;
        }

        ListNode segmentStart = segmentPrevious.next;
        ListNode current = segmentStart;

        for (int position = left; position <= right; position++) {
            ListNode next = current.next;
            current.next = segmentPrevious;
            segmentPrevious = current;
            current = next;
        }

        ListNode segmentTail = segmentStart;
        ListNode afterSegment = current;

        // Reconnect the reversed segment with the remaining list.
        ListNode newSegmentHead = segmentPrevious;
        ListNode beforeSegment = dummy;

        for (int position = 1; position < left; position++) {
            beforeSegment = beforeSegment.next;
        }

        beforeSegment.next = newSegmentHead;
        segmentTail.next = afterSegment;

        return dummy.next;
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    ListNode* reverseBetween(ListNode* head, int left, int right) {
        if (head == nullptr || left == right) return head;

        ListNode dummy(0);
        dummy.next = head;
        ListNode* segmentPrevious = &dummy;

        for (int position = 1; position < left; position++) {
            segmentPrevious = segmentPrevious->next;
        }

        ListNode* segmentStart = segmentPrevious->next;
        ListNode* current = segmentStart;

        for (int position = left; position <= right; position++) {
            ListNode* next = current->next;
            current->next = segmentPrevious;
            segmentPrevious = current;
            current = next;
        }

        ListNode* newSegmentHead = segmentPrevious;
        ListNode* segmentTail = segmentStart;
        ListNode* beforeSegment = &dummy;

        for (int position = 1; position < left; position++) {
            beforeSegment = beforeSegment->next;
        }

        beforeSegment->next = newSegmentHead;
        segmentTail->next = current;

        return dummy.next;
    }
};
class Solution:
    def reverseBetween(self, head, left, right):
        if not head or left == right:
            return head

        dummy = ListNode(0)
        dummy.next = head
        segment_previous = dummy

        for _ in range(1, left):
            segment_previous = segment_previous.next

        segment_start = segment_previous.next
        current = segment_start

        for _ in range(left, right + 1):
            next_node = current.next
            current.next = segment_previous
            segment_previous = current
            current = next_node

        new_segment_head = segment_previous
        segment_tail = segment_start
        before_segment = dummy

        for _ in range(1, left):
            before_segment = before_segment.next

        before_segment.next = new_segment_head
        segment_tail.next = current

        return dummy.next

Why this works: The nodes from left through right are reversed one by one. The original first node of the segment becomes its tail, so it is connected to the node after the segment. The node before the segment is connected to the new segment head. The rest of the list keeps its original order.

Extensions

92

Reverse Between

Reverse one continuous segment between two positions.

24

Swap Pairs

Rewire adjacent nodes repeatedly, effectively reversing groups of two.

25

K-Group

Extend segment reversal to repeated groups of k nodes.

Common Mistakes

  • Losing the remaining list because the next pointer was not saved before reversal.
  • Forgetting to reconnect the node before the reversed segment.
  • Forgetting that the original segment start becomes the segment tail.
  • Reversing nodes outside the required segment.
  • Handling the head as a special case instead of using a dummy node.

Complexity

Time

O(n) — the list is traversed only a constant number of times.

Space

O(1) extra space — reversal uses only a constant number of pointers.

Pattern Progression

LC 92 → LC 24 → LC 25
Start with reversing one bounded segment, then reinforce pointer rewiring with pairs, and finally extend the same idea to repeated groups of k nodes.

Mental Trigger

When you see linked list + reverse a segment + groups / positions / k nodes, think: Reverse in Groups.

LINKED LIST PATTERN

Linked List Intersection & Cycle

This pattern uses pointer synchronization to reason about linked lists that share nodes or contain cycles. Instead of comparing every possible pair of nodes, pointers are moved in a coordinated way so that different path lengths are naturally equalized.

Pattern Overview

The core idea is to synchronize pointer movement. For intersection problems, pointers switch to the other list after reaching the end, causing both to travel the same total distance. For cycle problems, synchronized movement helps detect whether a cycle exists and locate its entry.

Core idea: Let pointers traverse equivalent total paths so that differences in starting positions or path lengths cancel out.

Mental Model

01

Shared Node

Two linked lists may eventually merge into the exact same node objects.

02

Synchronize

Move pointers in a way that removes the effect of different path lengths.

03

Detect / Locate

Pointer relationships reveal an intersection or the location of a cycle.

Recognition Clues

IntersectionTwo linked lists may share a common tail or node.
CycleThe list may eventually point back to an earlier node.
Shared NodeThe problem asks for the exact node where two paths meet.

How the Pattern Works

  • For intersection, start one pointer at each list head.
  • Move each pointer one node at a time.
  • When a pointer reaches the end of its list, redirect it to the other list's head.
  • Both pointers then travel the same combined distance.
  • If the lists intersect, the pointers eventually reference the same node.
  • For cycle problems, fast and slow pointers can first detect a meeting point, which can then be used to locate the cycle entry.

Coding Template

Pointer Synchronization
ListNode pointerA = headA;
ListNode pointerB = headB;

while (pointerA != pointerB) {
    pointerA = pointerA == null ? headB : pointerA.next;
    pointerB = pointerB == null ? headA : pointerB.next;
}

return pointerA;
ListNode* pointerA = headA;
ListNode* pointerB = headB;

while (pointerA != pointerB) {
    pointerA = pointerA == nullptr ? headB : pointerA->next;
    pointerB = pointerB == nullptr ? headA : pointerB->next;
}

return pointerA;
pointer_a = head_a
pointer_b = head_b

while pointer_a is not pointer_b:
    pointer_a = head_b if pointer_a is None else pointer_a.next
    pointer_b = head_a if pointer_b is None else pointer_b.next

return pointer_a

Practical Example — LC 160: Intersection of Two Linked Lists

Question: Given the heads of two singly linked lists, return the node at which the two lists intersect. If they do not intersect, return null.

How to read the problem: The important word is intersection. We are looking for the same node object, not merely two nodes containing the same value. The two lists can have different lengths before they merge.

Why this pattern fits: If pointer A finishes list A, send it to list B. If pointer B finishes list B, send it to list A. Each pointer therefore travels the length of both lists, so the extra distance of the longer prefix is automatically cancelled.
List A: 4 → 1 ↘
8 → 4 → 5
List B: 5 → 6 → 1 ↗
Intersection = node 8
Solution — Java
public class Solution {
    public ListNode getIntersectionNode(ListNode headA, ListNode headB) {
        ListNode pointerA = headA;
        ListNode pointerB = headB;

        while (pointerA != pointerB) {
            pointerA = pointerA == null ? headB : pointerA.next;
            pointerB = pointerB == null ? headA : pointerB.next;
        }

        return pointerA;
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    ListNode* getIntersectionNode(ListNode* headA, ListNode* headB) {
        ListNode* pointerA = headA;
        ListNode* pointerB = headB;

        while (pointerA != pointerB) {
            pointerA = pointerA == nullptr ? headB : pointerA->next;
            pointerB = pointerB == nullptr ? headA : pointerB->next;
        }

        return pointerA;
    }
};
class Solution:
    def getIntersectionNode(self, headA, headB):
        pointer_a = headA
        pointer_b = headB

        while pointer_a is not pointer_b:
            pointer_a = headB if pointer_a is None else pointer_a.next
            pointer_b = headA if pointer_b is None else pointer_b.next

        return pointer_a

Why this works: Suppose list A has a longer unique prefix than list B. Pointer A initially travels that extra distance, but after reaching the end it switches to B. Pointer B switches to A after reaching the end of B. After both switches, each pointer has traveled the total length of both lists before reaching the shared section at the same time. If there is no intersection, both eventually become null together.

Extensions

160

Intersection

Synchronize two pointers by switching heads after reaching the opposite list's end.

141

Cycle Detection

Use synchronized fast and slow movement to determine whether a cycle exists.

142

Cycle Entry

After detecting a meeting point, synchronize pointers again to locate the cycle start.

Common Mistakes

  • Comparing node values instead of comparing node references.
  • Forgetting to switch a pointer to the other list after reaching the end.
  • Assuming two nodes with the same value represent an intersection.
  • Confusing cycle detection with finding the cycle entry point.
  • Using extra sets when pointer synchronization can solve the problem in O(1) extra space.

Complexity

Time

O(n + m) — each pointer traverses at most both lists.

Space

O(1) extra space — only a constant number of pointers are used.

Pattern Progression

LC 160 → LC 141 → LC 142
Start with pointer synchronization for shared nodes, then detect cycles, and finally extend the idea to locate the cycle entry point.

Mental Trigger

When you see linked lists + intersection / shared node / cycle start, think: Pointer Synchronization.

HEAP PATTERN

Top K Elements

The Top K pattern uses a heap to keep only the most important K elements instead of sorting or processing every element repeatedly. The same idea works for K largest, K smallest, most frequent, and dynamically arriving elements.

Pattern Overview

The key idea is to maintain a heap containing only the K elements that currently matter. For K largest elements, a min heap is useful because the smallest element among the current top K stays at the root and can be removed when a larger candidate arrives.

Core idea: Keep only K candidates → use the heap root as the weakest candidate → replace it when a better candidate appears.

Mental Model

01

Choose K

Only the best K elements need to remain in the heap.

02

Track the Boundary

The heap root represents the weakest element currently inside the top K.

03

Replace

When a stronger candidate appears, remove the weakest and insert the new candidate.

Recognition Clues

Top K / K LargestFind only the K largest elements instead of fully sorting the input.
K SmallestKeep the K smallest candidates using the opposite heap strategy.
FrequentCombine frequency counting with a heap when the most frequent K elements are required.

How the Pattern Works

  • Choose the heap type based on what you want to keep.
  • For K largest elements, maintain a min heap of size K.
  • Add each candidate to the heap.
  • If the heap grows beyond K, remove its root.
  • The heap now contains the best K candidates seen so far.
  • For K smallest elements, reverse the heap strategy and use a max heap.

Coding Template

Top K — K Largest with Min Heap
PriorityQueue<Integer> minHeap = new PriorityQueue<>();

for (int value : values) {
    minHeap.offer(value);

    if (minHeap.size() > k) {
        minHeap.poll();
    }
}

// minHeap contains the K largest elements
priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>> minHeap;

for (int value : values) {
    minHeap.push(value);

    if (minHeap.size() > k) {
        minHeap.pop();
    }
}

// minHeap contains the K largest elements
import heapq

min_heap = []

for value in values:
    heapq.heappush(min_heap, value)

    if len(min_heap) > k:
        heapq.heappop(min_heap)

# min_heap contains the K largest elements

Practical Example — LC 215: Kth Largest Element in an Array

Question: Given an unsorted array, return the Kth largest element. The element is defined by its position in sorted order, not by distinct values.

How to read the problem: We do not need the entire array sorted. We only need enough information to know which element belongs at position K from the largest side. A min heap of size K keeps exactly the K largest elements seen so far, and its root becomes the Kth largest.

Why this pattern fits: The heap never needs to contain more than K elements. Whenever a new value enters the top K, the smallest value currently inside the heap is removed. At the end, the root is the Kth largest element.
nums = [3,2,1,5,6,4], k = 2
Keep top 2 → [5,6]
Answer = heap root = 5
Solution — Java
class Solution {
    public int findKthLargest(int[] nums, int k) {
        PriorityQueue<Integer> minHeap = new PriorityQueue<>();

        for (int value : nums) {
            minHeap.offer(value);

            if (minHeap.size() > k) {
                minHeap.poll();
            }
        }

        return minHeap.peek();
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    int findKthLargest(vector<int>& nums, int k) {
        priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>> minHeap;

        for (int value : nums) {
            minHeap.push(value);

            if (minHeap.size() > k) {
                minHeap.pop();
            }
        }

        return minHeap.top();
    }
};
import heapq

class Solution:
    def findKthLargest(self, nums, k):
        min_heap = []

        for value in nums:
            heapq.heappush(min_heap, value)

            if len(min_heap) > k:
                heapq.heappop(min_heap)

        return min_heap[0]

Why this works: The heap contains the K largest values encountered so far. If there are more than K values, removing the smallest one ensures that only the strongest K remain. Therefore, after processing the entire array, the smallest value inside the heap is exactly the Kth largest value overall.

Extensions

215

Kth Largest

Maintain a min heap of size K.

703

Kth Largest Stream

Keep the same bounded heap while new values arrive dynamically.

347

Top K Frequent

Count frequencies first, then use a heap to retain the K strongest frequency candidates.

Common Mistakes

  • Using a max heap when a min heap of size K is the simpler choice for K largest elements.
  • Keeping more than K elements in the heap.
  • Confusing Kth largest with the Kth distinct largest element.
  • Fully sorting the array when only K elements are required and a heap is more appropriate.
  • Forgetting that the heap root represents the weakest element among the current top K.

Complexity

Time

O(n log k) — each of the n elements is inserted and may cause one heap removal, with heap size limited to k.

Space

O(k) — the heap stores at most K elements.

Pattern Progression

LC 215 → LC 703 → LC 347
Start with a bounded heap for Kth largest, then maintain it dynamically in a stream, and finally combine frequency counting with the same Top K idea.

Mental Trigger

When you see Top K + largest / smallest / frequent, think: Heap of K Candidates.

HEAP PATTERN

Merge Multiple Sorted Collections

When multiple collections are already sorted, a Min Heap lets us repeatedly select the smallest available element across all collections without scanning every collection each time.

Pattern Overview

The key idea is to put the current smallest element from every sorted collection into a Min Heap. The heap tells us which collection currently has the globally smallest available element. After removing it, we insert the next element from that same collection.

Core idea: Put one candidate from each sorted source into a Min Heap → extract the smallest → advance only that source → repeat.

Mental Model

01

One Candidate

Keep the current smallest available element from each sorted collection.

02

Global Minimum

The heap root is the smallest element across all current candidates.

03

Advance Source

After extracting a value, add the next value from the same collection.

Recognition Clues

Merge KMultiple sorted arrays, lists, or streams must be combined.
Smallest ElementRepeatedly find the smallest available value across several sorted sources.
Sorted SourcesEach individual collection is already sorted, so only one new candidate is needed after each extraction.

How the Pattern Works

  • Insert the first element from every non-empty sorted collection into a Min Heap.
  • Each heap entry should remember which collection produced the value and where that value came from.
  • Remove the smallest heap entry.
  • Add that value to the merged result.
  • Advance to the next element in the same collection and insert it into the heap.
  • Continue until the heap becomes empty.

Coding Template

Merge Multiple Sorted Sources
PriorityQueue<Entry> minHeap = new PriorityQueue<>();

// Add the first element from every sorted source.
for (int sourceIndex = 0; sourceIndex < sources.length; sourceIndex++) {
    if (!sources[sourceIndex].isEmpty()) {
        minHeap.offer(new Entry(sources[sourceIndex].get(0), sourceIndex, 0));
    }
}

while (!minHeap.isEmpty()) {
    Entry current = minHeap.poll();

    // Use current.value

    int nextIndex = current.elementIndex + 1;
    if (nextIndex < sources[current.sourceIndex].size()) {
        minHeap.offer(new Entry(
            sources[current.sourceIndex].get(nextIndex),
            current.sourceIndex,
            nextIndex
        ));
    }
}
priority_queue<Entry, vector<Entry>, greater<Entry>> minHeap;

// Add the first element from every sorted source.
for (int sourceIndex = 0; sourceIndex < sources.size(); sourceIndex++) {
    if (!sources[sourceIndex].empty()) {
        minHeap.push({sources[sourceIndex][0], sourceIndex, 0});
    }
}

while (!minHeap.empty()) {
    Entry current = minHeap.top();
    minHeap.pop();

    // Use current.value

    int nextIndex = current.elementIndex + 1;
    if (nextIndex < sources[current.sourceIndex].size()) {
        minHeap.push({
            sources[current.sourceIndex][nextIndex],
            current.sourceIndex,
            nextIndex
        });
    }
}
import heapq

min_heap = []

# Add the first element from every sorted source.
for source_index, source in enumerate(sources):
    if source:
        heapq.heappush(min_heap, (source[0], source_index, 0))

while min_heap:
    value, source_index, element_index = heapq.heappop(min_heap)

    # Use value

    next_index = element_index + 1
    if next_index < len(sources[source_index]):
        next_value = sources[source_index][next_index]
        heapq.heappush(min_heap, (next_value, source_index, next_index))

Practical Example — LC 23: Merge k Sorted Lists

Question: Given k sorted linked lists, merge them into one sorted linked list.

How to read the problem: Every list is already sorted. At any moment, only the first unmerged node of each list can be the next smallest node in the final answer. Therefore, we only need those current candidates in the heap.

Why this pattern fits: Put the head node of every list into a Min Heap. The smallest head must be the next node in the merged result. After removing it, add the next node from that same list.
1 → 4 → 5
1 → 3 → 4
2 → 6

Min Heap chooses: 1 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 4 → 5 → 6
Solution — Java
class Solution {
    public ListNode mergeKLists(ListNode[] lists) {
        PriorityQueue<ListNode> minHeap = new PriorityQueue<>(
            (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a.val, b.val)
        );

        for (ListNode head : lists) {
            if (head != null) {
                minHeap.offer(head);
            }
        }

        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0);
        ListNode current = dummy;

        while (!minHeap.isEmpty()) {
            ListNode smallestNode = minHeap.poll();
            current.next = smallestNode;
            current = current.next;

            if (smallestNode.next != null) {
                minHeap.offer(smallestNode.next);
            }
        }

        return dummy.next;
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    ListNode* mergeKLists(vector<ListNode*>& lists) {
        priority_queue<ListNode*, vector<ListNode*>, Compare> minHeap;

        for (ListNode* head : lists) {
            if (head != nullptr) {
                minHeap.push(head);
            }
        }

        ListNode dummy(0);
        ListNode* current = &dummy;

        while (!minHeap.empty()) {
            ListNode* smallestNode = minHeap.top();
            minHeap.pop();

            current->next = smallestNode;
            current = current->next;

            if (smallestNode->next != nullptr) {
                minHeap.push(smallestNode->next);
            }
        }

        return dummy.next;
    }
};
import heapq

class Solution:
    def mergeKLists(self, lists):
        min_heap = []
        unique_id = 0

        for head in lists:
            if head:
                heapq.heappush(min_heap, (head.val, unique_id, head))
                unique_id += 1

        dummy = ListNode(0)
        current = dummy

        while min_heap:
            value, _, smallest_node = heapq.heappop(min_heap)

            current.next = smallest_node
            current = current.next

            if smallest_node.next:
                heapq.heappush(
                    min_heap,
                    (smallest_node.next.val, unique_id, smallest_node.next)
                )
                unique_id += 1

        return dummy.next

Why this works: The heap contains at most one candidate from each list. Because every list is already sorted, once the smallest current node is removed, only its next node can become a new candidate from that list. Thus the heap always represents the smallest available node from every source.

Extensions

23

Merge K Lists

Keep the current head of every sorted linked list in a Min Heap.

378

Sorted Matrix

Extract the smallest matrix candidate and advance within its sorted row.

373

Smallest Pairs

Use a heap to generate and expand the currently smallest pair candidates.

Common Mistakes

  • Putting every element from every collection into the heap instead of only the current candidates.
  • Forgetting to add the next element from the source that produced the extracted minimum.
  • Failing to store enough information to identify the source and position of each candidate.
  • Ignoring that the input collections are already sorted and therefore provide a natural next candidate.

Complexity

Time

O(N log k) — each of the N total elements is inserted and removed from a heap containing at most k candidates.

Space

O(k) auxiliary heap space, excluding the output structure.

Pattern Progression

LC 23 → LC 378 → LC 373
Start by merging multiple sorted lists, then apply the same smallest-candidate extraction to a sorted matrix, and finally extend the idea to generating smallest pairs.

Mental Trigger

When you see multiple sorted sources + repeatedly need the smallest available element, think: Min Heap + One Candidate per Source.

HEAP PATTERN

Scheduling & Greedy with Heap

A Priority Queue helps greedy scheduling problems make the best local decision efficiently. Instead of repeatedly scanning all available tasks or resources, the heap keeps the most important current choice at the top.

Pattern Overview

The key idea is to combine a greedy decision with a heap. As events become available, add their relevant values to a priority queue and repeatedly choose the option that gives the best immediate result.

Core idea: Identify what is currently available → store those choices in a heap → repeatedly select the best current choice → update the available choices.

Mental Model

01

Available Choices

Only tasks, meetings, or opportunities that are currently eligible enter the heap.

02

Priority

The heap keeps the most useful current choice immediately accessible.

03

Greedy Decision

Take the best available option, then update the state and continue.

Recognition Clues

Meeting / IntervalMultiple activities compete for a limited number of resources.
Task / ScheduleYou repeatedly choose from tasks that are currently available.
Resource AllocationResources such as rooms, bricks, ladders, or capital must be allocated efficiently.

How the Pattern Works

  • Sort or process events so that new choices become available in the correct order.
  • Add every currently available choice to the priority queue.
  • Use the heap root to make the best greedy decision.
  • Remove or consume that choice.
  • Update the available resources or events.
  • Repeat until all relevant decisions have been processed.

Coding Template

Greedy + Priority Queue
PriorityQueue<Integer> priorityQueue = new PriorityQueue<>();

for (Event event : events) {
    // Add choices that are now available.
    priorityQueue.offer(event.value);

    // Greedily choose the best available option.
    int bestChoice = priorityQueue.poll();

    // Update the current state.
}
priority_queue<int> priorityQueue;

for (const Event& event : events) {
    // Add choices that are now available.
    priorityQueue.push(event.value);

    // Greedily choose the best available option.
    int bestChoice = priorityQueue.top();
    priorityQueue.pop();

    // Update the current state.
}
import heapq

priority_queue = []

for event in events:
    # Add choices that are now available.
    heapq.heappush(priority_queue, -event.value)

    # Greedily choose the best available option.
    best_choice = -heapq.heappop(priority_queue)

    # Update the current state.

Practical Example — LC 253: Meeting Rooms II

Question: Given an array of meeting time intervals, return the minimum number of conference rooms required so that all meetings can take place without overlap.

How to read the problem: Meetings have start and end times. When a new meeting begins, we need to know whether an existing room has already become free. Among all active rooms, the one that becomes free earliest is the most useful resource to check first.

Why this pattern fits: Sort meetings by start time and keep the end time of every currently occupied room in a Min Heap. The heap root is the room that becomes free earliest. If it is free before the current meeting starts, reuse it; otherwise, another room is required.
Meetings: [0,30] [5,10] [15,20]
Start 0 → room ends 30
Start 5 → earliest end 30 → need room 2
Start 15 → earliest end 10 → reuse room 2
Answer = 2 rooms
Solution — Java
class Solution {
    public int minMeetingRooms(int[][] intervals) {
        if (intervals.length == 0) return 0;

        Arrays.sort(intervals, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]));

        PriorityQueue<Integer> roomEndTimes = new PriorityQueue<>();

        for (int[] meeting : intervals) {
            if (!roomEndTimes.isEmpty() &&
                roomEndTimes.peek() <= meeting[0]) {
                roomEndTimes.poll();
            }

            roomEndTimes.offer(meeting[1]);
        }

        return roomEndTimes.size();
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    int minMeetingRooms(vector<vector<int>>& intervals) {
        if (intervals.empty()) return 0;

        sort(intervals.begin(), intervals.end());

        priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>> roomEndTimes;

        for (const auto& meeting : intervals) {
            if (!roomEndTimes.empty() &&
                roomEndTimes.top() <= meeting[0]) {
                roomEndTimes.pop();
            }

            roomEndTimes.push(meeting[1]);
        }

        return roomEndTimes.size();
    }
};
import heapq

class Solution:
    def minMeetingRooms(self, intervals):
        if not intervals:
            return 0

        intervals.sort()
        room_end_times = []

        for start_time, end_time in intervals:
            if room_end_times and room_end_times[0] <= start_time:
                heapq.heappop(room_end_times)

            heapq.heappush(room_end_times, end_time)

        return len(room_end_times)

Why this works: The heap always contains the ending time of every room currently occupied. The smallest ending time is the earliest room that could become available. If that time is less than or equal to the current meeting's start, that room can be reused. Otherwise, every existing room is still occupied, so a new room is required.

Extensions

253

Meeting Rooms II

Use a Min Heap to track the earliest room that becomes available.

1642

Furthest Building

Use a heap to allocate limited ladders to the largest climbs while using bricks for the others.

502

IPO

Use a heap to repeatedly choose the most profitable project that is currently affordable.

Common Mistakes

  • Using a heap without first identifying what the heap priority should represent.
  • Choosing from tasks that are not yet available.
  • Forgetting to update the heap after a greedy decision changes the current state.
  • Using a heap when the problem does not actually require repeated best-choice selection.
  • Forgetting that the heap strategy depends on the greedy decision: earliest finish, largest benefit, smallest cost, or another problem-specific priority.

Complexity

Time

O(n log n) for the scheduling example — sorting takes O(n log n), and each meeting performs at most one heap insertion and removal.

Space

O(n) in the worst case when all meetings overlap and every active resource remains in the heap.

Pattern Progression

LC 253 → LC 1642 → LC 502
Start with resource scheduling, then apply heap-based allocation to limited resources, and finally use the heap to make greedy choices among currently affordable opportunities.

Mental Trigger

When you see scheduling / tasks / intervals + limited resources + repeatedly choose the best available option, think: Greedy + Priority Queue.

learning.html:
HEAP PATTERN

Two Heaps

The Two Heaps pattern maintains a dynamic ordered set by splitting its elements into two balanced halves: a max heap stores the smaller half and a min heap stores the larger half. By keeping their sizes balanced, the median can be read directly from the heap tops.

Pattern Overview

When a problem asks for a median while values are continuously added, repeatedly sorting the entire collection is unnecessary. Two heaps maintain the middle of the data efficiently as the collection changes.

Core idea: Keep the smaller half in a max heap and the larger half in a min heap. Balance their sizes so the heap tops always represent the middle values.

Mental Model

MAX

Smaller Half

Stores the smaller values.

maxHeap.peek()
MIN

Larger Half

Stores the larger values.

minHeap.peek()
MID

Median

The heap tops expose the middle.

median = middle value(s)

Recognition Clues

MedianFind the median of a changing collection.
Running MedianReturn the median after each insertion.
BalanceMaintain two groups around a middle boundary.
Data StreamValues arrive one at a time.
Middle ElementRepeatedly access the central value without full sorting.
Two Priority StructuresOne structure manages the lower half and one manages the upper half.

How the Pattern Works

  1. Add the new value to the appropriate heap based on the current boundary.
  2. Restore the ordering relationship between the heaps.
  3. Balance their sizes so neither side becomes too large.
  4. If the total size is odd, the larger heap provides the median.
  5. If the total size is even, the median is the average of both heap tops.
maxHeap.peek()≤minHeap.peek()
|size(maxHeap) − size(minHeap)|≤1

Coding Template

Use this structure when values arrive dynamically and you need to maintain their median.

Two Heaps Template
PriorityQueue<Integer> smaller = new PriorityQueue<>(Collections.reverseOrder());
PriorityQueue<Integer> larger = new PriorityQueue<>();

void add(int value) {
    if (smaller.isEmpty() || value <= smaller.peek()) {
        smaller.offer(value);
    } else {
        larger.offer(value);
    }

    if (smaller.size() > larger.size() + 1) {
        larger.offer(smaller.poll());
    } else if (larger.size() > smaller.size() + 1) {
        smaller.offer(larger.poll());
    }

    if (!smaller.isEmpty() && !larger.isEmpty() && smaller.peek() > larger.peek()) {
        int left = smaller.poll();
        int right = larger.poll();
        smaller.offer(right);
        larger.offer(left);
    }
}
priority_queue<int> smaller;
priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>> larger;

void add(int value) {
    if (smaller.empty() || value <= smaller.top()) {
        smaller.push(value);
    } else {
        larger.push(value);
    }

    if (smaller.size() > larger.size() + 1) {
        larger.push(smaller.top());
        smaller.pop();
    } else if (larger.size() > smaller.size() + 1) {
        smaller.push(larger.top());
        larger.pop();
    }

    if (!smaller.empty() && !larger.empty() && smaller.top() > larger.top()) {
        int left = smaller.top();
        int right = larger.top();
        smaller.pop();
        larger.pop();
        smaller.push(right);
        larger.push(left);
    }
}
import heapq

smaller = []
larger = []

def add(value):
    if not smaller or value <= -smaller[0]:
        heapq.heappush(smaller, -value)
    else:
        heapq.heappush(larger, value)

    if len(smaller) > len(larger) + 1:
        heapq.heappush(larger, -heapq.heappop(smaller))
    elif len(larger) > len(smaller) + 1:
        heapq.heappush(smaller, -heapq.heappop(larger))

    if smaller and larger and -smaller[0] > larger[0]:
        left = -heapq.heappop(smaller)
        right = heapq.heappop(larger)
        heapq.heappush(smaller, -right)
        heapq.heappush(larger, left)

Practical Example — LC 295: Find Median from Data Stream

Question: Numbers arrive one at a time. After each insertion, return the median of all numbers seen so far.

How to Read the Problem

The data is arriving as a stream, so repeatedly sorting every value would waste work. The important requirement is not just finding a median once, but maintaining the middle efficiently after every insertion.

Why Two Heaps Fit

Split the numbers into two halves. The max heap gives the largest value of the smaller half, while the min heap gives the smallest value of the larger half. Those two values are exactly what we need to determine the median.

Smaller Half → [1, 3, 5]|[7, 9, 12] ← Larger Half
LC 295 — Find Median from Data Stream
class MedianFinder {
    private PriorityQueue<Integer> smaller =
        new PriorityQueue<>(Collections.reverseOrder());
    private PriorityQueue<Integer> larger = new PriorityQueue<>();

    public void addNum(int num) {
        if (smaller.isEmpty() || num <= smaller.peek()) {
            smaller.offer(num);
        } else {
            larger.offer(num);
        }

        if (smaller.size() > larger.size() + 1) {
            larger.offer(smaller.poll());
        } else if (larger.size() > smaller.size() + 1) {
            smaller.offer(larger.poll());
        }
    }

    public double findMedian() {
        if (smaller.size() > larger.size()) {
            return smaller.peek();
        }
        if (larger.size() > smaller.size()) {
            return larger.peek();
        }
        return ((double) smaller.peek() + larger.peek()) / 2.0;
    }
}
class MedianFinder {
private:
    priority_queue<int> smaller;
    priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>> larger;

public:
    void addNum(int num) {
        if (smaller.empty() || num <= smaller.top()) {
            smaller.push(num);
        } else {
            larger.push(num);
        }

        if (smaller.size() > larger.size() + 1) {
            larger.push(smaller.top());
            smaller.pop();
        } else if (larger.size() > smaller.size() + 1) {
            smaller.push(larger.top());
            larger.pop();
        }
    }

    double findMedian() {
        if (smaller.size() > larger.size()) {
            return smaller.top();
        }
        if (larger.size() > smaller.size()) {
            return larger.top();
        }
        return ((double) smaller.top() + larger.top()) / 2.0;
    }
};
import heapq

class MedianFinder:
    def __init__(self):
        self.smaller = []
        self.larger = []

    def addNum(self, num):
        if not self.smaller or num <= -self.smaller[0]:
            heapq.heappush(self.smaller, -num)
        else:
            heapq.heappush(self.larger, num)

        if len(self.smaller) > len(self.larger) + 1:
            heapq.heappush(self.larger, -heapq.heappop(self.smaller))
        elif len(self.larger) > len(self.smaller) + 1:
            heapq.heappush(self.smaller, -heapq.heappop(self.larger))

    def findMedian(self):
        if len(self.smaller) > len(self.larger):
            return -self.smaller[0]
        if len(self.larger) > len(self.smaller):
            return self.larger[0]
        return (-self.smaller[0] + self.larger[0]) / 2.0

Why This Works

The max heap contains the lower half, so its top is the largest value on the lower side. The min heap contains the upper half, so its top is the smallest value on the upper side. Once the sizes differ by at most one, the middle value or middle pair is immediately available.

The real pattern: Do not think “two heaps because the problem asks for a median.” Think “I need to maintain two balanced ordered halves so the boundary between them stays accessible.”

Extensions

  • LC 480 — Sliding Window Median: Apply the two-halves idea while values enter and leave a moving window.
  • LC 2102 — Sequentially Ordinal Rank Tracker: Reinforces maintaining useful ordering information with priority structures.

Common Mistakes

  • Using two min heaps or two max heaps instead of opposite heap types.
  • Forgetting to rebalance after insertion.
  • Allowing one heap to contain more than one extra element.
  • Confusing “smaller half” with “all values smaller than the median” without maintaining the boundary correctly.
  • Forgetting that an even-sized collection requires averaging the two middle values.
  • Using integer division when the median can be fractional.

Complexity

Insertion

O(log n)

Each insertion and possible rebalance moves an element through a heap.

Find Median

O(1)

The middle value(s) are already at the heap tops.

Problem Progression

LC 295 — Running Median→LC 480 — Sliding Window Median→LC 2102 — Rank Tracking

Mental Trigger

When you see: “median”, “running median”, “data stream”, “middle value”, or “maintain two balanced sides” → think Two Heaps.

TREE TRAVERSAL PATTERN

DFS Traversal — Preorder, Inorder & Postorder

Depth-First Search on a binary tree explores one subtree completely before moving to the other. The three fundamental traversals differ only in when the current node is processed relative to its left and right subtrees.

Pattern Overview

Recursive DFS gives a natural way to traverse every node of a binary tree. The key decision is the position of the current node's processing relative to the recursive calls.

Core idea: The recursive structure stays the same. Only the position of visit(root) changes: before both children, between them, or after both children.

Mental Model

PRE

Preorder

Root → Left → Right

visit(root) → left → right
IN

Inorder

Left → Root → Right

left → visit(root) → right
POST

Postorder

Left → Right → Root

left → right → visit(root)

Recognition Clues

TraverseVisit every node of a tree in a specific order.
Root, Left, RightThe problem explicitly describes the order of traversal.
Visit Every NodeEach node must be processed exactly once.
SubtreesThe same operation must be repeated for left and right children.
Binary TreeEach node can have a left and right subtree.
Recursive StructureThe left and right children are themselves smaller binary trees.

How the Pattern Works

  1. If the current node is null, stop.
  2. Decide when the current node should be processed.
  3. Recursively process the left subtree.
  4. Recursively process the right subtree.
  5. The only difference between preorder, inorder, and postorder is where the visit occurs.
PreorderRoot → Left → Right
InorderLeft → Root → Right
PostorderLeft → Right → Root

Coding Template

The recursive skeleton is almost identical for all three traversals. Move the visit operation to change the traversal order.

DFS Traversal Template
void dfs(TreeNode root) {
    if (root == null) return;

    // Preorder: process root here

    dfs(root.left);

    // Inorder: process root here

    dfs(root.right);

    // Postorder: process root here
}
void dfs(TreeNode* root) {
    if (root == nullptr) return;

    // Preorder: process root here

    dfs(root->left);

    // Inorder: process root here

    dfs(root->right);

    // Postorder: process root here
}
def dfs(root):
    if root is None:
        return

    # Preorder: process root here

    dfs(root.left)

    # Inorder: process root here

    dfs(root.right)

    # Postorder: process root here

Practical Example — LC 94: Binary Tree Inorder Traversal

Question: Given the root of a binary tree, return the inorder traversal of its nodes' values.

How to Read the Problem

The required order is Left → Root → Right. That immediately identifies recursive inorder DFS. For every node, completely traverse its left subtree first, then record the current node, then traverse its right subtree.

Why This Pattern Fits

A binary tree is recursively composed of smaller binary trees. Once we know how to perform inorder traversal on one subtree, the same logic can be applied to every subtree.

Left Subtree→Root→Right Subtree
LC 94 — Binary Tree Inorder Traversal
class Solution {
    public List<Integer> inorderTraversal(TreeNode root) {
        List<Integer> traversal = new ArrayList<>();
        dfs(root, traversal);
        return traversal;
    }

    private void dfs(TreeNode root, List<Integer> traversal) {
        if (root == null) return;

        dfs(root.left, traversal);
        traversal.add(root.val);
        dfs(root.right, traversal);
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    vector<int> inorderTraversal(TreeNode* root) {
        vector<int> traversal;
        dfs(root, traversal);
        return traversal;
    }

private:
    void dfs(TreeNode* root, vector<int>& traversal) {
        if (root == nullptr) return;

        dfs(root->left, traversal);
        traversal.push_back(root->val);
        dfs(root->right, traversal);
    }
};
class Solution:
    def inorderTraversal(self, root):
        traversal = []

        def dfs(node):
            if node is None:
                return

            dfs(node.left)
            traversal.append(node.val)
            dfs(node.right)

        dfs(root)
        return traversal

Why It Works

Each recursive call is responsible for exactly one subtree. The base case stops at null children. For inorder traversal, the current node is added only after its left subtree has been completely processed and before its right subtree is processed.

The real pattern: Do not memorize three separate algorithms. Memorize the recursive DFS skeleton and recognize where the node is processed: before the children, between them, or after them.

Extensions

  • LC 144 — Binary Tree Preorder Traversal: Move the root visit before the left recursive call.
  • LC 145 — Binary Tree Postorder Traversal: Move the root visit after both recursive calls.

Common Mistakes

  • Using the wrong position for processing the current node.
  • Forgetting the null base case.
  • Mixing up left and right recursive calls.
  • Thinking preorder, inorder, and postorder require completely different algorithms.
  • Forgetting that recursion uses the call stack, which grows with tree height.

Complexity

Time

O(n)

Every node is visited exactly once.

Space

O(h)

The recursive call stack depends on the tree height h.

Problem Progression

LC 94 — Inorder→LC 144 — Preorder→LC 145 — Postorder

Mental Trigger

When you see: “traverse”, “visit every node”, “root-left-right”, “left-root-right”, or “left-right-root” → think DFS Traversal and identify where the root is processed.

learning.html:
TREE TRAVERSAL PATTERN

BFS / Level Order Traversal

Breadth-First Search explores a binary tree level by level, visiting all nodes at the current depth before moving to the next. A queue naturally maintains this left-to-right layer order.

Pattern Overview

When a tree problem asks you to process nodes by level, depth, layer, or breadth, use BFS with a queue. The queue holds the nodes waiting to be processed and naturally preserves the order needed to move across one level before entering the next.

Core idea: Put the root into a queue. Repeatedly process the current level, add its children to the queue, and then continue with the next level.

Mental Model

Q

Queue

Stores nodes waiting to be processed.

queue<TreeNode*>
LVL

Current Level

Process exactly the nodes currently in the queue.

levelSize = queue.size()
NEXT

Next Level

Children are added for the next round.

left → right

Recognition Clues

LevelProcess or return nodes level by level.
BreadthExplore all nodes at one depth before going deeper.
LayerThe answer is organized around tree layers.
QueueA queue is the natural structure for breadth-first processing.
DepthGroup nodes according to their distance from the root.
ViewProblems ask what is visible from a side or across levels.

How the Pattern Works

  1. If the root is null, return an empty result.
  2. Put the root into the queue.
  3. Record the number of nodes currently in the queue. This is the size of the current level.
  4. Process exactly that many nodes.
  5. For each node, process its value and add its non-null children to the queue.
  6. After the current level is finished, the queue contains the next level.
Current Level→Process all queued nodes
Children→Become the Next Level

Coding Template

Use this template whenever the problem requires explicit level-by-level processing.

BFS Level Order Template
Queue<TreeNode> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
queue.offer(root);

while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
    int levelSize = queue.size();

    for (int i = 0; i < levelSize; i++) {
        TreeNode current = queue.poll();

        // Process current node

        if (current.left != null) queue.offer(current.left);
        if (current.right != null) queue.offer(current.right);
    }
}
queue<TreeNode*> queue;
queue.push(root);

while (!queue.empty()) {
    int levelSize = queue.size();

    for (int i = 0; i < levelSize; i++) {
        TreeNode* current = queue.front();
        queue.pop();

        // Process current node

        if (current->left) queue.push(current->left);
        if (current->right) queue.push(current->right);
    }
}
from collections import deque

queue = deque([root])

while queue:
    level_size = len(queue)

    for _ in range(level_size):
        current = queue.popleft()

        # Process current node

        if current.left:
            queue.append(current.left)
        if current.right:
            queue.append(current.right)

Practical Example — LC 102: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal

Question: Given the root of a binary tree, return the level order traversal of its nodes' values, from left to right, level by level.

How to Read the Problem

The phrase level order is the key clue. We must finish processing one depth before moving to the next. A queue gives exactly this behavior: nodes from the current level are removed first, while their children are added behind them.

Why This Pattern Fits

At the beginning of each loop, the queue contains exactly the nodes belonging to one level. Saving levelSize lets us process only those nodes before starting the next level.

Level 0→Level 1→Level 2→Level 3
LC 102 — Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
class Solution {
    public List<List<Integer>> levelOrder(TreeNode root) {
        List<List<Integer>> result = new ArrayList<>();
        if (root == null) return result;

        Queue<TreeNode> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
        queue.offer(root);

        while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
            int levelSize = queue.size();
            List<Integer> level = new ArrayList<>();

            for (int i = 0; i < levelSize; i++) {
                TreeNode current = queue.poll();
                level.add(current.val);

                if (current.left != null) queue.offer(current.left);
                if (current.right != null) queue.offer(current.right);
            }

            result.add(level);
        }

        return result;
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    vector<vector<int>> levelOrder(TreeNode* root) {
        vector<vector<int>> result;
        if (root == nullptr) return result;

        queue<TreeNode*> queue;
        queue.push(root);

        while (!queue.empty()) {
            int levelSize = queue.size();
            vector<int> level;

            for (int i = 0; i < levelSize; i++) {
                TreeNode* current = queue.front();
                queue.pop();
                level.push_back(current->val);

                if (current->left) queue.push(current->left);
                if (current->right) queue.push(current->right);
            }

            result.push_back(level);
        }

        return result;
    }
};
from collections import deque

class Solution:
    def levelOrder(self, root):
        if root is None:
            return []

        result = []
        queue = deque([root])

        while queue:
            level_size = len(queue)
            level = []

            for _ in range(level_size):
                current = queue.popleft()
                level.append(current.val)

                if current.left:
                    queue.append(current.left)
                if current.right:
                    queue.append(current.right)

            result.append(level)

        return result

Why It Works

The queue preserves breadth-first order. The crucial levelSize boundary separates the current layer from the next one. Every node already in the queue belongs to the current level, while children added during that level are processed only in the next iteration.

The real pattern: Do not memorize “use a queue.” Think “process the current layer completely, while building the next layer.” The queue is what makes that possible.

Extensions

  • LC 107 — Binary Tree Level Order Traversal II: Use the same BFS levels, then return the collected levels in reverse order.
  • LC 199 — Binary Tree Right Side View: Use level boundaries and capture the last node processed at each level.

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting to save levelSize before processing the level.
  • Processing newly added children in the same level.
  • Using DFS when the problem specifically requires level-by-level ordering.
  • Forgetting to check for a null root.
  • Mixing up queue order and accidentally processing children before all current-level nodes.

Complexity

Time

O(n)

Every node enters and leaves the queue exactly once.

Space

O(w)

The queue holds nodes from the current or next level, where w is the maximum width of the tree.

Problem Progression

LC 102 — Level Order→LC 107 — Bottom-Up→LC 199 — Right Side View

Mental Trigger

When you see: “level”, “breadth”, “layer”, “level order”, “nodes at each depth”, or “view from a side” → think BFS + Queue, and ask whether you need to process one complete level at a time.

learning.html:
TREE RECURSION PATTERN

Recursive Divide & Conquer

Recursive Divide & Conquer solves a tree problem by asking each subtree to solve its own smaller version of the problem, then combining the returned information at the current node. This is especially powerful for height, balance, diameter, depth, and other bottom-up tree problems.

Pattern Overview

Many binary-tree problems cannot be solved correctly by looking only at the current node. The answer depends on information from the left and right subtrees. Recursive divide and conquer lets each subtree compute its own result, then lets the parent combine those results.

Core idea: Ask the left subtree for its answer, ask the right subtree for its answer, then combine both answers to solve the current node.

Mental Model

L

Left Result

Recursively solve the left subtree.

leftResult = dfs(root.left)
R

Right Result

Recursively solve the right subtree.

rightResult = dfs(root.right)
↗

Combine

Use both results at the current node.

answer = combine(left, right)

Recognition Clues

HeightThe answer depends on the height of subtrees.
BalancedCompare information from the left and right sides.
DiameterThe answer may pass through the current node using both subtrees.
DepthEach node depends on the depth or height returned by its children.
Bottom-UpChildren must be solved before the parent can be solved.
Subtree InformationThe current node needs results computed by its child subtrees.

How the Pattern Works

  1. Define exactly what the recursive function should return for one subtree.
  2. Handle the base case, usually a null node.
  3. Recursively solve the left subtree.
  4. Recursively solve the right subtree.
  5. Combine the two returned results at the current node.
  6. Return the information required by the parent.
Left Result+Right Result→Current Result
Key question: Before writing recursion, ask “What information does my parent need from me?” That answer usually becomes the return value of the recursive function.

Coding Template

The exact returned value depends on the problem. The important structure is bottom-up: solve both children first, then compute the current node's result.

Recursive Divide & Conquer Template
int dfs(TreeNode root) {
    if (root == null) {
        return 0;
    }

    int leftResult = dfs(root.left);
    int rightResult = dfs(root.right);

    // Combine leftResult and rightResult
    return combine(leftResult, rightResult, root);
}
int dfs(TreeNode* root) {
    if (root == nullptr) {
        return 0;
    }

    int leftResult = dfs(root->left);
    int rightResult = dfs(root->right);

    // Combine leftResult and rightResult
    return combine(leftResult, rightResult, root);
}
def dfs(root):
    if root is None:
        return 0

    left_result = dfs(root.left)
    right_result = dfs(root.right)

    # Combine left_result and right_result
    return combine(left_result, right_result, root)

Practical Example — LC 104: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree

Question: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth.

How to Read the Problem

The depth of a node depends on how deep its left and right subtrees are. Therefore, the parent cannot determine its depth until both children have returned their depths.

Why This Pattern Fits

For every node, recursively find the maximum depth of the left subtree and the maximum depth of the right subtree. The current node adds one level to the larger of those two depths.

Left Depth→max←Right Depth→+ 1
LC 104 — Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
class Solution {
    public int maxDepth(TreeNode root) {
        if (root == null) {
            return 0;
        }

        int leftDepth = maxDepth(root.left);
        int rightDepth = maxDepth(root.right);

        return 1 + Math.max(leftDepth, rightDepth);
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    int maxDepth(TreeNode* root) {
        if (root == nullptr) {
            return 0;
        }

        int leftDepth = maxDepth(root->left);
        int rightDepth = maxDepth(root->right);

        return 1 + max(leftDepth, rightDepth);
    }
};
class Solution:
    def maxDepth(self, root):
        if root is None:
            return 0

        left_depth = self.maxDepth(root.left)
        right_depth = self.maxDepth(root.right)

        return 1 + max(left_depth, right_depth)

Why It Works

A null subtree has depth 0. Every non-null node has a left depth and a right depth. The deeper subtree determines how far the current node can reach, so the current depth is one more than the larger child depth.

The real pattern: Do not think “recursion means calling the function again.” Think “each subtree returns useful information, and the parent combines those results.”

Extensions

  • LC 110 — Balanced Binary Tree: Recursively obtain subtree heights and determine whether the current node is balanced.
  • LC 543 — Diameter of Binary Tree: Recursively obtain subtree heights while also using the two heights to update the best diameter.

Returning One Result vs Multiple Pieces of Information

Some problems need only one value from each subtree, such as height in LC 104. Harder problems may need the recursive function to return multiple pieces of information, or return one value while updating a separate global answer.

Simple→Subtree Height
Advanced→Subtree Information + Global Answer

Common Mistakes

  • Choosing the wrong meaning for the recursive function's return value.
  • Trying to solve the parent before obtaining information from both children.
  • Forgetting the null base case.
  • Confusing tree height with node depth.
  • Returning only the final answer when the parent actually needs different subtree information.
  • Recomputing the same subtree repeatedly, causing unnecessary time complexity.

Complexity

Time

O(n)

Each node is processed once when its subtree result is computed.

Space

O(h)

The recursive call stack depends on the height h of the tree.

Problem Progression

LC 104 — Maximum Depth→LC 110 — Balanced Tree→LC 543 — Diameter

Mental Trigger

When you see: “height”, “balanced”, “diameter”, “depth”, or a parent answer that depends on both child subtrees → think Recursive Divide & Conquer and ask what each subtree should return.
