TREE PATH PATTERN

Path Problems

Path problems track information while moving through a binary tree. The key is to carry the required state along the DFS path, decide when a path is complete, and sometimes maintain a global answer when the best path can occur anywhere in the tree.

Pattern Overview

Tree path problems become easier when you think about what information must travel with the current DFS path. Depending on the problem, that state may be a remaining target sum, the values collected along the current root-to-leaf path, or a global best answer.

Core idea: During DFS, maintain the state of the current path. For root-to-leaf problems, the path usually becomes complete at a leaf. For maximum-path problems, combine information from child paths while maintaining a global answer.

Mental Model

SUM

Path State

Carry the information required by the current path.

remainingSum
PATH

Current Path

Track nodes when the complete path itself matters.

path.add(root.val)
BEST

Global Answer

Maintain the best path found anywhere.

globalMax

Recognition Clues

Path SumFind whether a path reaches a target total.
Root to LeafThe path starts at the root and ends at a leaf.
Maximum PathFind the highest-value path anywhere in the tree.
Track StateInformation must be carried from parent to child during DFS.
Complete PathThe answer is evaluated when a valid path reaches its endpoint.
Global BestThe optimal path may start and end away from the root.

How the Pattern Works

  1. Define what state the current DFS path needs.
  2. Update that state when entering the current node.
  3. Recursively continue into the children.
  4. For root-to-leaf problems, evaluate the state when a leaf is reached.
  5. If the complete path must be returned, add the current node to a path list and backtrack after exploring its children.
  6. If the best path can occur anywhere, maintain a global answer while recursion returns useful path information upward.
Parent State→Update at Node→Child State
Key question: Ask “What information about the path so far must the child know?” That information becomes the DFS state.

Coding Template

Use the template that matches the type of path problem. The most common root-to-leaf version carries a path condition or remaining target.

DFS with Path State Template
void dfs(TreeNode root, int state) {
    if (root == null) return;

    state = updateState(state, root.val);

    if (root.left == null && root.right == null) {
        // Evaluate complete root-to-leaf path
        return;
    }

    dfs(root.left, state);
    dfs(root.right, state);
}
void dfs(TreeNode* root, int state) {
    if (root == nullptr) return;

    state = updateState(state, root->val);

    if (root->left == nullptr && root->right == nullptr) {
        // Evaluate complete root-to-leaf path
        return;
    }

    dfs(root->left, state);
    dfs(root->right, state);
}
def dfs(root, state):
    if root is None:
        return

    state = update_state(state, root.val)

    if root.left is None and root.right is None:
        # Evaluate complete root-to-leaf path
        return

    dfs(root.left, state)
    dfs(root.right, state)

Practical Example — LC 112: Path Sum

Question: Given the root of a binary tree and a target sum, determine whether the tree has a root-to-leaf path whose node values add up to the target sum.

How to Read the Problem

The path must start at the root and end at a leaf. As DFS moves downward, subtract each node's value from the remaining target. Only when a leaf is reached do we know whether the complete root-to-leaf path satisfies the target.

Why This Pattern Fits

The child does not need the entire path. It only needs the remaining sum. Passing that state through recursion makes each subtree responsible for checking whether its continuation can complete the required path.

Target→Remaining Sum→Leaf Check
LC 112 — Path Sum
class Solution {
    public boolean hasPathSum(TreeNode root, int targetSum) {
        if (root == null) {
            return false;
        }

        int remainingSum = targetSum - root.val;

        if (root.left == null && root.right == null) {
            return remainingSum == 0;
        }

        return hasPathSum(root.left, remainingSum)
            || hasPathSum(root.right, remainingSum);
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    bool hasPathSum(TreeNode* root, int targetSum) {
        if (root == nullptr) {
            return false;
        }

        int remainingSum = targetSum - root->val;

        if (root->left == nullptr && root->right == nullptr) {
            return remainingSum == 0;
        }

        return hasPathSum(root->left, remainingSum)
            || hasPathSum(root->right, remainingSum);
    }
};
class Solution:
    def hasPathSum(self, root, targetSum):
        if root is None:
            return False

        remaining_sum = targetSum - root.val

        if root.left is None and root.right is None:
            return remaining_sum == 0

        return (self.hasPathSum(root.left, remaining_sum)
                or self.hasPathSum(root.right, remaining_sum))

Why It Works

Every recursive call represents one possible continuation of the current root-to-leaf path. Subtracting the current node's value keeps exactly the amount still required. At a leaf, the path is complete, so the remaining sum determines whether the path is valid.

The real pattern: Do not think “DFS on a tree.” Think “DFS while carrying the state of the current path.” The state changes depending on what the path problem asks you to track.

Extensions

  • LC 113 — Path Sum II: Track the actual node values in the current path and backtrack after exploring each subtree.
  • LC 124 — Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum: Use recursive child contributions and maintain a global maximum because the best path can occur anywhere in the tree.

Root-to-Leaf vs Global Path

R→L

Root to Leaf

The path has a fixed starting point and must end at a leaf.

state travels downward
ANY

Any Path

The optimal path may start and end anywhere.

combine child contributions
MAX

Global State

Maintain the best answer found during recursion.

globalMax = best

Common Mistakes

  • Checking the target sum before reaching a leaf when the problem specifically requires root-to-leaf paths.
  • Forgetting to carry the updated path state into both recursive calls.
  • Confusing a root-to-leaf path with an arbitrary path anywhere in the tree.
  • Forgetting to backtrack when storing the actual path for problems like LC 113.
  • Assuming the best path must pass through the root when solving maximum-path problems.
  • For global-answer problems, forgetting to update the best answer while recursion explores different nodes.

Complexity

Time

O(n)

Each node is visited at most once in the standard DFS solution.

Space

O(h)

The recursion stack depends on the tree height. Explicit path storage may also require O(h).

Problem Progression

LC 112 — Path Sum→LC 113 — Path Sum II→LC 124 — Maximum Path Sum

Mental Trigger

When you see: “path sum”, “root to leaf”, “path”, “maximum path”, or a condition that must be carried along a tree path → think DFS with State and ask what information the current path must carry.

TREE RECURSION PATTERN

Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA)

The Lowest Common Ancestor pattern finds the deepest node that is an ancestor of two target nodes. Recursive search lets each subtree report what it found, allowing the current node to identify where the two target paths meet.

Pattern Overview

When two nodes are given and the problem asks for their lowest common ancestor, search both sides of the tree and determine where information from the two target nodes comes together.

Core idea: Recursively search the tree. If one target is found in the left subtree and the other is found in the right subtree, the current node is their Lowest Common Ancestor.

Mental Model

L

Left Search

Check whether a target exists in the left subtree.

left = dfs(root.left)
R

Right Search

Check whether a target exists in the right subtree.

right = dfs(root.right)
↗

Meeting Point

If both sides find a target, the current node is the LCA.

left != null && right != null

Recognition Clues

AncestorThe problem asks for an ancestor of target nodes.
Common ParentFind the lowest node connecting two targets.
Two NodesTwo target nodes must be related through the tree.
Recursive SearchSearch both subtrees for the targets.
Split PointThe answer occurs where the two target searches meet.
Binary Search TreeBST ordering can provide a faster directional search.

How the Pattern Works

  1. If the current node is null, return null.
  2. If the current node is one of the target nodes, return the current node.
  3. Recursively search the left subtree.
  4. Recursively search the right subtree.
  5. If both searches return a node, the current node is the common ancestor where the two paths meet.
  6. If only one side returns a node, propagate that result upward.
Left finds target+Right finds target→Current node = LCA

Coding Template

The recursive function returns the useful node found below. The parent combines the left and right results.

Recursive LCA Template
TreeNode dfs(TreeNode root, TreeNode first, TreeNode second) {
    if (root == null || root == first || root == second) {
        return root;
    }

    TreeNode left = dfs(root.left, first, second);
    TreeNode right = dfs(root.right, first, second);

    if (left != null && right != null) {
        return root;
    }

    return left != null ? left : right;
}
TreeNode* dfs(TreeNode* root, TreeNode* first, TreeNode* second) {
    if (root == nullptr || root == first || root == second) {
        return root;
    }

    TreeNode* left = dfs(root->left, first, second);
    TreeNode* right = dfs(root->right, first, second);

    if (left != nullptr && right != nullptr) {
        return root;
    }

    return left != nullptr ? left : right;
}
def dfs(root, first, second):
    if root is None or root is first or root is second:
        return root

    left = dfs(root.left, first, second)
    right = dfs(root.right, first, second)

    if left is not None and right is not None:
        return root

    return left if left is not None else right

Practical Example — LC 236: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree

Question: Given the root of a binary tree and two nodes p and q, find their lowest common ancestor.

Example Input

Tree: [3,5,1,6,2,0,8,null,null,7,4], p = 5, q = 1

Example Output

3

Short Dry Run

  1. Start at node 3. It is neither p nor q, so search both subtrees.
  2. Left subtree reaches node 5. Since 5 = p, return 5.
  3. Right subtree reaches node 1. Since 1 = q, return 1.
  4. Back at node 3: left returned 5 and right returned 1.
  5. Both sides are non-null, so 3 is the LCA.
left = 5+right = 1→LCA = 3
LC 236 — Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
class Solution {
    public TreeNode lowestCommonAncestor(TreeNode root, TreeNode p, TreeNode q) {
        if (root == null || root == p || root == q) {
            return root;
        }

        TreeNode left = lowestCommonAncestor(root.left, p, q);
        TreeNode right = lowestCommonAncestor(root.right, p, q);

        if (left != null && right != null) {
            return root;
        }

        return left != null ? left : right;
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    TreeNode* lowestCommonAncestor(TreeNode* root, TreeNode* p, TreeNode* q) {
        if (root == nullptr || root == p || root == q) {
            return root;
        }

        TreeNode* left = lowestCommonAncestor(root->left, p, q);
        TreeNode* right = lowestCommonAncestor(root->right, p, q);

        if (left != nullptr && right != nullptr) {
            return root;
        }

        return left != nullptr ? left : right;
    }
};
class Solution:
    def lowestCommonAncestor(self, root, p, q):
        if root is None or root is p or root is q:
            return root

        left = self.lowestCommonAncestor(root.left, p, q)
        right = self.lowestCommonAncestor(root.right, p, q)

        if left is not None and right is not None:
            return root

        return left if left is not None else right

Why It Works

If the current node is one of the targets, it is returned upward. Otherwise, recursion searches both subtrees. When both sides return non-null results, one target was found on each side, so the current node is the lowest node where their paths meet.

The real pattern: Do not think “search for two nodes.” Think “let each subtree report what it found, then identify the node where both reports meet.”

Extensions

  • LC 235 — Lowest Common Ancestor of a BST: Use BST ordering to move left or right instead of searching both subtrees.
  • LC 1644 — Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree II: Add state to verify that both target nodes actually exist.

Binary Tree vs BST

BT

Binary Tree

No ordering guarantee, so both subtrees may need to be searched.

search left + right
BST

Binary Search Tree

Values tell you which direction contains the targets.

left / right decision
II

Missing Nodes

Extra state may verify both targets exist.

foundFirst + foundSecond

Common Mistakes

  • Assuming a normal binary tree has BST ordering.
  • Returning the first target found without checking the other subtree.
  • Forgetting the base case when the current node is one of the targets.
  • Confusing the LCA with simply the first common ancestor found from one search path.
  • Using the basic LC 236 solution when the problem requires verifying that both nodes actually exist.

Complexity

Time

O(n)

The tree may need to be searched to find both targets.

Space

O(h)

The recursive call stack depends on the tree height.

Problem Progression

LC 236 — Binary Tree LCA→LC 235 — BST LCA→LC 1644 — Missing Nodes

Mental Trigger

When you see: “ancestor”, “common parent”, “lowest common ancestor”, or “two nodes meet in a tree” → think Recursive LCA Search and ask what each subtree can report to its parent.

learning.html:
TREE CONSTRUCTION PATTERN

Tree Construction & Serialization

Reconstruct a binary tree from traversal information, then extend the same recursive thinking to serialize and deserialize a tree. The core idea is to use one traversal to determine the root and another traversal to determine how the remaining nodes split into left and right subtrees.

Pattern Overview

Tree construction problems give you traversal sequences and ask you to rebuild the original binary tree. The key is that traversal orders contain structural information: Preorder gives the root first, Inorder tells you which nodes belong to the left and right subtrees, and Postorder gives the root last.

Core pattern: Choose the root from one traversal, locate that root in the second traversal, split the remaining range into left and right subtrees, then recursively construct both sides.

Mental Model

ROOT

Find the Root

Preorder starts with the root. Postorder ends with the root.

root = traversal value
SPLIT

Split the Tree

Use the root's position in inorder to separate left and right subtrees.

left | root | right
BUILD

Build Recursively

Repeat the same process on each subtree range until the range becomes empty.

build(left), build(right)

Recognition Clues

ReconstructBuild a binary tree from traversal sequences.
Preorder + InorderRoot comes first, then inorder splits the tree.
Inorder + PostorderRoot comes last, then inorder splits the tree.
SerializeConvert a tree structure into a storable sequence.
DeserializeRebuild the exact tree from the serialized representation.
Recursive BuildThe same construction rule repeats for every subtree.

How the Pattern Works

Type A — Preorder + Inorder

Preorder tells you the next root because the root appears first. Find that root in inorder. Everything before it belongs to the left subtree, and everything after it belongs to the right subtree.

Preorder → Root+Inorder → Split→Recursive Build
Template — Preorder + Inorder
Map<Integer, Integer> inorderPosition = new HashMap<>();
int preorderIndex = 0;

TreeNode build(int left, int right, int[] preorder, int[] inorder) {
    if (left > right) return null;

    int rootValue = preorder[preorderIndex++];
    TreeNode root = new TreeNode(rootValue);
    int split = inorderPosition.get(rootValue);

    root.left = build(left, split - 1, preorder, inorder);
    root.right = build(split + 1, right, preorder, inorder);
    return root;
}
unordered_map<int, int> inorderPosition;
int preorderIndex = 0;

TreeNode* build(int left, int right, vector<int>& preorder, vector<int>& inorder) {
    if (left > right) return nullptr;

    int rootValue = preorder[preorderIndex++];
    TreeNode* root = new TreeNode(rootValue);
    int split = inorderPosition[rootValue];

    root->left = build(left, split - 1, preorder, inorder);
    root->right = build(split + 1, right, preorder, inorder);
    return root;
}
inorder_position = {value: i for i, value in enumerate(inorder)}
preorder_index = 0

def build(left, right):
    global preorder_index
    if left > right:
        return None

    root_value = preorder[preorder_index]
    preorder_index += 1
    root = TreeNode(root_value)
    split = inorder_position[root_value]

    root.left = build(left, split - 1)
    root.right = build(split + 1, right)
    return root

Example: preorder = [3,9,20,15,7], inorder = [9,3,15,20,7]. Root = 3. Inorder splits into [9] and [15,20,7]. Recursively build both sides using the same rule.

Type B — Inorder + Postorder

Postorder tells you the root because the root appears last. Find that root in inorder and split the remaining nodes into left and right subtrees. When consuming postorder from the end, build the right subtree first, then the left subtree.

Postorder → Root+Inorder → Split→Right → Left
Template — Inorder + Postorder
Map<Integer, Integer> inorderPosition = new HashMap<>();
int postorderIndex;

TreeNode build(int left, int right, int[] postorder) {
    if (left > right) return null;

    int rootValue = postorder[postorderIndex--];
    TreeNode root = new TreeNode(rootValue);
    int split = inorderPosition.get(rootValue);

    root.right = build(split + 1, right, postorder);
    root.left = build(left, split - 1, postorder);
    return root;
}
unordered_map<int, int> inorderPosition;
int postorderIndex;

TreeNode* build(int left, int right, vector<int>& postorder) {
    if (left > right) return nullptr;

    int rootValue = postorder[postorderIndex--];
    TreeNode* root = new TreeNode(rootValue);
    int split = inorderPosition[rootValue];

    root->right = build(split + 1, right, postorder);
    root->left = build(left, split - 1, postorder);
    return root;
}
inorder_position = {value: i for i, value in enumerate(inorder)}
postorder_index = len(postorder) - 1

def build(left, right):
    global postorder_index
    if left > right:
        return None

    root_value = postorder[postorder_index]
    postorder_index -= 1
    root = TreeNode(root_value)
    split = inorder_position[root_value]

    root.right = build(split + 1, right)
    root.left = build(left, split - 1)
    return root

Example: inorder = [9,3,15,20,7], postorder = [9,15,7,20,3]. Root = 3 because it is last in postorder. Inorder splits into [9] and [15,20,7]. From the end of postorder, build the right subtree first, then the left subtree.

Type C — Serialization & Deserialization

Serialization converts a tree into a sequence that preserves both values and structure. Deserialization reads that sequence and recursively rebuilds the same tree. Null markers are essential because they tell us where missing children occur.

Tree→Value + Null Markers→Serialized Data
Template — Serialization & Deserialization
void serialize(TreeNode root, StringBuilder result) {
    if (root == null) {
        result.append("#,");
        return;
    }

    result.append(root.val).append(",");
    serialize(root.left, result);
    serialize(root.right, result);
}

TreeNode deserialize(Queue<String> values) {
    String value = values.poll();
    if (value.equals("#")) return null;

    TreeNode root = new TreeNode(Integer.parseInt(value));
    root.left = deserialize(values);
    root.right = deserialize(values);
    return root;
}
void serialize(TreeNode* root, string& result) {
    if (root == nullptr) {
        result += "#,";
        return;
    }

    result += to_string(root->val) + ",";
    serialize(root->left, result);
    serialize(root->right, result);
}

TreeNode* deserialize(queue<string>& values) {
    string value = values.front();
    values.pop();

    if (value == "#") return nullptr;

    TreeNode* root = new TreeNode(stoi(value));
    root->left = deserialize(values);
    root->right = deserialize(values);
    return root;
}
def serialize(root, result):
    if root is None:
        result.append("#")
        return

    result.append(str(root.val))
    serialize(root.left, result)
    serialize(root.right, result)

def deserialize(values):
    value = next(values)
    if value == "#":
        return None

    root = TreeNode(int(value))
    root.left = deserialize(values)
    root.right = deserialize(values)
    return root

Example: A tree with root 1, left child 2, and right child 3 with children 4 and 5 can be serialized in preorder as 1,2,#,#,3,4,#,#,5,#,#. During deserialization, read each value in order; when # appears, return null.

Template — Tree Construction

Preorder + Inorder Construction
Map<Integer, Integer> inorderPosition = new HashMap<>();
int preorderIndex = 0;

TreeNode build(int left, int right, int[] preorder, int[] inorder) {
    if (left > right) return null;

    int rootValue = preorder[preorderIndex++];
    TreeNode root = new TreeNode(rootValue);
    int split = inorderPosition.get(rootValue);

    root.left = build(left, split - 1, preorder, inorder);
    root.right = build(split + 1, right, preorder, inorder);
    return root;
}
unordered_map<int, int> inorderPosition;
int preorderIndex = 0;

TreeNode* build(int left, int right, vector<int>& preorder, vector<int>& inorder) {
    if (left > right) return nullptr;

    int rootValue = preorder[preorderIndex++];
    TreeNode* root = new TreeNode(rootValue);
    int split = inorderPosition[rootValue];

    root->left = build(left, split - 1, preorder, inorder);
    root->right = build(split + 1, right, preorder, inorder);
    return root;
}
inorder_position = {value: i for i, value in enumerate(inorder)}
preorder_index = 0

def build(left, right):
    global preorder_index
    if left > right:
        return None

    root_value = preorder[preorder_index]
    preorder_index += 1
    root = TreeNode(root_value)
    split = inorder_position[root_value]

    root.left = build(left, split - 1)
    root.right = build(split + 1, right)
    return root

Practical Example — LC 105

Problem: Given preorder and inorder traversals of a binary tree, construct the original binary tree.

How to read it: Because preorder gives the root first and inorder tells us where that root splits the tree, this is a direct application of the Root → Split → Recurse pattern.

Example Input: preorder = [3,9,20,15,7], inorder = [9,3,15,20,7]

Example Output: The reconstructed tree has root 3, left child 9, and right subtree 20 → 15, 7.

Short Dry Run:

  1. Preorder starts with 3, so 3 is the root.
  2. In inorder, 3 appears between 9 and 20, so 9 is the left subtree and [15,20,7] is the right subtree.
  3. The next preorder value is 9, so it becomes the left child.
  4. The next root for the right range is 20; inorder splits it into 15 on the left and 7 on the right.
  5. All ranges are exhausted, so the tree is reconstructed.
Root = 3→9 | 3 | 15,20,7→Recurse
LC 105 — Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
class Solution {
    private int preorderIndex = 0;
    private Map<Integer, Integer> inorderPosition = new HashMap<>();

    public TreeNode buildTree(int[] preorder, int[] inorder) {
        for (int i = 0; i < inorder.length; i++) {
            inorderPosition.put(inorder[i], i);
        }
        return build(0, inorder.length - 1, preorder);
    }

    private TreeNode build(int left, int right, int[] preorder) {
        if (left > right) return null;

        int rootValue = preorder[preorderIndex++];
        TreeNode root = new TreeNode(rootValue);
        int split = inorderPosition.get(rootValue);

        root.left = build(left, split - 1, preorder);
        root.right = build(split + 1, right, preorder);
        return root;
    }
}
class Solution {
    unordered_map<int, int> inorderPosition;
    int preorderIndex = 0;

    TreeNode* build(int left, int right, vector<int>& preorder) {
        if (left > right) return nullptr;

        int rootValue = preorder[preorderIndex++];
        TreeNode* root = new TreeNode(rootValue);
        int split = inorderPosition[rootValue];

        root->left = build(left, split - 1, preorder);
        root->right = build(split + 1, right, preorder);
        return root;
    }

public:
    TreeNode* buildTree(vector<int>& preorder, vector<int>& inorder) {
        for (int i = 0; i < inorder.size(); i++) {
            inorderPosition[inorder[i]] = i;
        }
        return build(0, inorder.size() - 1, preorder);
    }
};
class Solution:
    def buildTree(self, preorder, inorder):
        inorder_position = {value: i for i, value in enumerate(inorder)}
        preorder_index = 0

        def build(left, right):
            nonlocal preorder_index
            if left > right:
                return None

            root_value = preorder[preorder_index]
            preorder_index += 1
            root = TreeNode(root_value)
            split = inorder_position[root_value]

            root.left = build(left, split - 1)
            root.right = build(split + 1, right)
            return root

        return build(0, len(inorder) - 1)

Why This Works

The traversal pair gives two different pieces of information. One traversal identifies which node is the root, while inorder identifies how the tree is divided. Once those two decisions are made, the left and right subtrees become smaller versions of the exact same problem.

Recursive rule: Root → find root in inorder → split into left/right ranges → recursively build both ranges.

Serialization & Deserialization Extension

LC 297 takes the same recursive tree thinking one step further. During serialization, visit each node and record null children using a marker. During deserialization, read the sequence in the same order and recursively rebuild the tree.

Tree→Value + Null Markers→Serialized Data
Serialized Data→Read Next→Recursive Tree

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting that preorder gives the root from the front, while postorder gives the root from the back.
  • Using the inorder position incorrectly and mixing up the left and right ranges.
  • Advancing the traversal index at the wrong time.
  • When consuming postorder backwards, building the left subtree before the right subtree.
  • Reconstructing without preserving subtree boundaries.
  • Assuming values alone are enough for serialization; null children must preserve structure.
  • Ignoring the duplicate-value constraint when using a value-to-index map; LC 105/106 assume unique node values.

Complexity

Construction

Time: O(n)

Space: O(n) for the map and recursion stack in the worst case.

Serialization

Time: O(n)

Space: O(n) for the serialized data and recursion.

Problem Progression

105

Construct from Preorder + Inorder

Learn the basic root-and-split reconstruction rule.

106

Construct from Inorder + Postorder

Reinforce the same structure using a different root position.

297

Serialize + Deserialize

Extend recursive construction into persistent tree representation.

Mental Trigger

Think: “One traversal tells me the root. Inorder tells me the split. Then recurse.”
When the problem asks you to reconstruct, serialize, or deserialize a binary tree, look for the information that identifies the root and the information that preserves subtree boundaries.

learning.html:
BINARY SEARCH TREE PATTERN

Binary Search Tree (BST)

Use the ordering property of a Binary Search Tree to search, validate, and reason about node positions efficiently. The central idea is simple: values smaller than a node belong to its left subtree, values larger belong to its right subtree, and inorder traversal visits BST values in sorted order.

Pattern Overview

A BST is not just a binary tree with two children. It has an ordering rule that lets you eliminate half of the search space at every decision. The same ordering property also gives powerful validation and traversal techniques.

Core pattern: Compare the target or current value with the node, use the BST ordering to choose a subtree, and use inorder traversal when the problem asks for sorted order or rank.

Mental Model

<

Left Subtree

Every value in a node's left subtree must be smaller than that node.

left < root
>

Right Subtree

Every value in a node's right subtree must be larger than that node.

right > root
IN

Inorder = Sorted

Inorder traversal of a valid BST produces values in strictly increasing order.

left → root → right

Recognition Clues

BSTThe problem explicitly gives a Binary Search Tree.
SearchFind a value and repeatedly choose left or right.
ValidateCheck whether the entire tree satisfies BST ordering.
Kth SmallestUse inorder because BST values appear in sorted order.
Sorted OrderInorder traversal exposes the BST's natural ordering.
Range ConstraintA node must satisfy bounds inherited from all its ancestors.

How the Pattern Works

Type A — BST Search

At each node, compare the target with the current value. If the target is smaller, move left. If it is larger, move right. If they are equal, the target is found.

target < root → left|target > root → right|equal → found
Template — BST Search
TreeNode searchBST(TreeNode root, int target) {
    while (root != null) {
        if (target == root.val) return root;
        if (target < root.val) root = root.left;
        else root = root.right;
    }
    return null;
}
TreeNode* searchBST(TreeNode* root, int target) {
    while (root != nullptr) {
        if (target == root->val) return root;
        if (target < root->val) root = root->left;
        else root = root->right;
    }
    return nullptr;
}
def search_bst(root, target):
    while root:
        if target == root.val:
            return root
        if target < root.val:
            root = root.left
        else:
            root = root.right
    return None

Example: Search for 7 in a BST rooted at 8. Since 7 < 8, move left. At 3, 7 > 3, move right. At 7, the target is found.

Type B — BST Validation

Checking only the immediate children is not enough. A node must satisfy restrictions created by every ancestor. Carry a valid range down the recursion and ensure every node stays inside that range.

lower bound≤node≤upper bound
Template — Validate BST
boolean isValidBST(TreeNode root) {
    return validate(root, Long.MIN_VALUE, Long.MAX_VALUE);
}

boolean validate(TreeNode node, long lowerBound, long upperBound) {
    if (node == null) return true;
    if (node.val <= lowerBound || node.val >= upperBound) return false;

    return validate(node.left, lowerBound, node.val) &&
           validate(node.right, node.val, upperBound);
}
bool validate(TreeNode* node, long long lowerBound, long long upperBound) {
    if (node == nullptr) return true;
    if (node->val <= lowerBound || node->val >= upperBound) return false;

    return validate(node->left, lowerBound, node->val) &&
           validate(node->right, node->val, upperBound);
}

bool isValidBST(TreeNode* root) {
    return validate(root, LLONG_MIN, LLONG_MAX);
}
def is_valid_bst(root):
    def validate(node, lower_bound, upper_bound):
        if not node:
            return True
        if not (lower_bound < node.val < upper_bound):
            return False

        return (validate(node.left, lower_bound, node.val) and
                validate(node.right, node.val, upper_bound))

    return validate(root, float('-inf'), float('inf'))

Example: If a node with value 6 appears inside the right subtree of 5, it is valid relative to 5. But if that same node appears inside the right subtree of 10, it violates the inherited lower bound because 6 must be greater than 10.

Type C — Kth Smallest Using Inorder

Inorder traversal of a BST visits nodes in sorted ascending order. Therefore, the kth visited node is the kth smallest value. You do not need to store the entire sorted sequence; stop as soon as the kth node is reached.

Inorder→1st smallest→2nd→...→kth
Template — Kth Smallest
int kthSmallest(TreeNode root, int k) {
    Stack<TreeNode> stack = new Stack<>();

    while (root != null || !stack.isEmpty()) {
        while (root != null) {
            stack.push(root);
            root = root.left;
        }

        root = stack.pop();
        k--;
        if (k == 0) return root.val;
        root = root.right;
    }

    return -1;
}
int kthSmallest(TreeNode* root, int k) {
    stack<TreeNode*> nodes;

    while (root != nullptr || !nodes.empty()) {
        while (root != nullptr) {
            nodes.push(root);
            root = root->left;
        }

        root = nodes.top();
        nodes.pop();
        k--;
        if (k == 0) return root->val;
        root = root->right;
    }

    return -1;
}
def kth_smallest(root, k):
    stack = []

    while root or stack:
        while root:
            stack.append(root)
            root = root.left

        root = stack.pop()
        k -= 1
        if k == 0:
            return root.val
        root = root.right

    return -1

Example: For BST values 3, 5, 6, 7, 8 and k = 3, inorder visits 3 → 5 → 6, so the 3rd smallest value is 6.

Practical Example — LC 98

Problem: Given the root of a binary tree, determine whether it is a valid Binary Search Tree.

How to read it: A BST rule applies to the entire subtree, not only to direct children. Therefore, each node needs the valid range created by its ancestors.

Example Input: root = [5,1,4,null,null,3,6]

Example Output: false

Short Dry Run:

  1. Start at 5 with range (−∞, +∞).
  2. Move left to 1, so its range becomes (−∞, 5); 1 is valid.
  3. Move right to 4, so its range becomes (5, +∞).
  4. 4 is not greater than 5, so it violates the inherited lower bound.
  5. Therefore the tree is not a valid BST.
4must be > 5→Violation
LC 98 — Validate Binary Search Tree
class Solution {
    public boolean isValidBST(TreeNode root) {
        return validate(root, Long.MIN_VALUE, Long.MAX_VALUE);
    }

    private boolean validate(TreeNode node, long lowerBound, long upperBound) {
        if (node == null) return true;
        if (node.val <= lowerBound || node.val >= upperBound) return false;

        return validate(node.left, lowerBound, node.val) &&
               validate(node.right, node.val, upperBound);
    }
}
class Solution {
    bool validate(TreeNode* node, long long lowerBound, long long upperBound) {
        if (node == nullptr) return true;
        if (node->val <= lowerBound || node->val >= upperBound) return false;

        return validate(node->left, lowerBound, node->val) &&
               validate(node->right, node->val, upperBound);
    }

public:
    bool isValidBST(TreeNode* root) {
        return validate(root, LLONG_MIN, LLONG_MAX);
    }
};
class Solution:
    def isValidBST(self, root):
        def validate(node, lower_bound, upper_bound):
            if not node:
                return True
            if not (lower_bound < node.val < upper_bound):
                return False

            return (validate(node.left, lower_bound, node.val) and
                    validate(node.right, node.val, upper_bound))

        return validate(root, float('-inf'), float('inf'))

Why This Works

The three problems look different, but they all exploit the same BST property. Search uses ordering to eliminate a subtree. Validation carries ordering constraints from ancestors. Kth smallest uses inorder because the BST's ordering makes inorder traversal sorted.

Same structure, different use: Search → use ordering to choose a path. Validate → enforce ordering constraints. Kth Smallest → exploit sorted inorder traversal.

Important BST Detail — Local vs Global Rules

A common mistake is checking only whether left child < parent < right child. That is not enough. Every node must satisfy the constraints imposed by all of its ancestors.

Left subtree→values below ancestor bounds|Right subtree→values above ancestor bounds

Common Mistakes

  • Checking only immediate children instead of maintaining global bounds.
  • Forgetting that a BST's inorder traversal is sorted.
  • Using normal binary-tree traversal logic when BST ordering can eliminate an entire subtree.
  • Forgetting to move left when target < current value and right when target > current value.
  • Using integer bounds that can overflow when node values are at the integer limits; wider bounds such as long are safer.
  • Assuming duplicate values are valid when the problem expects the strict BST rule.

Complexity

BST Search

Average: O(log n)

Worst case: O(n) for a skewed BST.

Validation

Time: O(n)

Space: O(h) for recursion, where h is tree height.

Kth Smallest

Time: O(h + k) in the iterative inorder approach.

Space: O(h) for the stack.

Balanced BST

Height: O(log n)

BST search benefits from small height; a skewed tree can degrade to O(n).

Problem Progression

98

Validate BST

Learn global ordering constraints and recursive bounds.

700

Search in BST

Reinforce using BST ordering to choose the next subtree.

230

Kth Smallest

Extend the pattern using inorder traversal and sorted order.

Mental Trigger

Think: “BST gives me an ordering advantage.”
If the problem asks you to search, validate ordering, or find a rank such as kth smallest, look for the BST property first: left < root < right, and remember that inorder traversal is sorted.

learning.html:
GRAPH TRAVERSAL PATTERN

Graph Representation & Traversal (DFS/BFS)

Traverse a graph systematically by visiting connected nodes while keeping track of what has already been explored. The same DFS/BFS foundation applies to grids, connected components, reachability, flood fill, and problems where you collect information during traversal.

Pattern Overview

Graph traversal is about systematically exploring a set of connected states. A graph can be represented using an adjacency list, while a grid can be treated as a graph where each cell is a node connected to its valid neighboring cells.

Core pattern: Start from a node or cell, mark it visited, explore its neighbors using DFS or BFS, and continue until every reachable state has been processed.

Mental Model

G

Graph Representation

Store which nodes are connected so traversal can quickly access neighbors.

node → neighbors
V

Visited State

Mark nodes or cells when they are discovered so they are not processed repeatedly.

visited[node] = true
T

Traverse

Use DFS for depth-first exploration or BFS for level-by-level exploration.

DFS / BFS → neighbors

Recognition Clues

ConnectedFind or count regions of connected nodes or cells.
ReachableDetermine whether states can be reached from a starting point.
VisitExplore every node or cell exactly once.
ComponentsCount separate connected groups in a graph or grid.
Flood FillSpread from one cell through valid neighboring cells.
Collect InformationCalculate area, count nodes, or gather other information during traversal.

How the Pattern Works

Type A — DFS Traversal

DFS explores one path as deeply as possible before backtracking. It is naturally expressed using recursion or an explicit stack.

Start→Mark Visited→Explore Neighbor→Recurse
Template — DFS Traversal
void dfs(int node, List<List<Integer>> graph, boolean[] visited) {
    visited[node] = true;

    for (int neighbor : graph.get(node)) {
        if (!visited[neighbor]) {
            dfs(neighbor, graph, visited);
        }
    }
}
void dfs(int node, vector<vector<int>>& graph, vector<bool>& visited) {
    visited[node] = true;

    for (int neighbor : graph[node]) {
        if (!visited[neighbor]) {
            dfs(neighbor, graph, visited);
        }
    }
}
def dfs(node, graph, visited):
    visited.add(node)

    for neighbor in graph[node]:
        if neighbor not in visited:
            dfs(neighbor, graph, visited)

Example: If 1 is connected to 2 and 3, DFS starts at 1, marks it visited, explores one neighbor deeply, then returns and explores the remaining neighbor.

Type B — BFS Traversal

BFS explores nodes level by level using a queue. It is especially useful when the traversal needs the nearest or shortest number of steps in an unweighted graph.

Start→Queue→Pop→Visit Neighbors
Template — BFS Traversal
void bfs(int start, List<List<Integer>> graph) {
    Queue<Integer> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
    boolean[] visited = new boolean[graph.size()];

    queue.offer(start);
    visited[start] = true;

    while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
        int node = queue.poll();

        for (int neighbor : graph.get(node)) {
            if (!visited[neighbor]) {
                visited[neighbor] = true;
                queue.offer(neighbor);
            }
        }
    }
}
void bfs(int start, vector<vector<int>>& graph) {
    queue<int> nodes;
    vector<bool> visited(graph.size(), false);

    nodes.push(start);
    visited[start] = true;

    while (!nodes.empty()) {
        int node = nodes.front();
        nodes.pop();

        for (int neighbor : graph[node]) {
            if (!visited[neighbor]) {
                visited[neighbor] = true;
                nodes.push(neighbor);
            }
        }
    }
}
from collections import deque

def bfs(start, graph):
    queue = deque([start])
    visited = {start}

    while queue:
        node = queue.popleft()

        for neighbor in graph[node]:
            if neighbor not in visited:
                visited.add(neighbor)
                queue.append(neighbor)

Example: Starting from node 1, BFS visits all nodes directly connected to 1 before moving to nodes one more edge away.

Type C — Grid DFS/BFS & Information Collection

A grid can be treated as an implicit graph. Each cell is a node and its valid neighboring cells are edges. During traversal, collect information such as the number of cells, area, or other properties of the connected component.

Cell→4 Directions→Valid Neighbor→Collect
Template — Grid Traversal
void dfs(int row, int col, int[][] grid) {
    if (row < 0 || row >= grid.length ||
        col < 0 || col >= grid[0].length ||
        grid[row][col] == 0) {
        return;
    }

    grid[row][col] = 0;

    dfs(row + 1, col, grid);
    dfs(row - 1, col, grid);
    dfs(row, col + 1, grid);
    dfs(row, col - 1, grid);
}
void dfs(int row, int col, vector<vector<int>>& grid) {
    if (row < 0 || row >= grid.size() ||
        col < 0 || col >= grid[0].size() ||
        grid[row][col] == 0) {
        return;
    }

    grid[row][col] = 0;

    dfs(row + 1, col, grid);
    dfs(row - 1, col, grid);
    dfs(row, col + 1, grid);
    dfs(row, col - 1, grid);
}
def dfs(row, col, grid):
    if (row < 0 or row >= len(grid) or
        col < 0 or col >= len(grid[0]) or
        grid[row][col] == 0):
        return

    grid[row][col] = 0

    dfs(row + 1, col, grid)
    dfs(row - 1, col, grid)
    dfs(row, col + 1, grid)
    dfs(row, col - 1, grid)

Example: Starting from one land cell, visit every connected land cell and increment an area counter for each visited cell. The same traversal can be reused for island counting, flood fill, or connected-region calculations.

Graph Representation

For explicit graphs, the adjacency list is the most common representation for traversal problems because it stores each node's neighbors directly and avoids allocating space for nonexistent edges.

0 → [1,2]|1 → [0,3]|2 → [0]|3 → [1]
Grid insight: You often do not need to build an adjacency list explicitly. The four or eight directional moves define the graph edges implicitly.

Practical Example — LC 200

Problem: Given a grid containing land and water, count the number of islands. An island is a group of connected land cells surrounded by water.

How to read it: Every unvisited land cell can be the start of a new connected component. Run DFS from it and mark the entire island visited.

Example Input: grid = [[1,1,0],[1,0,0],[0,0,1]]

Example Output: 2

Short Dry Run:

  1. Scan the grid and find the first land cell at (0,0).
  2. DFS visits its connected land cells: (0,0), (0,1), and (1,0).
  3. That entire region is one island, so increment the island count to 1.
  4. Continue scanning and find another unvisited land cell at (2,2).
  5. DFS visits that cell; increment the count to 2.
Unvisited Land→DFS Entire Component→count++
LC 200 — Number of Islands
class Solution {
    public int numIslands(char[][] grid) {
        int islands = 0;

        for (int row = 0; row < grid.length; row++) {
            for (int col = 0; col < grid[0].length; col++) {
                if (grid[row][col] == '1') {
                    islands++;
                    dfs(row, col, grid);
                }
            }
        }

        return islands;
    }

    private void dfs(int row, int col, char[][] grid) {
        if (row < 0 || row >= grid.length ||
            col < 0 || col >= grid[0].length ||
            grid[row][col] == '0') {
            return;
        }

        grid[row][col] = '0';

        dfs(row + 1, col, grid);
        dfs(row - 1, col, grid);
        dfs(row, col + 1, grid);
        dfs(row, col - 1, grid);
    }
}
class Solution {
    void dfs(int row, int col, vector<vector<char>>& grid) {
        if (row < 0 || row >= grid.size() ||
            col < 0 || col >= grid[0].size() ||
            grid[row][col] == '0') {
            return;
        }

        grid[row][col] = '0';

        dfs(row + 1, col, grid);
        dfs(row - 1, col, grid);
        dfs(row, col + 1, grid);
        dfs(row, col - 1, grid);
    }

public:
    int numIslands(vector<vector<char>>& grid) {
        int islands = 0;

        for (int row = 0; row < grid.size(); row++) {
            for (int col = 0; col < grid[0].size(); col++) {
                if (grid[row][col] == '1') {
                    islands++;
                    dfs(row, col, grid);
                }
            }
        }

        return islands;
    }
};
class Solution:
    def numIslands(self, grid):
        rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])
        islands = 0

        def dfs(row, col):
            if (row < 0 or row >= rows or
                col < 0 or col >= cols or
                grid[row][col] == '0'):
                return

            grid[row][col] = '0'

            dfs(row + 1, col)
            dfs(row - 1, col)
            dfs(row, col + 1)
            dfs(row, col - 1)

        for row in range(rows):
            for col in range(cols):
                if grid[row][col] == '1':
                    islands += 1
                    dfs(row, col)

        return islands

Why This Works

LC 200, LC 733, and LC 695 all use the same fundamental operation: explore every state belonging to a connected region exactly once. The difference is what the traversal does with the information it discovers.

Same traversal, different goal: LC 200 counts components. LC 733 spreads a replacement through a component. LC 695 collects the size of a component.

DFS vs BFS

DFS

Natural for recursive component exploration and problems where you fully process one region before returning.

Typical tools: recursion or stack.

BFS

Useful for level-by-level exploration and shortest-distance problems in unweighted graphs.

Typical tool: queue.

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting to mark a node or cell visited, causing repeated processing or infinite traversal.
  • Marking a grid cell visited too late instead of when it is discovered.
  • Using the wrong boundary checks for grid rows and columns.
  • Counting every land cell instead of counting each connected component once.
  • Building an explicit graph for a grid when directional movement already provides the edges.
  • Using recursion on extremely deep graphs or grids without considering stack depth.
  • Forgetting that BFS requires a queue while DFS uses recursion or a stack.

Complexity

Graph DFS / BFS

Time: O(V + E)

Space: O(V) for visited state and the traversal structure.

Grid Traversal

Time: O(R × C)

Space: O(R × C) in the worst case for visited state and traversal stack/queue.

Problem Progression

200

Number of Islands

Learn connected-component traversal on a grid.

733

Flood Fill

Reinforce traversal by modifying every reachable cell.

695

Max Area of Island

Extend traversal by collecting information from each component.

Mental Trigger

Think: “Start somewhere, mark it visited, explore neighbors, and process the whole connected region.”
When you see connected, reachable, visit, components, islands, flood fill, or a grid of neighboring states, think DFS/BFS traversal first.

GRAPH TRAVERSAL PATTERN

Multi-Source BFS

Use BFS when multiple starting points must spread simultaneously through a graph or grid. Instead of starting from one source, place every source into the queue at the beginning. BFS then expands all sources level by level, making the first time a state is reached equal to its shortest distance from the nearest source.

Pattern Overview

Multi-Source BFS is a variation of normal BFS where several nodes or cells are treated as starting points at distance 0. All sources enter the queue before traversal begins, so the search expands outward from every source simultaneously.

Core pattern: Put all sources into the queue first, mark them visited, then run normal BFS. Because BFS processes states level by level, each newly reached state gets its shortest distance from the nearest source.

Mental Model

S

Multiple Sources

Every starting source enters the queue before BFS begins.

queue ← all sources
0

Distance Zero

All source nodes begin at distance 0 because they are already reached.

distance[source] = 0
→

Level Expansion

BFS expands outward one level at a time from all sources simultaneously.

next = distance + 1

Recognition Clues

Shortest DistanceFind the minimum number of steps from any source.
NearestFind the closest source, gate, cell, or object.
RottingA state spreads simultaneously from multiple starting positions.
SpreadSomething expands outward one step at a time.
Multiple Starting PointsSeveral cells or nodes are active at time 0.
Minimum TimeCalculate how long it takes for a process to reach all possible states.

How the Pattern Works

Type A — Multi-Source BFS on a Grid

Scan the grid and put every source into the queue before starting BFS. Then process the queue level by level. Every neighboring unvisited cell is reached at the current distance plus one.

All Sources→Queue→Expand Level→Expand Again
Template — Multi-Source BFS
Queue<int[]> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();

// Add every source first.
for (int row = 0; row < rows; row++) {
    for (int col = 0; col < cols; col++) {
        if (isSource(row, col)) {
            queue.offer(new int[]{row, col});
        }
    }
}

int distance = 0;
while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
    int levelSize = queue.size();

    for (int i = 0; i < levelSize; i++) {
        int[] cell = queue.poll();

        for (int[] direction : directions) {
            int nextRow = cell[0] + direction[0];
            int nextCol = cell[1] + direction[1];

            if (isValid(nextRow, nextCol) && isUnvisited(nextRow, nextCol)) {
                markVisited(nextRow, nextCol);
                queue.offer(new int[]{nextRow, nextCol});
            }
        }
    }

    distance++;
}
queue<pair<int, int>> nodes;

// Add every source first.
for (int row = 0; row < rows; row++) {
    for (int col = 0; col < cols; col++) {
        if (isSource(row, col)) {
            nodes.push({row, col});
        }
    }
}

int distance = 0;
while (!nodes.empty()) {
    int levelSize = nodes.size();

    for (int i = 0; i < levelSize; i++) {
        auto [row, col] = nodes.front();
        nodes.pop();

        for (auto [dr, dc] : directions) {
            int nextRow = row + dr;
            int nextCol = col + dc;

            if (isValid(nextRow, nextCol) && isUnvisited(nextRow, nextCol)) {
                markVisited(nextRow, nextCol);
                nodes.push({nextRow, nextCol});
            }
        }
    }

    distance++;
}
from collections import deque

queue = deque()

# Add every source first.
for row in range(rows):
    for col in range(cols):
        if is_source(row, col):
            queue.append((row, col))

 distance = 0
while queue:
    level_size = len(queue)

    for _ in range(level_size):
        row, col = queue.popleft()

        for dr, dc in directions:
            next_row = row + dr
            next_col = col + dc

            if is_valid(next_row, next_col) and is_unvisited(next_row, next_col):
                mark_visited(next_row, next_col)
                queue.append((next_row, next_col))

    distance += 1

Example: If cells A, B, and C are all sources, put A, B, and C into the queue first. BFS then explores their distance-1 neighbors together, followed by their distance-2 neighbors.

Type B — Shortest Distance from the Nearest Source

When every source begins at distance 0, the first time BFS reaches another node or cell is through the shortest possible route from any source. Store the distance when the state is discovered.

Source = 0→Neighbor = 1→Next = 2→...
Template — Nearest Source Distance
Queue<int[]> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
int[][] distance = new int[rows][cols];

for (int row = 0; row < rows; row++) {
    Arrays.fill(distance[row], -1);
}

for (int row = 0; row < rows; row++) {
    for (int col = 0; col < cols; col++) {
        if (isSource(row, col)) {
            queue.offer(new int[]{row, col});
            distance[row][col] = 0;
        }
    }
}

while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
    int[] cell = queue.poll();

    for (int[] direction : directions) {
        int nextRow = cell[0] + direction[0];
        int nextCol = cell[1] + direction[1];

        if (isValid(nextRow, nextCol) && distance[nextRow][nextCol] == -1) {
            distance[nextRow][nextCol] = distance[cell[0]][cell[1]] + 1;
            queue.offer(new int[]{nextRow, nextCol});
        }
    }
}
queue<pair<int, int>> nodes;
vector<vector<int>> distance(rows, vector<int>(cols, -1));

for (int row = 0; row < rows; row++) {
    for (int col = 0; col < cols; col++) {
        if (isSource(row, col)) {
            nodes.push({row, col});
            distance[row][col] = 0;
        }
    }
}

while (!nodes.empty()) {
    auto [row, col] = nodes.front();
    nodes.pop();

    for (auto [dr, dc] : directions) {
        int nextRow = row + dr;
        int nextCol = col + dc;

        if (isValid(nextRow, nextCol) && distance[nextRow][nextCol] == -1) {
            distance[nextRow][nextCol] = distance[row][col] + 1;
            nodes.push({nextRow, nextCol});
        }
    }
}
from collections import deque

queue = deque()
distance = [[-1] * cols for _ in range(rows)]

for row in range(rows):
    for col in range(cols):
        if is_source(row, col):
            queue.append((row, col))
            distance[row][col] = 0

while queue:
    row, col = queue.popleft()

    for dr, dc in directions:
        next_row = row + dr
        next_col = col + dc

        if is_valid(next_row, next_col) and distance[next_row][next_col] == -1:
            distance[next_row][next_col] = distance[row][col] + 1
            queue.append((next_row, next_col))

Example: If two sources are at distances 0, a cell reached from source A in 2 steps and source B in 4 steps receives distance 2 because BFS reaches it from the nearest source first.

Type C — BFS Spread / Time Simulation

Some problems describe a process that spreads simultaneously every minute or every round. Each BFS level represents one unit of time. Process the current queue as one complete time step, then process everything newly added as the next step.

Time 0→All Sources→Time 1→Time 2
Template — BFS Spread Simulation
int time = 0;

while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
    int levelSize = queue.size();

    for (int i = 0; i < levelSize; i++) {
        int[] current = queue.poll();

        for (int[] direction : directions) {
            int nextRow = current[0] + direction[0];
            int nextCol = current[1] + direction[1];

            if (isValid(nextRow, nextCol) && canSpread(nextRow, nextCol)) {
                spread(nextRow, nextCol);
                queue.offer(new int[]{nextRow, nextCol});
            }
        }
    }

    time++;
}
int time = 0;

while (!nodes.empty()) {
    int levelSize = nodes.size();

    for (int i = 0; i < levelSize; i++) {
        auto [row, col] = nodes.front();
        nodes.pop();

        for (auto [dr, dc] : directions) {
            int nextRow = row + dr;
            int nextCol = col + dc;

            if (isValid(nextRow, nextCol) && canSpread(nextRow, nextCol)) {
                spread(nextRow, nextCol);
                nodes.push({nextRow, nextCol});
            }
        }
    }

    time++;
}
time = 0

    for _ in range(level_size):
        row, col = queue.popleft()

        for dr, dc in directions:
            next_row = row + dr
            next_col = col + dc

            if is_valid(next_row, next_col) and can_spread(next_row, next_col):
                spread(next_row, next_col)
                queue.append((next_row, next_col))

    time += 1

Example: In a spreading process, all currently active cells affect their neighbors during the same minute. The newly affected cells do not spread again until the next BFS level.

Why Multiple Sources Matter

Running separate BFS searches from every source would repeat work and can become inefficient. Multi-Source BFS combines all sources into one traversal. Because they all start in the queue together, the first arrival at every state automatically represents the nearest source.

Key insight: Instead of asking “How far is this cell from source A, then source B, then source C?”, let all sources compete simultaneously through one BFS.

Practical Example — LC 994

Problem: Given a grid containing fresh and rotten oranges, every minute a rotten orange makes adjacent fresh oranges rotten. Return the minimum number of minutes until no fresh orange remains, or -1 if some fresh orange can never rot.

How to read it: Every rotten orange is a source at time 0. Put all rotten oranges into the queue first. Each BFS level represents one minute of spreading.

Example Input: grid = [[2,1,1],[1,1,0],[0,1,1]]

Example Output: 4

Short Dry Run:

  1. Time 0: the rotten orange at (0,0) is the initial source.
  2. Time 1: its neighbors (0,1) and (1,0) become rotten.
  3. Time 2: newly rotten oranges spread to the next fresh cells.
  4. Time 3: the spread reaches the remaining fresh oranges.
  5. Time 4: the final fresh orange becomes rotten, so the answer is 4.
All Rotten→Queue→1 min / level→Answer = 4
LC 994 — Rotting Oranges
class Solution {
    public int orangesRotting(int[][] grid) {
        int rows = grid.length;
        int cols = grid[0].length;
        Queue<int[]> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
        int fresh = 0;

        for (int row = 0; row < rows; row++) {
            for (int col = 0; col < cols; col++) {
                if (grid[row][col] == 2) {
                    queue.offer(new int[]{row, col});
                } else if (grid[row][col] == 1) {
                    fresh++;
                }
            }
        }

        int minutes = 0;
        int[][] directions = {{1,0},{-1,0},{0,1},{0,-1}};

        while (!queue.isEmpty() && fresh > 0) {
            int levelSize = queue.size();

            for (int i = 0; i < levelSize; i++) {
                int[] current = queue.poll();

                for (int[] direction : directions) {
                    int nextRow = current[0] + direction[0];
                    int nextCol = current[1] + direction[1];

                    if (nextRow < 0 || nextRow >= rows ||
                        nextCol < 0 || nextCol >= cols ||
                        grid[nextRow][nextCol] != 1) {
                        continue;
                    }

                    grid[nextRow][nextCol] = 2;
                    fresh--;
                    queue.offer(new int[]{nextRow, nextCol});
                }
            }

            minutes++;
        }

        return fresh == 0 ? minutes : -1;
    }
}

from collections import deque

class Solution:
    def orangesRotting(self, grid):
        rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])
        queue = deque()
        fresh = 0

        for row in range(rows):
            for col in range(cols):
                if grid[row][col] == 2:
                    queue.append((row, col))
                elif grid[row][col] == 1:
                    fresh += 1

        minutes = 0
        directions = [(1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)]

        while queue and fresh > 0:
            for _ in range(len(queue)):
                row, col = queue.popleft()

                for dr, dc in directions:
                    next_row = row + dr
                    next_col = col + dc

                    if (next_row < 0 or next_row >= rows or
                        next_col < 0 or next_col >= cols or
                        grid[next_row][next_col] != 1):
                        continue

                    grid[next_row][next_col] = 2
                    fresh -= 1
                    queue.append((next_row, next_col))

            minutes += 1

        return minutes if fresh == 0 else -1

Why This Works

LC 994, LC 542, and LC 286 all rely on the same principle: multiple starting points expand simultaneously, and BFS guarantees that the first time a state is reached is through the minimum number of steps from the nearest source.

Same traversal, different goal: LC 994 measures spread time. LC 542 records nearest-source distance. LC 286 propagates distances through a grid while respecting blocked cells.

Important BFS Detail — Level Size

When the problem asks for time, minutes, rounds, or levels, capture queue.size() before processing the current level. Every item already in the queue belongs to the same time step. Newly added states belong to the next time step.

levelSize = queue.size()→process exactly this level→time++

Common Mistakes

  • Starting BFS separately from every source instead of putting all sources into one queue.
  • Forgetting that every source begins at distance 0.
  • Marking a state visited when it is removed instead of when it is discovered, which can enqueue it multiple times.
  • Incrementing time for every node instead of every BFS level.
  • Forgetting to check whether unreachable targets remain after BFS finishes.
  • Confusing “nearest source” with an arbitrary source; Multi-Source BFS guarantees the nearest one because of BFS ordering.
  • Forgetting obstacle or boundary checks when traversing a grid.

Complexity

Graph Multi-Source BFS

Time: O(V + E)

Space: O(V) for the queue and visited or distance state.

Grid Multi-Source BFS

Time: O(R × C)

Space: O(R × C) in the worst case.

Problem Progression

994

Rotting Oranges

Learn to start BFS from multiple sources and measure spread time.

542

01 Matrix

Reinforce shortest distance to the nearest source.

286

Walls and Gates

Extend the pattern to distance propagation with obstacles.

Mental Trigger

Think: “Many sources start at the same time.”
When you see shortest distance, nearest, rotting, spread, minimum time, or several starting points, put all sources into the BFS queue first and let the levels propagate outward.

GRAPH DEPENDENCY PATTERN

Topological Sort

Topological Sort orders the vertices of a directed acyclic graph so that every dependency appears before the node that depends on it. The pattern is especially useful for prerequisites, dependency resolution, scheduling, build systems, and directed cycle detection.

Pattern Overview

A directed edge A → B means B depends on A, so A must come before B. A topological ordering is possible only when the directed graph contains no cycle. The two standard approaches are Kahn's Algorithm, which repeatedly removes nodes with zero indegree, and DFS, which detects cycles using the recursion state of each node.

Core pattern: Represent dependencies as directed edges, identify nodes that currently have no unresolved prerequisites, process them, and update the remaining dependency counts. If every node can be processed, a valid topological order exists; otherwise, a cycle blocks the ordering.

Mental Model

IN

Indegree

Indegree tells you how many prerequisites are still blocking a node.

indegree[node] = prerequisites
Q

Ready Queue

Nodes with indegree 0 have no remaining dependencies and can be processed now.

indegree == 0 → queue
→

Remove Dependency

Processing a node removes one dependency from each of its outgoing neighbors.

indegree[neighbor]--

Recognition Clues

DependencyOne task must happen before another.
PrerequisiteA course, task, or state requires another first.
Course ScheduleDetermine whether prerequisites can all be satisfied.
DAGThe graph is directed and should contain no cycles.
Valid OrderReturn an ordering that respects every dependency.
Cycle DetectionDetermine whether circular dependencies make ordering impossible.

How the Pattern Works

Type A — Kahn's Algorithm / Indegree BFS

Kahn's Algorithm repeatedly chooses nodes with indegree 0. These nodes have no unresolved prerequisites, so they can safely be added to the topological order. After processing one, decrease the indegree of its outgoing neighbors.

Indegree 0→Queue→Process→Decrease Neighbors
Template — Kahn's Algorithm
int[] indegree = new int[n];
List<List<Integer>> graph = new ArrayList<>();

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    graph.add(new ArrayList<>());
}

for (int[] edge : edges) {
    int from = edge[0];
    int to = edge[1];
    graph.get(from).add(to);
    indegree[to]++;
}

Queue<Integer> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
for (int node = 0; node < n; node++) {
    if (indegree[node] == 0) {
        queue.offer(node);
    }
}

while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
    int node = queue.poll();

    for (int neighbor : graph.get(node)) {
        indegree[neighbor]--;
        if (indegree[neighbor] == 0) {
            queue.offer(neighbor);
        }
    }
}
vector<vector<int>> graph(n);
vector<int> indegree(n, 0);

for (auto& edge : edges) {
    int from = edge[0];
    int to = edge[1];
    graph[from].push_back(to);
    indegree[to]++;
}

queue<int> nodes;
for (int node = 0; node < n; node++) {
    if (indegree[node] == 0) {
        nodes.push(node);
    }
}

while (!nodes.empty()) {
    int node = nodes.front();
    nodes.pop();

    for (int neighbor : graph[node]) {
        indegree[neighbor]--;
        if (indegree[neighbor] == 0) {
            nodes.push(neighbor);
        }
    }
}
from collections import deque

graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]
indegree = [0] * n

for source, target in edges:
    graph[source].append(target)
    indegree[target] += 1

queue = deque()
for node in range(n):
    if indegree[node] == 0:
        queue.append(node)

while queue:
    node = queue.popleft()

    for neighbor in graph[node]:
        indegree[neighbor] -= 1
        if indegree[neighbor] == 0:
            queue.append(neighbor)

Example: If A → B and B → C, A starts with indegree 0. Process A, which makes B's indegree 0. Then process B, which makes C's indegree 0. The order becomes A → B → C.

Type B — DFS Topological Sort

DFS can build a topological ordering by placing a node after all of its outgoing neighbors have been completely explored. A three-state array detects cycles: 0 = unvisited, 1 = currently visiting, and 2 = completely processed.

Unvisited→Visiting→Processed→Reverse Finish Order
Template — DFS Topological Sort
boolean dfs(int node, List<List<Integer>> graph, int[] state, List<Integer> order) {
    if (state[node] == 1) return false;
    if (state[node] == 2) return true;

    state[node] = 1;

    for (int neighbor : graph.get(node)) {
        if (!dfs(neighbor, graph, state, order)) {
            return false;
        }
    }

    state[node] = 2;
    order.add(node);
    return true;
}
bool dfs(int node, vector<vector<int>>& graph,
         vector<int>& state, vector<int>& order) {
    if (state[node] == 1) return false;
    if (state[node] == 2) return true;

    state[node] = 1;

    for (int neighbor : graph[node]) {
        if (!dfs(neighbor, graph, state, order)) {
            return false;
        }
    }

    state[node] = 2;
    order.push_back(node);
    return true;
}
def dfs(node, graph, state, order):
    if state[node] == 1:
        return False
    if state[node] == 2:
        return True

    state[node] = 1

    for neighbor in graph[node]:
        if not dfs(neighbor, graph, state, order):
            return False

    state[node] = 2
    order.append(node)
    return True

Example: For A → B → C, DFS reaches C first and finishes it, then B, then A. The finish order is C, B, A, so reversing it gives A, B, C.

Type C — Cycle Detection & Eventual Safe States

A directed cycle means there is no valid topological ordering for the nodes trapped in that cycle. In LC 802, a node is eventually safe if every path starting from it eventually reaches a terminal node instead of entering a cycle. This can be understood through reverse-graph topological processing.

Terminal→Safe←Reverse Edges←Safe Dependency
Template — Reverse Graph / Safe States
List<List<Integer>> reverseGraph = new ArrayList<>();
int[] outdegree = new int[n];

for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    reverseGraph.add(new ArrayList<>());
    outdegree[i] = graph[i].size();
}

Queue<Integer> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
for (int node = 0; node < n; node++) {
    if (outdegree[node] == 0) {
        queue.offer(node);
    }
}

while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
    int safeNode = queue.poll();

    for (int previous : reverseGraph.get(safeNode)) {
        outdegree[previous]--;
        if (outdegree[previous] == 0) {
            queue.offer(previous);
        }
    }
}
vector<vector<int>> reverseGraph(n);
vector<int> outdegree(n, 0);

for (int node = 0; node < n; node++) {
    outdegree[node] = graph[node].size();
    for (int neighbor : graph[node]) {
        reverseGraph[neighbor].push_back(node);
    }
}

queue<int> nodes;
for (int node = 0; node < n; node++) {
    if (outdegree[node] == 0) {
        nodes.push(node);
    }
}

while (!nodes.empty()) {
    int safeNode = nodes.front();
    nodes.pop();

    for (int previous : reverseGraph[safeNode]) {
        outdegree[previous]--;
        if (outdegree[previous] == 0) {
            nodes.push(previous);
        }
    }
}
from collections import deque

reverse_graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]
outdegree = [len(graph[node]) for node in range(n)]

for node in range(n):
    for neighbor in graph[node]:
        reverse_graph[neighbor].append(node)

queue = deque()
for node in range(n):
    if outdegree[node] == 0:
        queue.append(node)

while queue:
    safe_node = queue.popleft()

    for previous in reverse_graph[safe_node]:
        outdegree[previous] -= 1
        if outdegree[previous] == 0:
            queue.append(previous)

Example: A terminal node has no outgoing edges, so it is safe. Any node whose every outgoing path eventually reaches a safe node can also become safe. Nodes remaining with unresolved outgoing edges belong to or lead into cycles.

Practical Example — LC 207

Problem: Given a number of courses and prerequisite pairs, determine whether it is possible to finish all courses.

How to read it: Each prerequisite creates a directed dependency. If a cycle exists, every course in that cycle remains blocked. Kahn's Algorithm detects this because those nodes never reach indegree 0.

Example Input: numCourses = 2, prerequisites = [[1,0]]

Example Output: true

Short Dry Run:

  1. Edge 0 → 1 means course 0 must be completed before course 1.
  2. Indegree of course 0 is 0, so put 0 into the queue.
  3. Process course 0 and decrease course 1's indegree from 1 to 0.
  4. Course 1 is now ready, so add it to the queue.
  5. Both courses are processed, so there is no cycle and all courses can be completed.
0 → 1→0 first→1 becomes ready
LC 207 — Course Schedule
class Solution {
    public boolean canFinish(int numCourses, int[][] prerequisites) {
        List<List<Integer>> graph = new ArrayList<>();
        int[] indegree = new int[numCourses];

        for (int i = 0; i < numCourses; i++) {
            graph.add(new ArrayList<>());
        }

        for (int[] prerequisite : prerequisites) {
            int course = prerequisite[0];
            int required = prerequisite[1];
            graph.get(required).add(course);
            indegree[course]++;
        }

        Queue<Integer> queue = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (int course = 0; course < numCourses; course++) {
            if (indegree[course] == 0) {
                queue.offer(course);
            }
        }

        int processed = 0;

        while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
            int course = queue.poll();
            processed++;

            for (int nextCourse : graph.get(course)) {
                indegree[nextCourse]--;
                if (indegree[nextCourse] == 0) {
                    queue.offer(nextCourse);
                }
            }
        }

        return processed == numCourses;
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    bool canFinish(int numCourses, vector<vector<int>>& prerequisites) {
        vector<vector<int>> graph(numCourses);
        vector<int> indegree(numCourses, 0);

        for (auto& prerequisite : prerequisites) {
            int course = prerequisite[0];
            int required = prerequisite[1];
            graph[required].push_back(course);
            indegree[course]++;
        }

        queue<int> courses;
        for (int course = 0; course < numCourses; course++) {
            if (indegree[course] == 0) {
                courses.push(course);
            }
        }

        int processed = 0;

        while (!courses.empty()) {
            int course = courses.front();
            courses.pop();
            processed++;

            for (int nextCourse : graph[course]) {
                indegree[nextCourse]--;
                if (indegree[nextCourse] == 0) {
                    courses.push(nextCourse);
                }
            }
        }

        return processed == numCourses;
    }
};
from collections import deque

class Solution:
    def canFinish(self, numCourses, prerequisites):
        graph = [[] for _ in range(numCourses)]
        indegree = [0] * numCourses

        for course, required in prerequisites:
            graph[required].append(course)
            indegree[course] += 1

        queue = deque()
        for course in range(numCourses):
            if indegree[course] == 0:
                queue.append(course)

        processed = 0

        while queue:
            course = queue.popleft()
            processed += 1

            for next_course in graph[course]:
                indegree[next_course] -= 1
                if indegree[next_course] == 0:
                    queue.append(next_course)

        return processed == numCourses

Why This Works

LC 207, LC 210, and LC 802 all use dependency structure. LC 207 asks whether every node can be processed, LC 210 asks for the actual processing order, and LC 802 identifies nodes that can eventually reach terminal states without entering a cycle.

Same dependency idea, different output: LC 207 → can an order exist? LC 210 → what is the order? LC 802 → which nodes are guaranteed to avoid cycles?

Important Detail — Cycle Detection with Kahn's Algorithm

If the graph contains a cycle, every node inside that cycle has at least one unresolved incoming dependency. Therefore, those nodes never reach indegree 0. The easiest check is to compare the number of processed nodes with n.

processed == n→No Cycle|processed < n→Cycle Exists

Kahn's Algorithm vs DFS

Kahn's Algorithm

Uses indegree and a queue. Naturally produces a topological ordering and makes cycle detection easy by counting processed nodes.

Core state: indegree + queue.

DFS

Uses recursion states to detect back edges and places nodes after their dependencies finish.

Core state: 0 / 1 / 2 visitation states.

Common Mistakes

  • Reversing the dependency edge. If A is a prerequisite for B, the graph should contain A → B.
  • Forgetting to increment indegree for every dependency edge.
  • Adding nodes to the queue before all their prerequisites have been processed.
  • Assuming any BFS order is automatically a topological order; only nodes with indegree 0 are currently safe to process.
  • Forgetting to check whether all nodes were processed when detecting cycles.
  • In DFS, confusing a currently visiting node with a completely processed node.
  • Forgetting to reverse DFS finish order when constructing the final topological ordering.

Complexity

Kahn's Algorithm

Time: O(V + E)

Space: O(V + E) for the graph, indegree array, and queue.

DFS Topological Sort

Time: O(V + E)

Space: O(V + E) for the graph, state array, result, and recursion stack.

Problem Progression

207

Course Schedule

Learn dependency modeling and cycle detection with Kahn's Algorithm.

210

Course Schedule II

Extend the pattern by returning an actual valid topological order.

802

Eventual Safe States

Reinforce cycle reasoning through reverse-graph dependency processing.

Mental Trigger

Think: “Dependency means directed edges; prerequisites mean indegree; no prerequisites means ready.”
When you see dependency, prerequisite, course schedule, DAG, valid ordering, or circular dependency, think Topological Sort. Start with Kahn's Algorithm unless DFS fits the problem more naturally.
