learning.html:
BACKTRACKING PATTERN

Constraint-Based Search

Build a solution step by step while continuously checking whether the current partial solution violates any constraint. The moment a placement becomes invalid, stop exploring that branch and backtrack.

Pattern Overview

Constraint-Based Search is a backtracking pattern where every choice must satisfy one or more rules before the search can continue. Instead of generating every possible arrangement and validating it at the end, we validate each decision immediately.

Core Idea: Choose → Validate → Explore → Undo. If a choice violates a constraint, reject it immediately and try another choice.

Mental Model

1

Choose

Place a candidate value, position, or object.

make a choice
2

Validate

Check whether the current state satisfies all constraints.

isValid(choice)
3

Backtrack

Undo the choice and try another possibility.

remove choice

Recognition Clues

N-QueensPlace queens without sharing a row, column, or diagonal.
SudokuFill cells while respecting row, column, and box constraints.
Valid PlacementEvery new placement must satisfy the current constraints.
Partial SolutionThe problem builds an answer one decision at a time.
Reject EarlyInvalid branches should stop immediately.
Undo & Try AgainAfter exploring a choice, restore the previous state.

How the Pattern Works

  1. Start with an empty or partially completed state.
  2. Choose the next position or variable that needs a value.
  3. Try each possible candidate.
  4. Validate the candidate against every relevant constraint.
  5. If valid, place it and recursively continue.
  6. If the recursive search fails, undo the choice.
  7. Try the next candidate.
  8. Stop when a complete valid solution is found or every possibility has been exhausted.
Choice→Validate→Recurse→Undo

Type A: Placement Constraint Search

Use this when the main task is to place objects into positions while maintaining constraints between already placed objects.

Example: In N-Queens, before placing a queen at (row, col), check whether another queen already occupies the same column or either diagonal.

Type B: Constraint Satisfaction with State Tracking

Use additional state structures when checking constraints repeatedly would otherwise require scanning the entire partial solution.

C

Columns

Track which columns are already occupied.

usedColumns
D

Diagonals

Track occupied diagonals using derived keys.

row - col
S

Secondary Diagonal

Track the opposite diagonal direction.

row + col

Type C: Counting Valid Solutions

Sometimes the task is not to return one valid configuration but to count how many valid configurations exist. The same constraint-based search is used, but every complete valid state contributes to the answer.

Difference: Find one solution → stop at the first complete state. Count solutions → continue searching after every complete valid state.

Type D: Constraint Filling

Problems such as Sudoku extend the same idea from placement into value assignment. At each empty position, try possible values, validate the row, column, and subgrid constraints, then continue recursively.

Practical Example — LC 51: N-Queens

Question: Place n queens on an n × n chessboard so that no two queens attack each other.

How to read it: We are building a board one row at a time. For every row, we need to choose a column that does not conflict with previously placed queens.

Why this pattern fits: Every placement creates constraints for future placements. If a queen cannot be placed safely, that branch is invalid and we backtrack.

Example Input: n = 4

Example Output: [[".Q..","...Q","Q...","..Q."],["..Q.","Q...","...Q",".Q.."]]

Short Dry Run: Start with row 0. Try column 0 and place a queen. Move to row 1 and test columns; conflicting positions are rejected. Continue until a row has no valid column, then remove the previous queen and try another column. When all 4 rows are filled, one valid board has been found.

LC 51 — Java Solution
class Solution {
    List<List<String>> result = new ArrayList<>();
    Set<Integer> usedColumns = new HashSet<>();
    Set<Integer> usedDiagonals = new HashSet<>();
    Set<Integer> usedAntiDiagonals = new HashSet<>();

    public List<List<String>> solveNQueens(int n) {
        char[][] board = new char[n][n];
        for (char[] row : board) Arrays.fill(row, '.');
        backtrack(0, n, board);
        return result;
    }

    private void backtrack(int row, int n, char[][] board) {
        if (row == n) {
            List<String> solution = new ArrayList<>();
            for (char[] currentRow : board) solution.add(new String(currentRow));
            result.add(solution);
            return;
        }

        for (int col = 0; col < n; col++) {
            int diagonal = row - col;
            int antiDiagonal = row + col;
            if (usedColumns.contains(col) || usedDiagonals.contains(diagonal) || usedAntiDiagonals.contains(antiDiagonal)) continue;

            board[row][col] = 'Q';
            usedColumns.add(col);
            usedDiagonals.add(diagonal);
            usedAntiDiagonals.add(antiDiagonal);

            backtrack(row + 1, n, board);

            board[row][col] = '.';
            usedColumns.remove(col);
            usedDiagonals.remove(diagonal);
            usedAntiDiagonals.remove(antiDiagonal);
        }
    }
}
class Solution {
    vector<vector<string>> result;
    unordered_set<int> usedColumns, usedDiagonals, usedAntiDiagonals;

public:
    vector<vector<string>> solveNQueens(int n) {
        vector<string> board(n, string(n, '.'));
        backtrack(0, n, board);
        return result;
    }

private:
    void backtrack(int row, int n, vector<string>& board) {
        if (row == n) {
            result.push_back(board);
            return;
        }

        for (int col = 0; col < n; col++) {
            int diagonal = row - col;
            int antiDiagonal = row + col;
            if (usedColumns.count(col) || usedDiagonals.count(diagonal) || usedAntiDiagonals.count(antiDiagonal)) continue;

            board[row][col] = 'Q';
            usedColumns.insert(col);
            usedDiagonals.insert(diagonal);
            usedAntiDiagonals.insert(antiDiagonal);

            backtrack(row + 1, n, board);

            board[row][col] = '.';
            usedColumns.erase(col);
            usedDiagonals.erase(diagonal);
            usedAntiDiagonals.erase(antiDiagonal);
        }
    }
};
class Solution:
    def solveNQueens(self, n: int) -> list[list[str]]:
        result = []
        used_columns = set()
        used_diagonals = set()
        used_anti_diagonals = set()
        board = [['.'] * n for _ in range(n)]

        def backtrack(row):
            if row == n:
                result.append([''.join(current_row) for current_row in board])
                return

            for col in range(n):
                diagonal = row - col
                anti_diagonal = row + col
                if col in used_columns or diagonal in used_diagonals or anti_diagonal in used_anti_diagonals:
                    continue

                board[row][col] = 'Q'
                used_columns.add(col)
                used_diagonals.add(diagonal)
                used_anti_diagonals.add(anti_diagonal)

                backtrack(row + 1)

                board[row][col] = '.'
                used_columns.remove(col)
                used_diagonals.remove(diagonal)
                used_anti_diagonals.remove(anti_diagonal)

        backtrack(0)
        return result

Why the Example Works

The search never explores a placement that already violates a column or diagonal constraint. The sets give constant-time average membership checks, allowing the algorithm to reject invalid positions before descending deeper into the search tree.

Templates

Constraint-Based Backtracking Template
void backtrack(State state) {
    if (isComplete(state)) {
        recordSolution(state);
        return;
    }

    for (Choice choice : choices) {
        if (!isValid(choice, state)) continue;

        makeChoice(choice, state);
        backtrack(state);
        undoChoice(choice, state);
    }
}
void backtrack(State& state) {
    if (isComplete(state)) {
        recordSolution(state);
        return;
    }

    for (const auto& choice : choices) {
        if (!isValid(choice, state)) continue;
        makeChoice(choice, state);
        backtrack(state);
        undoChoice(choice, state);
    }
}
def backtrack(state):
    if is_complete(state):
        record_solution(state)
        return

    for choice in choices:
        if not is_valid(choice, state):
            continue
        make_choice(choice, state)
        backtrack(state)
        undo_choice(choice, state)

Problem Progression

1

LC 51 — N-Queens

Learn constraint satisfaction through valid queen placement.

2

LC 52 — N-Queens II

Keep the same search but count every complete valid configuration.

3

LC 37 — Sudoku Solver

Extend constraint-based search to multiple simultaneous constraints.

Common Mistakes

  • Checking constraints only after completing a full candidate solution.
  • Forgetting to undo every piece of state modified before recursion.
  • Using the wrong diagonal keys or mixing up row and column relationships.
  • Failing to stop immediately when the current placement is invalid.
  • Confusing finding one valid solution with counting all valid solutions.
  • Mutating the board or constraint sets without restoring them during backtracking.

Complexity

Time

Typically exponential or factorial because the algorithm may explore a large search tree. Constraint checks reduce the number of branches explored but do not remove the worst-case combinatorial nature.

Space

Usually O(depth) recursion plus the state structures used for constraints and the board or partial solution.

Real Pattern

Mental Trigger: “I am building a solution step by step, and every new choice must satisfy constraints created by earlier choices.”

When you see N-Queens, Sudoku, valid placement, no two items can conflict, or partial assignment with rules, think: Backtracking + Validation + State Tracking.

BACKTRACKING PATTERN

Partitioning & String Backtracking

Build a string step by step by choosing where to split it or which character choice to take. Each recursive call advances through the input, stores the current path, and restores that path when the branch is complete.

Pattern Overview

Partitioning & String Backtracking is used when a string must be divided into valid segments or when a sequence must be generated by making one choice at a time. The important idea is that the recursion controls the current position in the string while the path stores the partial answer.

Core Idea: Choose a segment or character → validate it if necessary → add it to the path → recurse from the next position → remove it when returning.

Mental Model

1

Choose

Choose the next segment or character from the current position.

start → end
2

Build Path

Add the selected piece to the current partial answer.

path.add(choice)
3

Restore

Remove the choice before trying another branch.

path.remove(...)

Recognition Clues

PartitionSplit one string into multiple valid pieces.
RestoreReconstruct a value by choosing valid segments.
SplitTry different boundaries between characters.
PalindromeOnly accept segments satisfying a property such as palindrome.
Letter ChoicesEach input character can produce several recursive choices.
Generate AllReturn every valid combination or representation.

How the Pattern Works

  1. Start at the current index in the string.
  2. Choose the next possible segment or character choice.
  3. Validate the choice when the problem has a constraint.
  4. Add the choice to the current path.
  5. Recursively continue from the next index.
  6. When a complete answer is reached, record the path.
  7. Remove the last choice and try the next possibility.
Start Index→Choose Segment→Add to Path→DFS→Restore

Type A: String Partitioning

Use this when the string must be divided into contiguous pieces and every complete partition must satisfy a rule.

Example: For Palindrome Partitioning, try every possible substring beginning at the current index and recurse only when that substring is a palindrome.

Type B: Segmented Reconstruction

Use this when a string must be split into segments that follow a format or numerical constraint, then reconstructed from those selected segments.

P

Position

Track where the next segment begins.

index
S

Segment

Try a valid substring from the current position.

s.substring(start,end)
R

Restore

Remove the selected segment when backtracking.

path.remove(...)

Type C: Recursive Choice Generation

Not every string backtracking problem literally partitions the string. Some problems give several choices for each input character. The same path-based DFS structure generates every possible result.

Example: In Letter Combinations of a Phone Number, each digit maps to several letters. Choose one letter, recurse to the next digit, then restore the path.

Practical Example — LC 131: Palindrome Partitioning

Question: Given a string, partition it so that every substring in the partition is a palindrome. Return all possible palindrome partitions.

How to read it: At every index, we need to decide where the next piece ends. Every candidate substring becomes one possible branch.

Why this pattern fits: We build a partition from left to right. A substring is accepted only if it is a palindrome, and after exploring that choice we remove it and try another endpoint.

Example Input: s = "aab"

Example Output: [["a","a","b"],["aa","b"]]

Short Dry Run: Start at index 0. Try "a", which is a palindrome, so add it and continue from index 1. From index 1, choose "a", then "b", producing ["a","a","b"]. Backtrack and try "aa" from index 0, then choose "b", producing ["aa","b"].

LC 131 — Palindrome Partitioning Solution
class Solution {
    List<List<String>> result = new ArrayList<>();

    public List<List<String>> partition(String s) {
        backtrack(s, 0, new ArrayList<>());
        return result;
    }

    private void backtrack(String s, int start, List<String> path) {
        if (start == s.length()) {
            result.add(new ArrayList<>(path));
            return;
        }

        for (int end = start; end < s.length(); end++) {
            if (!isPalindrome(s, start, end)) continue;

            path.add(s.substring(start, end + 1));
            backtrack(s, end + 1, path);
            path.remove(path.size() - 1);
        }
    }

    private boolean isPalindrome(String s, int left, int right) {
        while (left < right) {
            if (s.charAt(left++) != s.charAt(right--)) return false;
        }
        return true;
    }
}
class Solution {
    vector<vector<string>> result;

public:
    vector<vector<string>> partition(string s) {
        vector<string> path;
        backtrack(s, 0, path);
        return result;
    }

private:
    void backtrack(const string& s, int start, vector<string>& path) {
        if (start == s.size()) {
            result.push_back(path);
            return;
        }

        for (int end = start; end < s.size(); end++) {
            if (!isPalindrome(s, start, end)) continue;

            path.push_back(s.substr(start, end - start + 1));
            backtrack(s, end + 1, path);
            path.pop_back();
        }
    }

    bool isPalindrome(const string& s, int left, int right) {
        while (left < right) {
            if (s[left++] != s[right--]) return false;
        }
        return true;
    }
};
class Solution:
    def partition(self, s: str) -> list[list[str]]:
        result = []
        path = []

        def is_palindrome(left, right):
            while left < right:
                if s[left] != s[right]:
                    return False
                left += 1
                right -= 1
            return True

        def backtrack(start):
            if start == len(s):
                result.append(path.copy())
                return

            for end in range(start, len(s)):

Why the Example Works

The recursion always moves forward through the string, so every partition covers the input exactly once. The palindrome check acts as the constraint, preventing invalid segments from entering the path. Backtracking restores the path so the next possible partition can be explored.

Templates

Partitioning & String Backtracking Template
void backtrack(String s, int start, List<String> path) {
    if (start == s.length()) {
        recordSolution(path);
        return;
    }

    for (int end = start; end < s.length(); end++) {
        String choice = s.substring(start, end + 1);
        if (!isValid(choice)) continue;

        path.add(choice);
        backtrack(s, end + 1, path);
        path.remove(path.size() - 1);
    }
}
void backtrack(const string& s, int start, vector<string>& path) {
    if (start == s.size()) {
        recordSolution(path);
        return;
    }

    for (int end = start; end < s.size(); end++) {
        string choice = s.substr(start, end - start + 1);
        if (!isValid(choice)) continue;

        path.push_back(choice);
        backtrack(s, end + 1, path);
        path.pop_back();
    }
}
def backtrack(s, start, path):
    if start == len(s):
        record_solution(path)
        return

    for end in range(start, len(s)):\
        choice = s[start:end + 1]
        if not is_valid(choice):
            continue
        path.append(choice)
        backtrack(s, end + 1, path)
        path.pop()

Problem Progression

1

LC 131 — Palindrome Partitioning

Learn recursive string partitioning with a validity constraint.

2

LC 93 — Restore IP Addresses

Reinforce segmented search by building a valid representation from string pieces.

3

LC 17 — Letter Combinations

Extend the same DFS path structure to multiple choices at every input position.

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting to advance the start index after choosing a segment.
  • Adding a segment to the path without validating it when the problem requires a constraint.
  • Forgetting to remove the last choice after returning from recursion.
  • Recording a solution before the entire string has been consumed.
  • Confusing contiguous substring partitioning with arbitrary subsequence selection.
  • Failing to copy the current path when storing a complete solution.

Complexity

Time

Usually exponential because many possible split points or character choices may be explored. Validation work such as palindrome checking can add additional cost.

Space

O(n) recursion depth and path storage for the current construction, excluding the space required to store all returned solutions.

Real Pattern

Mental Trigger: “I need to consume a string from left to right, choose the next segment or character, build a path, recurse, and restore the path.”

When you see partition, split, restore, palindrome, segmented string, letter combinations, or generate all string representations, think: DFS + Path + Start Index + Restore.

GREEDY PATTERN

Sorting + Greedy

Sort the input to expose the useful order, then make the locally best decision while processing each element. The key is to identify why the greedy choice is safe and how sorting makes that choice visible.

Pattern Overview

Sorting + Greedy combines two ideas: first arrange the data so related elements appear in a useful order, then process them using a greedy rule that makes the best decision available at the current step.

Core Idea: Sort → Scan in the useful order → Make the locally optimal choice → Keep the decision if it remains compatible with the current state.

Mental Model

1

Sort

Arrange the input according to the property that exposes the greedy structure.

sort(intervals)
2

Choose

Make the best decision for the current element based on the greedy rule.

take earliest finish
3

Commit

Keep the decision and update the state for the remaining elements.

update boundary

Recognition Clues

Sort FirstThe problem becomes easier after arranging the input.
IntervalsRanges overlap, conflict, merge, or need selection.
Earliest FinishChoosing the interval that ends earliest leaves more room for future choices.
Minimum ArrowsOne decision can cover multiple overlapping intervals.
Maximum Compatible SetSelect as many non-conflicting intervals as possible.
Local Best ChoiceA current choice should preserve the best possible future options.

How the Pattern Works

  1. Identify what decision must be made repeatedly.
  2. Determine which property should control the sorting order.
  3. Sort the input using that property.
  4. Scan the sorted elements from left to right.
  5. Apply the greedy rule to decide whether to select, skip, cover, merge, or update the current state.
  6. Update the state after committing the decision.
  7. Continue until every relevant element has been processed.
Sort→Greedy Choice→Update State→Continue

Type A: Sorting + Interval Merging

Use this when intervals must be combined whenever they overlap. Sorting by start time places intervals in an order where the current interval can be compared with the last merged interval.

Example: For Merge Intervals, sort by start time. If the next interval starts before or at the current merged end, extend the end; otherwise, start a new interval.

Type B: Sorting + Maximum Compatible Selection

Use this when the goal is to select the maximum number of non-overlapping intervals. Sorting by earliest finishing time makes the greedy choice safe because it leaves the most room for future intervals.

E

Earliest Finish

Choose the interval that finishes earliest.

min end
S

Select

Accept it when it does not overlap the previous selection.

start >= lastEnd
N

Next

Continue scanning the remaining sorted intervals.

count++

Type C: Sorting + Minimum Coverage

Use this when one decision can cover several overlapping intervals and the goal is to minimize the number of decisions. Sorting exposes which groups can be handled together.

Example: In Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons, sort by ending coordinate. Keep the current arrow position at the common end of the overlapping group and shoot another arrow only when the next balloon starts after it.

Why Sorting Matters

Sorting is not merely preprocessing. It creates the order in which the greedy decision becomes reliable. Different problems require different sorting keys, and choosing the wrong key can destroy the greedy property.

Merge Intervals→Sort by Start
Non-overlapping Intervals→Sort by End
Minimum Arrows→Sort by End

Practical Example — LC 435: Non-overlapping Intervals

Question: Given a collection of intervals, find the minimum number of intervals you need to remove to make the rest non-overlapping.

How to read it: The goal is to keep the maximum number of compatible intervals. Sort by ending time so that every selected interval leaves as much room as possible for future intervals.

Why this pattern fits: At each step, choosing the interval that finishes earliest is the greedy choice because it preserves the largest remaining range for future intervals.

Example Input: [[1,2],[2,3],[3,4],[1,3]]

Example Output: 1

Short Dry Run: Sort by end. Choose [1,2]. Then choose [2,3] because 2 >= 2. Then choose [3,4]. The interval [1,3] overlaps with the selected intervals, so remove it. Therefore, only 1 interval needs to be removed.

LC 435 — Non-overlapping Intervals Solution
class Solution {
    public int eraseOverlapIntervals(int[][] intervals) {
        Arrays.sort(intervals, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[1], b[1]));
        int count = 0;
        int lastEnd = Integer.MIN_VALUE;

        for (int[] interval : intervals) {
            if (interval[0] >= lastEnd) {
                lastEnd = interval[1];
            } else {
                count++;
            }
        }

        return count;
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    int eraseOverlapIntervals(vector<vector<int>>& intervals) {
        sort(intervals.begin(), intervals.end(), [](const vector<int>& a, const vector<int>& b) {
            return a[1] < b[1];
        });

        int count = 0;
        int lastEnd = INT_MIN;

        for (const auto& interval : intervals) {
            if (interval[0] >= lastEnd) {
                lastEnd = interval[1];
            } else {
                count++;
            }
        }

        return count;
    }
};
class Solution:
    def eraseOverlapIntervals(self, intervals: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        intervals.sort(key=lambda interval: interval[1])
        count = 0
        last_end = float('-inf')

        for start, end in intervals:
            if start >= last_end:
                last_end = end
            else:
                count += 1

        return count

Why the Example Works

After sorting by end time, the interval that finishes earliest is considered first. Keeping it leaves the maximum possible space for future intervals. Every overlapping interval that cannot be kept is removed, while compatible intervals update the current end.

Templates

Sorting + Greedy Template
Arrays.sort(items, (a, b) -> compareByGreedyKey(a, b));

State state = initializeState();

for (Item item : items) {
    if (isCompatible(item, state)) {
        makeGreedyChoice(item, state);
    }
}
sort(items.begin(), items.end(), compareByGreedyKey);

State state = initializeState();

for (const auto& item : items) {
    if (isCompatible(item, state)) {
        makeGreedyChoice(item, state);
    }
}
items.sort(key=greedy_key)

state = initialize_state()

for item in items:
    if is_compatible(item, state):
        make_greedy_choice(item, state)

Problem Progression

1

LC 435 — Non-overlapping Intervals

Learn earliest-finish selection to maximize the number of compatible intervals.

2

LC 452 — Minimum Number of Arrows

Extend interval greedy reasoning to minimize the number of covering decisions.

3

LC 56 — Merge Intervals

Understand sorting-based interval processing and how it differs from greedy interval selection.

Common Mistakes

  • Choosing a greedy rule without understanding why it preserves future options.
  • Sorting by the wrong property for the problem.
  • Confusing interval merging with interval selection.
  • Forgetting that different interval problems require different sorting keys.
  • Assuming every problem that involves sorting automatically has a greedy solution.

Complexity

Time

Usually O(n log n) because sorting dominates, followed by an O(n) greedy scan.

Space

Usually O(1) to O(n) auxiliary space depending on the sorting implementation.

Real Pattern

Mental Trigger: “If I sort the input in the right order, can I make a locally best decision that keeps the most useful options available for the future?”

When you see sort, intervals, earliest finish, non-overlapping, minimum arrows, or compatible choices, think: Sort + Identify Greedy Key + Scan + Commit.

learning.html:
GREEDY PATTERN

Local Optimal Choice

Make the best decision available at the current position while maintaining enough information about the future to complete the problem. The goal is to recognize when a local choice can safely lead to a globally optimal result.

Pattern Overview

Local Optimal Choice is a greedy pattern where we scan through the input and repeatedly make the best choice based on the current state. Unlike sorting-based greedy problems, the input order itself often provides the natural processing sequence.

Core Idea: Scan → Track the best reachable or feasible state → Make the local best choice → Continue until the goal is reached or the remaining choices become impossible.

Mental Model

1

Scan

Process positions, stations, or choices in their natural order.

for each position
2

Track Best

Maintain the strongest reachable or feasible state seen so far.

bestReach
3

Commit

Use the current best information to make the next greedy decision.

make choice

Recognition Clues

Reach EndDetermine whether a sequence of local moves can reach the final position.
JumpEach position provides a maximum reach or next set of choices.
Minimum JumpsReach the destination using the fewest possible moves.
Gas StationChoose a valid starting position while tracking a running resource balance.
Running StateA current balance or reach summarizes the useful past information.
Local BestA decision based on the current best state is enough to continue optimally.

How the Pattern Works

  1. Identify the quantity that represents the useful current state.
  2. Scan the input from left to right.
  3. Update the best reachable or feasible state using the current element.
  4. Determine whether the goal has already become reachable.
  5. If multiple moves are required, recognize when the current range or state must produce the next greedy decision.
  6. For feasibility problems, detect when the current state becomes impossible and use the greedy invariant to determine what can be discarded.
  7. Continue until the goal is reached or no valid continuation exists.
Scan→Track Best State→Greedy Decision→Continue

Type A: Greedy Reachability

Use this when each position gives you some ability to move forward and the question is whether the final position can be reached.

Example: In Jump Game, maintain the farthest position reachable from all positions processed so far. If the current index moves beyond that reach, the destination is impossible.

Type B: Minimum Number of Greedy Moves

Use this when the goal is not merely to reach the destination but to reach it using the minimum number of moves. The important idea is to treat all positions reachable with the current number of moves as one range and choose the next range greedily.

R

Current Range

Track the furthest position reachable using the current number of moves.

currentEnd
F

Farthest

Find the furthest next position available inside the current range.

farthest
J

Jump

When the current range ends, commit to another jump.

jumps++

Type C: Greedy Starting-Point Selection

Use this when a valid starting position must be found and the input provides a running resource balance. The key is to detect when the current candidate cannot possibly succeed and safely move the starting point forward.

Example: In Gas Station, maintain the running gas balance. If the balance becomes negative, the current starting position cannot complete the circuit, so the next station becomes the new candidate start.

Key Greedy Invariants

J

Jump Game

Invariant: bestReach represents the furthest index reachable from processed positions.

M

Jump Game II

Invariant: currentEnd represents the boundary reachable with the current number of jumps.

G

Gas Station

Invariant: a negative running tank proves the current candidate start cannot work.

Practical Example — LC 55: Jump Game

Question: Given an array where each value represents the maximum jump length from that position, determine whether you can reach the last index.

How to read it: Every index gives us a possible reach. We do not need to try every individual jump. We only need to know the furthest position reachable from the positions processed so far.

Why this pattern fits: The farthest reachable position summarizes all useful previous choices. If a new index is reachable, its jump can potentially extend that boundary.

Example Input: [2,3,1,1,4]

Example Output: true

Short Dry Run: Start with bestReach = 0. At index 0, value 2 extends reach to 2. At index 1, value 3 extends reach to 4. Since index 4 is now reachable, the answer is true.

LC 55 — Jump Game Solution
class Solution {
    public boolean canJump(int[] nums) {
        int bestReach = 0;

        for (int index = 0; index < nums.length; index++) {
            if (index > bestReach) return false;
            bestReach = Math.max(bestReach, index + nums[index]);
            if (bestReach >= nums.length - 1) return true;
        }

        return true;
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    bool canJump(vector<int>& nums) {
        int bestReach = 0;

        for (int index = 0; index < nums.size(); index++) {
            if (index > bestReach) return false;
            bestReach = max(bestReach, index + nums[index]);
            if (bestReach >= nums.size() - 1) return true;
        }

        return true;
    }
};
class Solution:
    def canJump(self, nums: list[int]) -> bool:
        best_reach = 0

        for index, jump_length in enumerate(nums):
            if index > best_reach:
                return False
            best_reach = max(best_reach, index + jump_length)
            if best_reach >= len(nums) - 1:
                return True

        return True

Why the Example Works

At every index that is reachable, we update the furthest position that can be reached from any processed index. We never need to remember the exact sequence of jumps because only the maximum reachable boundary matters for the feasibility question.

Templates

Local Optimal Choice Template
State bestState = initialState;

for (int index = 0; index < items.length; index++) {
    if (!isReachable(index, bestState)) return failure;
    bestState = updateBestState(bestState, items[index], index);

    if (goalReached(bestState)) return success;
}
State bestState = initialState;

for (int index = 0; index < items.size(); index++) {
    if (!isReachable(index, bestState)) return failure;
    bestState = updateBestState(bestState, items[index], index);

    if (goalReached(bestState)) return success;
}
best_state = initial_state

for index, item in enumerate(items):
    if not is_reachable(index, best_state):
        return failure
    best_state = update_best_state(best_state, item, index)

    if goal_reached(best_state):
        return success

Problem Progression

1

LC 55 — Jump Game

Learn greedy reachability by maintaining the furthest reachable position.

2

LC 45 — Jump Game II

Extend reachability into minimum jumps by processing reachable ranges greedily.

3

LC 134 — Gas Station

Learn how a failed candidate can be discarded and the next valid starting point selected.

Common Mistakes

  • Trying every possible jump instead of tracking the furthest useful reach.
  • Confusing maximum reach with the exact path used to achieve that reach.
  • For Jump Game II, counting every position as a jump instead of processing reachable ranges.
  • Choosing a new gas-station start without understanding why the failed range can be discarded.
  • Using greedy without identifying the invariant that makes the local choice safe.
  • Stopping the scan incorrectly when the current position is exactly at the reachable boundary.

Complexity

Time

Usually O(n) because the input is processed with one greedy scan and constant-time state updates.

Space

Usually O(1) auxiliary space because only a small amount of running state is maintained.

Real Pattern

Mental Trigger: “Can I summarize all useful previous choices with one best state, then make the next decision from that state instead of exploring every possibility?”

When you see reach the end, jump, minimum jumps, gas station, running balance, or choose the next position greedily, think: Greedy Scan + Strong Invariant + Local Optimal Choice.

GREEDY + HEAP PATTERN

Greedy with Heap

Use a heap to keep the most useful candidates available while making greedy decisions. The heap lets you repeatedly choose the best resource, earliest deadline, lowest cost, or largest available contribution needed to optimize the current state.

Pattern Overview

Greedy with Heap combines a greedy decision rule with a priority queue. The input is processed in an order such as time, deadline, position, or eligibility, while the heap dynamically stores candidates that can be chosen when the greedy decision is required.

Core Idea: Process in the required order → Add currently available candidates to a heap → Make the best greedy choice from the heap → Update the state → Continue.

Mental Model

1

Process

Move through events, stations, workers, or resources in the required order.

while available
2

Store

Put useful candidates into a heap so the best one can be retrieved efficiently.

heap.offer(candidate)
3

Choose

Extract the candidate that gives the best greedy outcome.

heap.poll()

Recognition Clues

SchedulingEvents or tasks must be selected while time moves forward.
ResourcesAvailable resources must be chosen dynamically as the process continues.
DeadlinesChoices become valid or invalid depending on the current time.
Best AvailableRepeatedly choose the most useful candidate among currently available options.
Dynamic CandidatesThe set of eligible choices changes as the scan progresses.
OptimizationMinimize cost, maximize events, or maximize progress using greedy choices.

How the Pattern Works

  1. Identify the order in which the input should be processed.
  2. Identify which candidates are currently eligible.
  3. Add those candidates to a heap using the property needed by the greedy decision.
  4. When a choice is required, inspect or remove the best candidate from the heap.
  5. Update the current resource, time, cost, or result.
  6. Continue adding newly eligible candidates as the state changes.
  7. Stop when the goal is reached or no valid candidate remains.
Process→Add Candidates→Heap→Greedy Choice→Update

Type A: Resource Maximization with a Heap

Use this when moving forward requires resources and you need to choose the best previously available resource when the current amount is insufficient.

Example: In Minimum Number of Refueling Stops, process stations by position. When fuel is insufficient to continue, choose the largest fuel amount among stations already passed.

Type B: Scheduling with Earliest Deadlines

Use this when events become available over time and each event has a deadline. Sort or process by start time, add currently available events to a heap, and greedily choose the event with the earliest ending deadline.

A

Available

Add every event whose start time has arrived.

start <= day
E

Earliest End

Choose the available event that ends earliest.

min end
D

Discard Expired

Remove events that can no longer be attended.

end < day

Type C: Greedy Optimization with a Heap

Use this when a greedy objective depends on dynamically selecting the best candidate among a changing collection. The heap maintains the candidates so the required minimum or maximum can be obtained efficiently.

Example: In Minimum Cost to Hire K Workers, sort workers by wage-to-quality ratio and use a max-heap of selected qualities. When more than K workers are selected, remove the largest quality to minimize the total quality while respecting the current ratio.

Choosing the Heap Direction

MIN

Min-Heap

Use when the smallest or earliest candidate should be selected first.

minimum value
MAX

Max-Heap

Use when the largest or most valuable candidate should be selected first.

maximum value
K

Size Control

Use heap size to maintain only the candidates needed by the optimization.

size <= k

Practical Example — LC 871: Minimum Number of Refueling Stops

Question: Given a target distance, starting fuel, and fuel stations along the route, determine the minimum number of refueling stops needed to reach the target.

How to read it: As we travel, every station we pass becomes a possible future refueling choice. If the current fuel is not enough to reach the next required position, we should take the largest fuel amount from all stations already passed.

Why this pattern fits: We do not know in advance which stations should be used. A max-heap keeps all previously reachable fuel amounts and lets us greedily choose the largest one whenever more fuel is required.

Example Input: target = 100, startFuel = 10, stations = [[10,60],[20,30],[30,30],[60,40]]

Example Output: 2

Short Dry Run: Start with 10 fuel and reach position 10, adding 60 to the max-heap. The next station at 20 cannot be reached with the remaining fuel, so refuel with 60. Continue and add the reachable stations. When more fuel is required later, take the largest available fuel again. Two refueling choices are enough to reach 100.

LC 871 — Minimum Number of Refueling Stops Solution
class Solution {
    public int minRefuelStops(int target, int startFuel, int[][] stations) {
        PriorityQueue<Integer> fuelHeap = new PriorityQueue<>(Collections.reverseOrder());
        int fuel = startFuel;
        int stops = 0;
        int stationIndex = 0;

        while (fuel < target) {
            while (stationIndex < stations.length && stations[stationIndex][0] <= fuel) {
                fuelHeap.offer(stations[stationIndex][1]);
                stationIndex++;
            }

            if (fuelHeap.isEmpty()) return -1;

            fuel += fuelHeap.poll();
            stops++;
        }

        return stops;
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    int minRefuelStops(int target, int startFuel, vector<vector<int>>& stations) {
        priority_queue<int> fuelHeap;
        long long fuel = startFuel;
        int stops = 0;
        int stationIndex = 0;

        while (fuel < target) {
            while (stationIndex < stations.size() && stations[stationIndex][0] <= fuel) {
                fuelHeap.push(stations[stationIndex][1]);
                stationIndex++;
            }

            if (fuelHeap.empty()) return -1;

            fuel += fuelHeap.top();
            fuelHeap.pop();
            stops++;
        }

        return stops;
    }
};
class Solution:
    def minRefuelStops(self, target: int, startFuel: int, stations: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        import heapq

        fuel = startFuel
        stops = 0
        station_index = 0
        fuel_heap = []

        while fuel < target:
            while station_index < len(stations) and stations[station_index][0] <= fuel:
                heapq.heappush(fuel_heap, -stations[station_index][1])
                station_index += 1

            if not fuel_heap:
                return -1

            fuel += -heapq.heappop(fuel_heap)
            stops += 1

        return stops

Why the Example Works

Every station that can already be reached is placed into the max-heap. When more fuel is needed, choosing the largest available fuel amount gives the greatest immediate extension of reach. This allows the algorithm to postpone smaller refueling choices unless they become necessary.

Templates

Greedy with Heap Template
PriorityQueue<Item> heap = new PriorityQueue<>(comparator);

while (!goalReached()) {
    while (hasNewCandidate()) {
        heap.offer(getCandidate());
    }

    if (heap.isEmpty()) return failure;

    Item best = heap.poll();
    applyGreedyChoice(best);
}
priority_queue<Item, vector<Item>, Compare> heap;

while (!goalReached()) {
    while (hasNewCandidate()) {
        heap.push(getCandidate());
    }

    if (heap.empty()) return failure;

    Item best = heap.top();
    heap.pop();
    applyGreedyChoice(best);
}
import heapq

heap = []

while not goal_reached():
    while has_new_candidate():
        heapq.heappush(heap, get_candidate())

    if not heap:
        return failure

    best = heapq.heappop(heap)
    apply_greedy_choice(best)

Problem Progression

1

LC 871 — Minimum Refueling Stops

Learn how a max-heap stores reachable resources and supports greedy refueling.

2

LC 1353 — Maximum Events

Learn dynamic scheduling where available events are selected by earliest deadline.

3

LC 857 — Minimum Cost to Hire K Workers

Extend heap-based greedy reasoning to a ratio-based optimization problem.

Common Mistakes

  • Using a heap without first identifying the correct greedy property.
  • Adding candidates before they become eligible or forgetting to add newly eligible candidates.
  • Choosing the wrong heap direction for the optimization objective.
  • Forgetting to remove expired or invalid candidates when the problem requires it.
  • Confusing the order used to process candidates with the order used to choose from the heap.
  • Assuming that a heap automatically makes a solution greedy; the greedy invariant still has to be understood.

Complexity

Time

Usually O(n log n) because each candidate is inserted into and removed from the heap at most once, with any required sorting also taking O(n log n).

Space

Usually O(n) for the heap in the worst case when many candidates are simultaneously available.

Real Pattern

Mental Trigger: “As the process moves forward, which candidates are currently available, and which one gives the best greedy choice right now?”

When you see scheduling, resources, deadlines, refueling, available events, minimum cost, or repeatedly choose the best available candidate, think: Process Order + Heap of Candidates + Greedy Extraction.

learning.html:
GREEDY PATTERN

String & Array Greedy

Use greedy decisions to partition, rearrange, remove, or order elements while preserving the best possible result. The key is to identify what information about the remaining input determines whether a local choice is safe.

Pattern Overview

String & Array Greedy problems often look like they require many possible arrangements or decisions. Instead of exploring every possibility, maintain the right information about the remaining elements and make the locally best choice whenever that choice can be proven safe.

Core Idea: Track the future → Identify the safest local choice → Commit to it → Update the remaining state → Continue.

Mental Model

1

Analyze Future

Track information such as last occurrence, remaining frequency, or available positions.

remainingState
2

Choose

Select the locally best element, partition boundary, or position.

greedyChoice
3

Commit

Make the choice permanent and update the state for future decisions.

updateState()

Recognition Clues

PartitionSplit an array or string into groups that satisfy a future-dependent condition.
RearrangeBuild a new ordering while optimizing a property of the result.
RemoveDelete elements while keeping the best possible remaining sequence.
LexicographicalConstruct the smallest or largest valid string under given constraints.
Last OccurrenceThe future positions of elements determine when a decision can safely be finalized.
Sorted PlacementSort by one property, then greedily place elements using another constraint.

How the Pattern Works

  1. Identify what the final answer is optimizing.
  2. Determine what information about the remaining input affects a local decision.
  3. Scan the input or process elements in a useful order.
  4. Choose the locally best valid element or boundary.
  5. Commit the choice when future information guarantees it is safe.
  6. Update the state and continue with the remaining elements.
  7. Repeat until the complete answer has been constructed.
Track Future→Greedy Choice→Commit→Update→Continue

Type A: Greedy Partitioning

Use this when a string or array must be divided into segments and a segment can be finalized once all elements that depend on it have been encountered.

Example: In Partition Labels, track the last occurrence of every character. A partition can end only when the current position has reached the last occurrence of every character seen in that partition.

Type B: Lexicographical Greedy Removal

Use this when characters must be removed or rearranged to produce the smallest valid lexicographical result. The important idea is to remove a character when a smaller future character can replace it without making the remaining character impossible to use.

L

Lexicographic Order

Prefer the smaller character when it is safe to do so.

smaller > current
R

Remaining

Check whether the current character appears again later.

lastIndex[c] > index
U

Used

Ensure every required character appears only when appropriate.

used[c]

Type C: Greedy Ordering After Sorting

Use this when sorting creates a useful processing order and each element must then be placed according to a remaining structural constraint.

Example: In Queue Reconstruction by Height, sort people by decreasing height and increasing k for equal heights. Then insert each person at index k, because taller people have already been placed and therefore determine the visible positions of shorter people.

Key Greedy Invariants

P

Partition Labels

Invariant: the current partition cannot end before the last occurrence of every character inside it.

D

Remove Duplicate Letters

Invariant: a larger character can be removed when a smaller character appears later and the larger character still remains available.

Q

Queue Reconstruction

Invariant: after sorting, inserting a person at position k preserves the required number of taller-or-equal people before them.

Practical Example — LC 763: Partition Labels

Question: Partition a string into as many parts as possible so that each letter appears in at most one part.

How to read it: Once a character appears inside a partition, that partition must continue until the character's final occurrence has been included.

Why this pattern fits: Last-occurrence information tells us exactly when a partition can safely end. We greedily close the partition at the earliest position where every character inside it has been fully contained.

Example Input: s = "ababcbacadefegdehijhklij"

Example Output: [9,7,8]

Short Dry Run: The first partition contains characters from a through f. Their last occurrences force the boundary to position 8, giving a length of 9. The scan then starts again and greedily closes the next valid partition at position 15, giving length 7. The remaining characters form the final partition of length 8.

LC 763 — Partition Labels Solution
class Solution {
    public List<Integer> partitionLabels(String s) {
        int[] lastIndex = new int[26];

        for (int index = 0; index < s.length(); index++) {
            lastIndex[s.charAt(index) - 'a'] = index;
        }

        List<Integer> result = new ArrayList<>();
        int partitionEnd = 0;
        int partitionStart = 0;

        for (int index = 0; index < s.length(); index++) {
            partitionEnd = Math.max(partitionEnd, lastIndex[s.charAt(index) - 'a']);

            if (index == partitionEnd) {
                result.add(partitionEnd - partitionStart + 1);
                partitionStart = index + 1;
            }
        }

        return result;
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    vector<int> partitionLabels(string s) {
        vector<int> lastIndex(26);

        for (int index = 0; index < s.size(); index++) {
            lastIndex[s[index] - 'a'] = index;
        }

        vector<int> result;
        int partitionEnd = 0;
        int partitionStart = 0;

        for (int index = 0; index < s.size(); index++) {
            partitionEnd = max(partitionEnd, lastIndex[s[index] - 'a']);

            if (index == partitionEnd) {
                result.push_back(partitionEnd - partitionStart + 1);
                partitionStart = index + 1;
            }
        }

        return result;
    }
};
class Solution:
    def partitionLabels(self, s: str) -> list[int]:
        last_index = {char: index for index, char in enumerate(s)}
        result = []
        partition_end = 0
        partition_start = 0

        for index, char in enumerate(s):
            partition_end = max(partition_end, last_index[char])

            if index == partition_end:
                result.append(partition_end - partition_start + 1)
                partition_start = index + 1

        return result

Why the Example Works

The last occurrence of every character tells us how far the current partition must extend. Once the scan reaches the maximum last occurrence among all characters in the current partition, no character from that partition can appear later, so closing the partition is safe and maximizes the number of partitions.

Templates

String & Array Greedy Template
State state = initializeState();

for (int index = 0; index < items.length; index++) {
    updateFutureInformation(items[index], state);

    if (isGreedyChoiceSafe(items[index], state)) {
        commitChoice(items[index], state);
    }
}
State state = initializeState();

for (int index = 0; index < items.size(); index++) {
    updateFutureInformation(items[index], state);

    if (isGreedyChoiceSafe(items[index], state)) {
        commitChoice(items[index], state);
    }
}
state = initialize_state()

for index, item in enumerate(items):
    update_future_information(item, state)

    if is_greedy_choice_safe(item, state):
        commit_choice(item, state)

Problem Progression

1

LC 763 — Partition Labels

Learn greedy partitioning using last-occurrence information.

2

LC 316 — Remove Duplicate Letters

Learn lexicographical greedy removal while preserving required characters.

3

LC 406 — Queue Reconstruction

Extend greedy ordering by sorting first and then placing elements according to a structural constraint.

Common Mistakes

  • Making a greedy choice without tracking the information that proves it is safe.
  • Ending a partition before every character inside it has reached its final occurrence.
  • Removing a character in LC 316 without checking whether it appears again later.
  • Forgetting that lexicographical optimization requires comparing the current character with a smaller future character.
  • Using the wrong sorting order before applying the insertion strategy in LC 406.
  • Confusing a locally attractive choice with a provably safe greedy choice.

Complexity

Time

Usually O(n) for direct greedy traversal problems such as Partition Labels, while sorting-based variants such as Queue Reconstruction are typically O(n log n).

Space

Usually O(n) for frequency, last-occurrence, or result structures, depending on the specific problem.

Real Pattern

Mental Trigger: “What information about the remaining input tells me that this element, boundary, or placement is now safe to finalize?”

When you see partition, rearrange, remove, lexicographical order, last occurrence, or sort then place, think: Track Future Information + Greedy Choice + Commit Safely.

DYNAMIC PROGRAMMING PATTERN

1D Dynamic Programming

Build the solution from smaller subproblems by defining a state that represents the best or number of ways to reach each position. Store previously computed results so the same subproblem is never solved repeatedly.

Pattern Overview

1D Dynamic Programming is used when a problem can be represented as a sequence of states, usually indexed by a position, step, or amount. The answer for the current state depends on answers from one or more smaller states that have already been computed.

Core Idea: Define the state → Identify the transition → Set base cases → Compute states in dependency order → Return the target state.

Mental Model

1

State

Define what each DP position represents.

dp[i] = answer at i
2

Transition

Express the current answer using smaller previously solved states.

dp[i] = f(dp[i-1], dp[i-2])
3

Build

Compute states in an order where their dependencies are already known.

for i = 1...n

Recognition Clues

WaysCount how many different ways can reach a state.
Minimum CostFind the cheapest way to reach a position or complete a sequence.
Maximum ProfitChoose actions that maximize the accumulated result.
ClimbMove through positions using a small set of previous states.
RobChoose between taking the current item and skipping it.
Repeated SubproblemsThe same smaller states appear repeatedly in a recursive formulation.

How the Pattern Works

  1. Identify the changing position, index, step, or amount.
  2. Define exactly what dp[i] means.
  3. Find the smaller states that can lead to the current state.
  4. Write the recurrence or transition formula.
  5. Initialize the smallest states with correct base cases.
  6. Compute the DP array from smaller states toward the target.
  7. Return the state representing the required answer.
State→Transition→Base Cases→Build→Answer

Type A: Counting Ways

Use this when the problem asks how many different ways can reach a position. The current state is usually formed by adding the number of ways from each valid previous state.

Example: In Climbing Stairs, you can reach step i from step i - 1 or i - 2, so dp[i] = dp[i - 1] + dp[i - 2].

Type B: Maximum Value with Choices

Use this when each position gives you a choice such as take or skip, and the goal is to maximize a total value.

T

Take

Include the current item and move to the previous compatible state.

value[i] + dp[i-2]
S

Skip

Ignore the current item and keep the best previous result.

dp[i-1]
M

Max

Choose the better of the available decisions.

max(take, skip)

Type C: Minimum Cost DP

Use this when every state has an associated cost and the goal is to reach the destination with minimum total cost. The transition chooses the cheaper path among the valid previous states.

Example: In Min Cost Climbing Stairs, reaching a step can come from either of the previous two positions, so the current cost depends on the minimum cost among those previous states.

State Design

The most important part of 1D DP is not writing the array. It is defining what the array means. A useful state should contain exactly enough information to calculate future states.

W

Ways

dp[i] = number of ways to reach state i.

M

Maximum

dp[i] = maximum value achievable up to state i.

C

Minimum

dp[i] = minimum cost required to reach state i.

Practical Example — LC 198: House Robber

Question: Given an array where each value represents the money in a house, determine the maximum amount you can rob without robbing two adjacent houses.

How to read it: At every house, there are two choices: rob it and skip the previous house, or skip it and keep the best result from the previous house.

Why this pattern fits: The answer at house i depends only on the best answers from earlier houses. The repeated choices create overlapping subproblems that can be stored in a 1D DP array.

Example Input: [2,7,9,3,1]

Example Output: 12

Short Dry Run: At house 0, the best is 2. At house 1, choose 7. At house 2, either keep 7 or rob 2 + 9 = 11, so the best is 11. At house 3, skip it and keep 11. At house 4, rob it with the result two positions back: 11 + 1 = 12. Therefore the answer is 12.

LC 198 — House Robber Solution
class Solution {
    public int rob(int[] nums) {
        if (nums.length == 1) return nums[0];

        int[] dp = new int[nums.length];
        dp[0] = nums[0];
        dp[1] = Math.max(nums[0], nums[1]);

        for (int i = 2; i < nums.length; i++) {
            int robCurrent = nums[i] + dp[i - 2];
            int skipCurrent = dp[i - 1];
            dp[i] = Math.max(robCurrent, skipCurrent);
        }

        return dp[nums.length - 1];
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    int rob(vector<int>& nums) {
        if (nums.size() == 1) return nums[0];

        vector<int> dp(nums.size());
        dp[0] = nums[0];
        dp[1] = max(nums[0], nums[1]);

        for (int i = 2; i < nums.size(); i++) {
            int robCurrent = nums[i] + dp[i - 2];
            int skipCurrent = dp[i - 1];
            dp[i] = max(robCurrent, skipCurrent);
        }

        return dp.back();
    }
};
class Solution:
    def rob(self, nums: list[int]) -> int:
        if len(nums) == 1:
            return nums[0]

        dp = [0] * len(nums)
        dp[0] = nums[0]
        dp[1] = max(nums[0], nums[1])

        for i in range(2, len(nums)):

Why the Example Works

For every house, the optimal answer must come from one of two possibilities: rob the current house and combine its value with the best answer from two houses earlier, or skip it and keep the previous best answer. Taking the maximum of these two choices captures every valid optimal solution.

Space Optimization

Often dp[i] depends only on a fixed number of previous states. In House Robber, only the previous two DP values are needed, so the full array can be replaced with two variables.

previousTwo→previousOne→current
1D DP — Space Optimized Template
int previousTwo = baseCase0;
int previousOne = baseCase1;

for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) {
    int current = transition(previousOne, previousTwo, i);
    previousTwo = previousOne;
    previousOne = current;
}
int previousTwo = baseCase0;
int previousOne = baseCase1;

for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) {
    int current = transition(previousOne, previousTwo, i);
    previousTwo = previousOne;
    previousOne = current;
}
previous_two = base_case_0
previous_one = base_case_1

for i in range(2, n + 1):
    current = transition(previous_one, previous_two, i)
    previous_two = previous_one
    previous_one = current

Templates

1D Dynamic Programming Template
int[] dp = new int[n + 1];
initializeBaseCases(dp);

for (int i = firstState; i <= n; i++) {
    dp[i] = transition(dp, i);
}

return dp[n];
vector<int> dp(n + 1);
initializeBaseCases(dp);

for (int i = firstState; i <= n; i++) {
    dp[i] = transition(dp, i);
}

return dp[n];
dp = [0] * (n + 1)
initialize_base_cases(dp)

for i in range(first_state, n + 1):
    dp[i] = transition(dp, i)

return dp[n]

Problem Progression

1

LC 70 — Climbing Stairs

Learn the basic DP mindset through counting ways from previous states.

2

LC 198 — House Robber

Learn state transitions where each position has competing take-or-skip choices.

3

LC 746 — Min Cost Climbing Stairs

Extend the same 1D state structure to minimum-cost optimization.

Common Mistakes

  • Writing code before clearly defining what dp[i] means.
  • Using an incorrect base case and therefore shifting every later state.
  • Writing a transition that uses states that are not actually valid dependencies.
  • Confusing the meaning of “up to i” with “exactly at i”.
  • Forgetting that the answer may require a final state different from the last array index.
  • Optimizing space before understanding the full DP recurrence.

Complexity

Time

Usually O(n) because each state is computed once and each transition takes constant time.

Space

O(n) with a full DP array. If only a fixed number of previous states are required, space can often be optimized to O(1).

Real Pattern

Mental Trigger: “Can I define the answer at position i using a small number of already-solved positions, and would storing those results avoid repeated work?”

When you see ways, minimum cost, maximum profit, climb, rob, take-or-skip, or repeated smaller subproblems along one dimension, think: 1D State + Transition + Base Cases + Bottom-Up DP.

DYNAMIC PROGRAMMING PATTERN

2D Grid Dynamic Programming

Solve matrix and grid problems by treating every cell as a DP state. Build each cell from previously solved neighboring states, allowing paths, costs, and expanding shapes to be computed without repeatedly exploring the same subproblems.

Pattern Overview

2D Grid Dynamic Programming is used when a problem is represented as rows and columns and the answer for one cell depends on neighboring cells or smaller rectangular regions. Instead of repeatedly exploring paths through the grid, store the answer for each cell in a 2D DP table.

Core Idea: Define what dp[row][col] means → Identify valid previous states → Write the transition → Initialize boundaries → Fill the grid in dependency order.

Mental Model

1

State

Each grid cell represents a subproblem.

dp[r][c]
2

Transition

Build the current cell from valid neighboring states.

dp[r][c] = f(neighbors)
3

Build

Process cells in an order where dependencies are already computed.

row → col

Recognition Clues

GridThe input is a matrix or rectangular board.
PathMove through cells using restricted directions such as right and down.
MatrixThe answer for a cell depends on neighboring cells or submatrices.
Minimum PathFind the cheapest route through a weighted grid.
Maximum SquareFind the largest valid square or rectangular structure.
Repeated PathsMany different routes reach the same cells or subproblems.

How the Pattern Works

  1. Identify the row and column that define the current subproblem.
  2. Define exactly what dp[row][col] represents.
  3. Determine which neighboring states can contribute to the current cell.
  4. Write the transition using those previously computed states.
  5. Initialize the first row, first column, or other boundary states.
  6. Fill the DP table in an order that respects the dependencies.
  7. Return the target cell or the best value found across the table.
Grid State→Neighbor States→Transition→Fill Table→Answer

Type A: Counting Grid Paths

Use this when the problem asks how many ways exist to travel from one part of the grid to another under restricted movement rules.

Example: In Unique Paths, each cell can be reached from the cell above or the cell to the left, so the number of paths is the sum of those two states.

Type B: Minimum or Maximum Path Value

Use this when cells have weights or values and the goal is to optimize the total accumulated value along a path.

P

Previous States

Use the neighboring cells that can reach the current cell.

dp[r-1][c], dp[r][c-1]
W

Weight

Add the current cell's cost or value to the selected previous state.

grid[r][c]
M

Optimize

Choose the minimum or maximum valid previous result.

min(...) / max(...)

Type C: Square Expansion DP

Use this when the problem asks for the largest square satisfying a condition. The current cell can represent the bottom-right corner of a square, and its size depends on neighboring square states.

Example: In Maximal Square, if the current matrix cell contains 1, the largest square ending there depends on the minimum of the top, left, and top-left square sizes, plus one.

State Design

As with every DP problem, the most important step is defining the state. The same grid can require completely different DP meanings depending on the question.

W

Ways

dp[r][c] = number of ways to reach cell (r,c).

C

Cost

dp[r][c] = minimum cost to reach cell (r,c).

S

Square

dp[r][c] = largest valid square ending at (r,c).

Practical Example — LC 64: Minimum Path Sum

Question: Given a grid of non-negative numbers, find a path from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner that minimizes the sum of all numbers along the path. You may only move right or down.

How to read it: To reach cell (r,c), the path must come from either the cell above or the cell to the left.

Why this pattern fits: The minimum cost of reaching the current cell depends only on the minimum costs already computed for its two possible predecessors.

Example Input: [[1,3,1],[1,5,1],[4,2,1]]

Example Output: 7

Short Dry Run: Start with cost 1 at the top-left. The first row and first column accumulate their only possible paths. For the middle cell 5, choose the cheaper cost from above or left, then add 5. Continue filling the grid until the bottom-right cell becomes 7.

LC 64 — Minimum Path Sum Solution
class Solution {
    public int minPathSum(int[][] grid) {
        int rows = grid.length;
        int cols = grid[0].length;
        int[][] dp = new int[rows][cols];

        dp[0][0] = grid[0][0];

        for (int col = 1; col < cols; col++) {
            dp[0][col] = dp[0][col - 1] + grid[0][col];
        }

        for (int row = 1; row < rows; row++) {
            dp[row][0] = dp[row - 1][0] + grid[row][0];
        }

        for (int row = 1; row < rows; row++) {
            for (int col = 1; col < cols; col++) {
                dp[row][col] = grid[row][col] + Math.min(dp[row - 1][col], dp[row][col - 1]);
            }
        }

        return dp[rows - 1][cols - 1];
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    int minPathSum(vector<vector<int>>& grid) {
        int rows = grid.size();
        int cols = grid[0].size();
        vector<vector<int>> dp(rows, vector<int>(cols));

        dp[0][0] = grid[0][0];

        for (int col = 1; col < cols; col++) {
            dp[0][col] = dp[0][col - 1] + grid[0][col];
        }

        for (int row = 1; row < rows; row++) {
            dp[row][0] = dp[row - 1][0] + grid[row][0];
        }

        for (int row = 1; row < rows; row++) {
            for (int col = 1; col < cols; col++) {
                dp[row][col] = grid[row][col] + min(dp[row - 1][col], dp[row][col - 1]);
            }
        }

        return dp[rows - 1][cols - 1];
    }
};
class Solution:
    def minPathSum(self, grid: list[list[int]]) -> int:
        rows = len(grid)
        cols = len(grid[0])
        dp = [[0] * cols for _ in range(rows)]

        dp[0][0] = grid[0][0]

        for col in range(1, cols):
            dp[0][col] = dp[0][col - 1] + grid[0][col]

        for row in range(1, rows):
            dp[row][0] = dp[row - 1][0] + grid[row][0]

        for row in range(1, rows):
            for col in range(1, cols):
                dp[row][col] = grid[row][col] + min(dp[row - 1][col], dp[row][col - 1])

        return dp[rows - 1][cols - 1]

Why the Example Works

Every valid path entering a cell must come from above or from the left. Therefore, once the minimum cost for those two cells is known, the minimum cost for the current cell is simply the smaller predecessor cost plus the current grid value.

Templates

2D Grid Dynamic Programming Template
int[][] dp = new int[rows][cols];
initializeBaseCases(dp);

for (int row = 0; row < rows; row++) {
    for (int col = 0; col < cols; col++) {
        if (isBaseCase(row, col)) continue;
        dp[row][col] = transition(dp, row, col);
    }
}

return dp[rows - 1][cols - 1];
vector<vector<int>> dp(rows, vector<int>(cols));
initializeBaseCases(dp);

for (int row = 0; row < rows; row++) {
    for (int col = 0; col < cols; col++) {
        if (isBaseCase(row, col)) continue;
        dp[row][col] = transition(dp, row, col);
    }
}

return dp[rows - 1][cols - 1];
dp = [[0] * cols for _ in range(rows)]
initialize_base_cases(dp)

for row in range(rows):
    for col in range(cols):
        if is_base_case(row, col):
            continue
        dp[row][col] = transition(dp, row, col)

return dp[rows - 1][cols - 1]

Space Optimization

Many grid DP problems only depend on the previous row and the current row. In those cases, the full 2D table can sometimes be compressed into a single 1D array, reducing auxiliary space from O(rows × cols) to O(cols).

2D Table→Previous Row Information→1D DP

Problem Progression

1

LC 62 — Unique Paths

Learn the basic grid DP structure by counting paths from neighboring cells.

2

LC 64 — Minimum Path Sum

Extend grid DP to weighted transitions and minimum-cost paths.

3

LC 221 — Maximal Square

Extend the state concept from paths to expanding square structures.

Common Mistakes

  • Defining dp[row][col] vaguely instead of giving it a precise meaning.
  • Forgetting to initialize the first row and first column when they have only one possible predecessor.
  • Reading from a neighboring state that has not been computed yet.
  • Confusing the current cell's value with the accumulated path cost.
  • Using the wrong neighboring states for the movement rules.
  • Optimizing the table to 1D before understanding the complete 2D transition.

Complexity

Time

Usually O(rows × cols) because each grid cell is computed once with a constant-time transition.

Space

O(rows × cols) with a full 2D DP table. Many problems can be optimized to O(cols) when only the previous row is required.

Real Pattern

Mental Trigger: “Can I define each cell as a smaller subproblem whose answer depends on a few neighboring cells that I can compute first?”

When you see grid, path, matrix, minimum path, maximum square, or repeated movement through cells, think: 2D State + Neighbor Transition + Boundary Initialization + Table Order.
