    char ch = board[row][col];
    if (node->children[ch - 'a'] == nullptr) return;
    TrieNode* next = node->children[ch - 'a'];
    // Continue DFS using next Trie node.
}
def dfs(row, col, node):
    ch = board[row][col]
    if ch not in node.children:
        return
    next_node = node.children[ch]
    # Continue DFS using next_node.

Template 3 — Reversed Trie for Suffix Sharing

Suffix Sharing
for (String word : words) {
    String reversed = new StringBuilder(word).reverse().toString();
    insert(reversed);
}
for (const string& word : words) {
    string reversed = word;
    reverse(reversed.begin(), reversed.end());
    insert(reversed);
}
for word in words:
    insert(word[::-1])

Problem Progression

212

LC 212

Combine Trie with DFS to search many dictionary words inside a character board.

648

LC 648

Use Trie prefix matching to replace words with their shortest dictionary roots.

820

LC 820

Reverse words so a Trie can exploit shared suffixes for compact encoding.

Common Mistakes

  • Using Trie without a reason: The Trie should remove repeated dictionary scanning or provide useful prefix structure.
  • Forgetting pruning: In Trie + DFS problems, a missing child should immediately stop that branch.
  • Returning the wrong prefix: Replacement problems usually require the shortest valid root, so stop at the first word-ending node.
  • Ignoring duplicates: In multi-word search, the same word may be discovered from multiple paths and should be handled according to the problem requirements.
  • Missing the transformation: When the problem is about suffix sharing, reversing the strings can turn suffixes into Trie-friendly prefixes.

Complexity

Build Trie

O(S) where S is the total number of characters inserted into the Trie.

Prefix Lookup

O(L) for a searched string or prefix of length L.

Trie + DFS

The total cost depends on board size, word lengths, and how much DFS is pruned by Trie paths.

Space

O(S) for the Trie in the worst case, with shared prefixes reducing actual node usage.

Real Pattern

When a problem gives you many words and repeatedly asks you to search, match prefixes, explore dictionary words, replace using roots, or exploit shared string structure, think Trie.

The key question is: Can I turn the dictionary into a character structure so the main algorithm can follow only valid string paths?

INTERVAL PATTERN

Merge Intervals

Merge Intervals is the core pattern for processing ranges that overlap in time, position, or value. Sort intervals first, then scan them once while maintaining the current merged interval.

Pattern Overview

An interval is represented by a start and an end, such as [1,5]. When intervals overlap, they can be combined into one larger interval. The central idea is to sort intervals by their starting point and then process them from left to right.

Core idea: Sort intervals by start time. Maintain the current merged interval. If the next interval overlaps it, extend the current end; otherwise, save the current interval and start a new one.

Mental Model

Think of every interval as occupying a segment on a number line. After sorting by start, the only interval that can affect the current merge is the next interval in order.

01

Sort

Order intervals by their starting value.

start ↑
02

Compare

Check whether the next interval overlaps the current merged interval.

nextStart <= currentEnd
03

Extend

If overlapping, extend the merged interval to the larger end.

max(currentEnd,nextEnd)

Recognition Clues

IntervalsThe input consists of [start, end] ranges.
OverlapThe problem asks which intervals intersect or conflict.
MergeOverlapping ranges need to become one continuous range.
SchedulingMeetings, events, reservations, or time blocks may overlap.
InsertA new interval must be placed into an existing sorted set of intervals.
Non-OverlappingThe goal may be to remove or count intervals that conflict.

How the Pattern Works

First sort the intervals by their start value. Take the first interval as the current merged interval. For every next interval, compare its start with the current end.

[1,3] + [2,6] → [1,6] → [8,10]

If nextStart <= currentEnd, the intervals overlap and can be merged. Otherwise, the current interval is complete and the next interval becomes the new current interval.

Type A — Basic Interval Merging

Given a collection of intervals, merge every pair of overlapping intervals into the smallest possible set of non-overlapping intervals.

overlap→newEnd = max(currentEnd, nextEnd)
Important: Sorting by start is what makes the one-pass scan possible. Without sorting, an interval that should merge may appear much later in the input.

Type B — Insert Interval

When inserting a new interval into an already sorted collection, divide the process into three phases: intervals completely before the new interval, intervals overlapping the new interval, and intervals completely after it.

  • Before: Add intervals whose end is smaller than the new interval's start.
  • Overlap: Expand the new interval using the minimum start and maximum end.
  • After: Add all remaining intervals unchanged.

Type C — Non-Overlapping Intervals

Some interval problems reverse the goal: instead of merging overlaps, determine how many intervals must be removed so the remaining intervals do not overlap.

Greedy connection: When choosing which overlapping interval to keep, prefer the interval with the smaller end. It leaves more room for future intervals.

Overlap Conditions

<

Before

The next interval ends before the current interval starts.

nextEnd < currentStart
↔

Overlap

The next interval begins before or exactly when the current interval ends.

nextStart <= currentEnd
>

After

The next interval starts after the current interval ends.

nextStart > currentEnd

Practical Example — LC 56: Merge Intervals

Question: Given an array of intervals, merge all overlapping intervals.

How to read it: The words intervals and overlapping are the main signals. We need to group ranges that intersect.

Why this pattern fits: After sorting by start, every future interval can be compared with the current merged interval in a single forward scan.

Example Input: [[1,3],[2,6],[8,10],[9,12]]

Example Output: [[1,6],[8,12]]

Short Dry Run: Start with [1,3]. The next interval [2,6] overlaps because 2 <= 3, so merge them into [1,6]. The next interval [8,10] does not overlap because 8 > 6, so save [1,6] and start [8,10]. Finally [9,12] overlaps with [8,10], so extend it to [8,12].

Java — Merge Intervals
class Solution {
    public int[][] merge(int[][] intervals) {
        Arrays.sort(intervals, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]));

        List<int[]> merged = new ArrayList<>();
        int currentStart = intervals[0][0];
        int currentEnd = intervals[0][1];

        for (int i = 1; i < intervals.length; i++) {
            int nextStart = intervals[i][0];
            int nextEnd = intervals[i][1];

            if (nextStart <= currentEnd) {
                currentEnd = Math.max(currentEnd, nextEnd);
            } else {
                merged.add(new int[]{currentStart, currentEnd});
                currentStart = nextStart;
                currentEnd = nextEnd;
            }
        }

        merged.add(new int[]{currentStart, currentEnd});
        return merged.toArray(new int[merged.size()][]);
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    vector<vector<int>> merge(vector<vector<int>>& intervals) {
        sort(intervals.begin(), intervals.end(), [](const auto& a, const auto& b) {
            return a[0] < b[0];
        });

        vector<vector<int>> merged;
        int currentStart = intervals[0][0];
        int currentEnd = intervals[0][1];

        for (int i = 1; i < intervals.size(); i++) {
            int nextStart = intervals[i][0];
            int nextEnd = intervals[i][1];

            if (nextStart <= currentEnd) {
                currentEnd = max(currentEnd, nextEnd);
            } else {
                merged.push_back({currentStart, currentEnd});
                currentStart = nextStart;
                currentEnd = nextEnd;
            }
        }

        merged.push_back({currentStart, currentEnd});
        return merged;
    }
};
class Solution:
    def merge(self, intervals):
        intervals.sort(key=lambda interval: interval[0])

        merged = []
        current_start, current_end = intervals[0]

        for next_start, next_end in intervals[1:]:
            if next_start <= current_end:
                current_end = max(current_end, next_end)
            else:
                merged.append([current_start, current_end])
                current_start = next_start
                current_end = next_end

        merged.append([current_start, current_end])
        return merged

Why the Example Works

Sorting guarantees that intervals are considered from left to right. Once an interval starts after the current end, no later interval can connect it back to the previous merged interval through an earlier start, so the current interval can safely be finalized.

Templates

Template 1 — Merge Overlapping Intervals

Basic Merge Template
Arrays.sort(intervals, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]));
int currentStart = intervals[0][0];
int currentEnd = intervals[0][1];

for (int i = 1; i < intervals.length; i++) {
    int nextStart = intervals[i][0];
    int nextEnd = intervals[i][1];
    if (nextStart <= currentEnd) {
        currentEnd = Math.max(currentEnd, nextEnd);
    } else {
        // Save current interval.
        currentStart = nextStart;
        currentEnd = nextEnd;
    }
}
sort(intervals.begin(), intervals.end(), [](const auto& a, const auto& b) {
    return a[0] < b[0];
});
int currentStart = intervals[0][0];
int currentEnd = intervals[0][1];

for (int i = 1; i < intervals.size(); i++) {
    int nextStart = intervals[i][0];
    int nextEnd = intervals[i][1];
    if (nextStart <= currentEnd) {
        currentEnd = max(currentEnd, nextEnd);
    } else {
        // Save current interval.
        currentStart = nextStart;
        currentEnd = nextEnd;
    }
}
intervals.sort(key=lambda interval: interval[0])
current_start, current_end = intervals[0]

for next_start, next_end in intervals[1:]:
    if next_start <= current_end:
        current_end = max(current_end, next_end)
    else:
        # Save current interval.
        current_start = next_start
        current_end = next_end

Template 2 — Insert and Merge an Interval

Insert Interval Template
while (i < intervals.length && intervals[i][1] < newStart) {
    // Add interval completely before new interval.
    i++;
}

while (i < intervals.length && intervals[i][0] <= newEnd) {
    newStart = Math.min(newStart, intervals[i][0]);
    newEnd = Math.max(newEnd, intervals[i][1]);
    i++;
}

// Add merged interval, then remaining intervals.
while (i < intervals.size() && intervals[i][1] < newStart) {
    // Add interval completely before new interval.
    i++;
}

while (i < intervals.size() && intervals[i][0] <= newEnd) {
    newStart = min(newStart, intervals[i][0]);
    newEnd = max(newEnd, intervals[i][1]);
    i++;
}

// Add merged interval, then remaining intervals.
while i < len(intervals) and intervals[i][1] < new_start:
    # Add interval completely before new interval.
    i += 1

while i < len(intervals) and intervals[i][0] <= new_end:
    new_start = min(new_start, intervals[i][0])
    new_end = max(new_end, intervals[i][1])
    i += 1

# Add merged interval, then remaining intervals.

Template 3 — Keep Non-Overlapping Intervals

Greedy Overlap Template
Arrays.sort(intervals, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[1], b[1]));
int previousEnd = intervals[0][1];

for (int i = 1; i < intervals.length; i++) {
    if (intervals[i][0] < previousEnd) {
        // Overlap: remove the interval with the later end.
    } else {
        previousEnd = intervals[i][1];
    }
}
sort(intervals.begin(), intervals.end(), [](const auto& a, const auto& b) {
    return a[1] < b[1];
});
int previousEnd = intervals[0][1];

for (int i = 1; i < intervals.size(); i++) {
    if (intervals[i][0] < previousEnd) {
        // Overlap: remove the interval with the later end.
    } else {
        previousEnd = intervals[i][1];
    }
}
intervals.sort(key=lambda interval: interval[1])
previous_end = intervals[0][1]

for i in range(1, len(intervals)):
    if intervals[i][0] < previous_end:
        # Overlap: remove the interval with the later end.
        pass
    else:
        previous_end = intervals[i][1]

Problem Progression

56

LC 56

Learn the core sort-and-merge technique for overlapping intervals.

57

LC 57

Apply interval overlap logic while inserting a new interval.

435

LC 435

Extend interval reasoning into greedy selection of non-overlapping ranges.

Common Mistakes

  • Not sorting first: The standard merge scan depends on intervals being ordered by start.
  • Wrong overlap condition: For closed intervals, nextStart <= currentEnd means they overlap.
  • Using min instead of max for the end: When merging, the new end must be the larger of the two ends.
  • Forgetting the final interval: The current merged interval must be added after the loop finishes.
  • Confusing merge and removal: LC 435 uses a different greedy decision: keep the interval with the earlier ending time.
  • Ignoring empty input: Always consider whether the interval list can be empty before accessing the first interval.

Complexity

Sorting

O(N log N) for N intervals because the intervals must be ordered first.

Scanning

O(N) after sorting because each interval is processed once.

Total Time

O(N log N) dominated by sorting.

Space

Typically O(N) for the output. Extra space depends on the language's sorting implementation.

Real Pattern

When you see ranges, schedules, time blocks, overlaps, conflicts, insertion into sorted intervals, or requests to make intervals non-overlapping, think Merge Intervals.

The key question is: Can I sort the intervals and then make one left-to-right decision based on the current interval's end?

INTERVAL PATTERN

Sweep Line / Events

The Sweep Line pattern converts intervals into start and end events, processes those events in order, and tracks how many intervals are active at each point.

Pattern Overview

Sweep Line is useful when the important question is not which intervals should be merged, but how many intervals are active simultaneously or how the active state changes over time.

Core idea: Convert every interval into events, sort the events by position or time, and sweep from left to right while maintaining the current number of active intervals.

Mental Model

Imagine moving a vertical line from left to right across a timeline. Every time the line reaches an interval's start, one interval becomes active. Every time it reaches an interval's end, one interval stops being active.

+1

Start Event

An interval becomes active at its starting point.

active++
-1

End Event

An interval stops being active at its ending point.

active--
MAX

Track Peak

The maximum active count represents the maximum simultaneous overlap.

maxActive

Recognition Clues

SimultaneousHow many intervals are active at the same time?
EventsThe important changes happen when an interval starts or ends.
Minimum ResourcesFind the minimum rooms, groups, servers, or resources needed.
TimelineIntervals represent activity over time or another ordered coordinate.
Overlap CountTrack how many ranges are currently active.
CapacityCheck whether active usage exceeds a limit.

How the Pattern Works

For every interval [start,end], create a start event and an end event. Sort all events by their position and process them from left to right.

start → +1    end → -1    sweep → active count

At each event, update the number of active intervals. The largest active count encountered during the sweep is the maximum overlap.

active→active + eventDelta

Type A — Maximum Simultaneous Overlap

When the question asks for the maximum number of intervals happening at the same time, represent each start as +1 and each end as -1.

Key idea: You do not need to compare every pair of intervals. The event sequence tells you exactly when the active count changes.

Type B — Minimum Number of Groups

When intervals must be divided into groups so that overlapping intervals cannot share a group, the answer is the maximum number of simultaneously active intervals.

This is why problems such as Meeting Rooms II and Divide Intervals Into Minimum Number of Groups can be solved with the same sweep-line reasoning.

Type C — Resource Capacity Tracking

In problems such as Car Pooling, each interval represents a resource change over time. A start event adds demand and an end event removes demand.

currentLoad→currentLoad + change

If the current load ever exceeds the available capacity, the constraint is violated.

Event Ordering

S

Start

Represents an interval becoming active.

+1
E

End

Represents an interval becoming inactive.

-1
⚠

Same Point

When starts and ends share a coordinate, tie-breaking depends on whether touching intervals overlap.

ordering matters
Important: Decide the endpoint convention before coding. For half-open intervals [start,end), an end event can be processed before a start event at the same time. For closed intervals, a start may need to be processed first.

Practical Example — LC 253: Meeting Rooms II

Question: Given meeting intervals, determine the minimum number of conference rooms required so that no meetings overlap in the same room.

How to read it: The important phrase is minimum number of rooms. Every simultaneous meeting requires a separate room, so we need the maximum number of active meetings.

Why this pattern fits: Every meeting creates a start event and an end event. Sweeping through those events tells us how many meetings are active at every moment.

Example Input: [[0,30],[5,10],[15,20]]

Example Output: 2

Short Dry Run: Start events occur at 0, 5, and 15. End events occur at 10, 20, and 30. At time 0, active becomes 1. At time 5, active becomes 2, which is the maximum. At time 10, active becomes 1. At time 15, active becomes 2 again. Therefore, 2 rooms are required.

Java — Sweep Line Events
class Solution {
    public int minMeetingRooms(int[][] intervals) {
        int n = intervals.length;
        int[][] events = new int[2 * n][2];

        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            events[2 * i] = new int[]{intervals[i][0], 1};
            events[2 * i + 1] = new int[]{intervals[i][1], -1};
        }

        Arrays.sort(events, (a, b) -> {
            if (a[0] != b[0]) return Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]);
            return Integer.compare(a[1], b[1]);
        });

        int active = 0;
        int maxActive = 0;

        for (int[] event : events) {
            active += event[1];
            maxActive = Math.max(maxActive, active);
        }

        return maxActive;
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    int minMeetingRooms(vector<vector<int>>& intervals) {
        vector<pair<int, int>> events;

        for (const auto& interval : intervals) {
            events.push_back({interval[0], 1});
            events.push_back({interval[1], -1});
        }

        sort(events.begin(), events.end());

        int active = 0;
        int maxActive = 0;

        for (auto [time, delta] : events) {
            active += delta;
            maxActive = max(maxActive, active);
        }

        return maxActive;
    }
};
class Solution:
    def minMeetingRooms(self, intervals):
        events = []

        for start, end in intervals:
            events.append((start, 1))
            events.append((end, -1))

        events.sort()

        active = 0
        max_active = 0

        for time, delta in events:
            active += delta
            max_active = max(max_active, active)

        return max_active

Why the Example Works

Each meeting contributes exactly one +1 event when it starts and one -1 event when it ends. The active count therefore represents the number of rooms occupied at that point in time. The highest active count is the minimum number of rooms required.

Templates

Template 1 — Start and End Events

Basic Sweep Line Template
List<int[]> events = new ArrayList<>();
for (int[] interval : intervals) {
    events.add(new int[]{interval[0], +1});
    events.add(new int[]{interval[1], -1});
}

events.sort((a, b) -> {
    if (a[0] != b[0]) return Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]);
    return Integer.compare(a[1], b[1]);
});

int active = 0;
for (int[] event : events) {
    active += event[1];
}
vector<pair<int, int>> events;
for (auto& interval : intervals) {
    events.push_back({interval[0], +1});
    events.push_back({interval[1], -1});
}

sort(events.begin(), events.end());

int active = 0;
for (auto [position, delta] : events) {
    active += delta;
}
events = []
for start, end in intervals:
    events.append((start, 1))
    events.append((end, -1))

events.sort()

active = 0
for position, delta in events:
    active += delta

Template 2 — Track Maximum Overlap

Maximum Active Count
int active = 0;
int maxActive = 0;

for (int[] event : events) {
    active += event[1];
    maxActive = Math.max(maxActive, active);
}
int active = 0;
int maxActive = 0;

for (auto [position, delta] : events) {
    active += delta;
    maxActive = max(maxActive, active);
}
active = 0
max_active = 0

for position, delta in events:
    active += delta
    max_active = max(max_active, active)

Template 3 — Track Resource Capacity

Capacity Constraint
int currentLoad = 0;
for (int[] event : events) {
    currentLoad += event[1];
    if (currentLoad > capacity) return false;
}
return true;
int currentLoad = 0;
for (auto [position, change] : events) {
    currentLoad += change;
    if (currentLoad > capacity) return false;
}
return true;
current_load = 0
for position, change in events:
    current_load += change
    if current_load > capacity:
        return False
return True

Alternative Implementation — Separate Starts and Ends

For problems such as Meeting Rooms II, another common implementation sorts all start times and all end times separately. Two pointers then determine whether a new meeting starts before the earliest ending meeting.

start < end→need another room
start >= end→reuse a room

Problem Progression

253

LC 253

Learn maximum simultaneous overlap and minimum resource allocation.

2406

LC 2406

Apply the same active-overlap reasoning to divide intervals into the minimum number of groups.

1094

LC 1094

Use events to track changing passenger load and enforce capacity.

Common Mistakes

  • Forgetting event ordering: When two events occur at the same position, tie-breaking can change whether touching intervals are considered simultaneous.
  • Mixing interval conventions: Be clear whether intervals are closed, open, or half-open.
  • Tracking only starts: The active count is correct only when end events also reduce the count.
  • Confusing maximum overlap with merged intervals: Sweep Line counts simultaneous activity; Merge Intervals combines overlapping ranges.
  • Ignoring capacity: In resource problems, the active count may represent passengers, machines, memory, or another changing load rather than simply intervals.
  • Using pairwise comparisons: The purpose of events is to avoid checking every interval against every other interval.

Complexity

Event Creation

O(N) because every interval produces two events.

Sorting

O(N log N) for 2N events.

Sweep

O(N) because every event is processed once.

Space

O(N) for the event list containing two events per interval.

Real Pattern

When you see intervals, simultaneous activity, minimum resources, changing load over time, capacity constraints, or questions about how many ranges are active at once, think Sweep Line / Events.

The key question is: Can I convert every interval into a small number of events and sweep through those events while maintaining the current state?

MATH PATTERN

GCD / LCM

GCD and LCM problems are built around divisibility and common factors. The key tool is Euclid's algorithm for finding the Greatest Common Divisor efficiently, with LCM derived from the relationship between GCD and the product of two numbers.

Pattern Overview

The Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) is the largest positive integer that divides two or more numbers without a remainder. The Least Common Multiple (LCM) is the smallest positive integer divisible by all given numbers.

Core idea: When numbers repeatedly need to share factors, divide cleanly, or reach a common multiple, think GCD/LCM. Euclid's algorithm reduces the problem using remainders instead of checking every possible divisor.

Mental Model

GCD asks: What is the largest size that can divide everything evenly? LCM asks: What is the smallest value that all numbers can divide into?

G

GCD

Largest positive integer that divides both values.

gcd(a,b)
L

LCM

Smallest positive value divisible by both numbers.

lcm(a,b)
E

Euclid

Repeatedly replace the larger problem using the remainder.

gcd(a,b)=gcd(b,a%b)

Recognition Clues

DivisibleThe problem repeatedly asks whether values divide evenly.
Common FactorSeveral values need to share a factor or divisor.
Common MultipleFind the smallest value divisible by multiple numbers.
Reduce FractionsA ratio or fraction needs to be simplified using a common divisor.
Repeating CyclesDifferent periodic processes must align at a common time.
Impossible ConditionsA construction may depend on whether a target is compatible with a GCD.

How the Pattern Works

Euclid's algorithm is based on the fact that the common divisors of a and b are the same as the common divisors of b and a % b.

gcd(a,b)→gcd(b,a % b)

Continue until the remainder becomes zero. The remaining non-zero value is the GCD.

gcd(48,18) → gcd(18,12) → gcd(12,6) → gcd(6,0) → 6

Type A — GCD of Multiple Numbers

For an array, compute the GCD progressively. Start with the first value and combine it with every next value.

gcd(a,b,c)→gcd(gcd(a,b),c)
Key idea: GCD is associative, so the entire array can be reduced one number at a time using the same two-number Euclidean algorithm.

Type B — GCD of Strings

String GCD problems use the same mathematical idea through repeated patterns. If one string can be formed by repeating another, the two strings must share a common repeating base.

Before finding the common divisor string, verify that str1 + str2 equals str2 + str1. If not, there is no common repeating pattern.

base length→gcd(len(str1), len(str2))

Type C — GCD-Based Reachability

Some problems use GCD as a mathematical invariant rather than directly asking for the GCD. The Water and Jug Problem is a classic example: the target amount must be compatible with the GCD of the jug capacities.

Reachability condition: A target amount can be measured only if it is divisible by gcd(jug1Capacity, jug2Capacity), and the target cannot exceed the combined capacity.

GCD and LCM Relationship

For two positive integers, GCD and LCM are connected by a useful identity.

gcd(a,b) × lcm(a,b)=a × b

Therefore, LCM can be calculated safely as (a / gcd(a,b)) × b, dividing first to reduce the risk of overflow.

Practical Example — LC 1979: Find Greatest Common Divisor of Array

Question: Given an integer array, find the GCD of the smallest number and the largest number in the array.

How to read it: The problem explicitly asks for a greatest common divisor. We only need to identify the minimum and maximum values, then apply Euclid's algorithm.

Why this pattern fits: GCD can be computed in logarithmic time with Euclid's algorithm instead of checking every possible divisor.

Example Input: nums = [2,5,6,9,10]

Example Output: 2

Short Dry Run: The smallest value is 2 and the largest is 10. Compute gcd(2,10): 10 % 2 = 0, so the GCD is 2.

Java — GCD with Euclid's Algorithm
class Solution {
    private int gcd(int a, int b) {
        while (b != 0) {
            int remainder = a % b;
            a = b;
            b = remainder;
        }
        return a;
    }

    public int findGCD(int[] nums) {
        int minimum = nums[0];
        int maximum = nums[0];

        for (int value : nums) {
            minimum = Math.min(minimum, value);
            maximum = Math.max(maximum, value);
        }

        return gcd(minimum, maximum);
    }
}
class Solution {
    int gcd(int a, int b) {
        while (b != 0) {
            int remainder = a % b;
            a = b;
            b = remainder;
        }
        return a;
    }

public:
    int findGCD(vector<int>& nums) {
        int minimum = nums[0];
        int maximum = nums[0];

        for (int value : nums) {
            minimum = min(minimum, value);
            maximum = max(maximum, value);
        }

        return gcd(minimum, maximum);
    }
};
class Solution:
    def gcd(self, a, b):
        while b != 0:
            a, b = b, a % b
        return a

    def findGCD(self, nums):
        minimum = min(nums)
        maximum = max(nums)
        return self.gcd(minimum, maximum)

Why the Example Works

The array only determines the smallest and largest values. Once those two values are known, Euclid's algorithm repeatedly replaces the larger number with the remainder until the remainder becomes zero. The final non-zero value is the greatest common divisor.

Templates

Template 1 — Euclid's GCD Algorithm

Basic GCD Template
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int remainder = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = remainder;
    }
    return a;
}
int gcd(int a, int b) {
    while (b != 0) {
        int remainder = a % b;
        a = b;
        b = remainder;
    }
    return a;
}
def gcd(a, b):
    while b != 0:
        a, b = b, a % b
    return a

Template 2 — GCD of Multiple Values

Progressive GCD
int runningGcd = values[0];
for (int i = 1; i < values.length; i++) {
    runningGcd = gcd(runningGcd, values[i]);
}
int runningGcd = values[0];
for (int i = 1; i < values.size(); i++) {
    runningGcd = gcd(runningGcd, values[i]);
}
running_gcd = values[0]
for value in values[1:]:
    running_gcd = gcd(running_gcd, value)

Template 3 — LCM Using GCD

GCD / LCM Relationship
long gcdValue = gcd(a, b);
long lcmValue = (a / gcdValue) * b;
long long gcdValue = gcd(a, b);
long long lcmValue = (a / gcdValue) * b;
gcd_value = gcd(a, b)
lcm_value = (a // gcd_value) * b

Template 4 — GCD-Based Reachability

Divisibility Condition
int commonFactor = gcd(capacityA, capacityB);
boolean possible = target <= capacityA + capacityB
        && target % commonFactor == 0;
int commonFactor = gcd(capacityA, capacityB);
bool possible = target <= capacityA + capacityB
        && target % commonFactor == 0;
common_factor = gcd(capacity_a, capacity_b)
possible = (target <= capacity_a + capacity_b
            and target % common_factor == 0)

Problem Progression

1979

LC 1979

Learn the basic GCD calculation using Euclid's algorithm.

1071

LC 1071

Recognize GCD reasoning in repeated string patterns and combine lengths with divisibility.

365

LC 365

Apply the GCD as a mathematical invariant for determining whether a target amount is reachable.

Common Mistakes

  • Brute-forcing divisors: Checking every possible divisor is unnecessary when Euclid's algorithm gives GCD efficiently.
  • Confusing GCD and LCM: GCD finds the largest common divisor; LCM finds the smallest common multiple.
  • Forgetting the zero case: Euclid's algorithm terminates when the second value becomes zero.
  • Computing LCM as a × b / gcd directly: Divide before multiplying when using fixed-width integer types to reduce overflow risk.
  • Missing the invariant: Some problems never explicitly ask for GCD but depend on divisibility by the GCD.
  • Assuming every string shares a common divisor: String GCD requires compatible repeating structures.

Complexity

Euclid's Algorithm

O(log min(a,b)) for two positive integers.

Array GCD

O(N log V) approximately for N values bounded by V, because each GCD operation is logarithmic.

LCM

O(log min(a,b)) when computed using GCD.

Space

O(1) auxiliary space for the iterative Euclidean algorithm.

Real Pattern

When you see divisibility, common factors, common multiples, repeating cycles, fraction reduction, or mathematical reachability, think GCD / LCM.

The key question is: Can I reduce the problem to common divisibility and use Euclid's algorithm instead of brute force?

learning.html:
MATH PATTERN

Prime & Modular Arithmetic

Prime and modular arithmetic problems use number properties to replace expensive simulation with mathematical structure. The key ideas are prime factorization, divisibility, remainders, modular reasoning, and fast exponentiation.

Pattern Overview

Many mathematical problems look computationally expensive because they involve repeatedly checking numbers, multiplying large values, or simulating a process. Number theory often gives a much smaller way to reason about the same problem.

Core idea: Look for mathematical structure before simulating. Prime numbers reveal factor structure, modular arithmetic reduces values to remainders, and exponentiation can be reduced from O(n) multiplications to O(log n).

Mental Model

Think of these problems as questions about properties rather than individual operations. Instead of asking how to perform every step, ask what must mathematically be true.

P

Prime

A number greater than 1 with exactly two positive divisors.

2,3,5,7,...
%

Modulo

Work with the remainder instead of the full value.

a % m
²

Fast Power

Repeatedly square the base and halve the exponent.

O(log n)

Recognition Clues

PrimeThe problem asks whether numbers are prime or how many primes exist.
DivisibilityA number must be divisible by a particular base or factor.
PowerA value is raised to a potentially very large exponent.
ModuloThe result is required under a modulus or depends on remainders.
Large ExponentDirect multiplication would require too many operations.
OptimizationA mathematical property can replace repeated computation.

How the Pattern Works

For prime-related problems, determine whether numbers have factors efficiently rather than testing every possible value blindly. For many numbers in a range, the Sieve of Eratosthenes marks multiples of each discovered prime.

prime p→mark p², p²+p, p²+2p,...

For exponentiation, use binary decomposition of the exponent. If the current exponent bit is 1, multiply the answer by the current base; then square the base and halve the exponent.

power→square + halve

Type A — Prime Detection & Sieve

To test whether one number is prime, only divisors up to its square root need to be checked. When many primes up to a limit are required, use the Sieve of Eratosthenes.

Why stop at √n? If n has a factor larger than √n, its matching factor must be smaller than √n. Therefore, if no divisor exists up to √n, n is prime.

Type B — Divisibility and Powers of a Base

LC 326 asks whether a number is a power of three. Instead of repeatedly generating powers or using floating-point logarithms, repeatedly divide by 3 while the number is divisible by 3.

n→n / 3→n / 9→...

Another mathematical observation is that for a fixed maximum value, the largest power of three in that range is divisible by every smaller power of three. The problem can therefore also be solved with a divisibility check.

Type C — Fast Modular Exponentiation

When computing x raised to the power n, multiplying x by itself n times is too slow for a large exponent. Binary exponentiation reduces the number of multiplications by repeatedly squaring the base.

Key idea: Every exponent can be represented in binary. Squaring gives powers x, x², x⁴, x⁸, ... and only the powers corresponding to set bits of n need to be multiplied into the answer.

Binary Exponentiation State

A

Answer

Stores the product of the powers selected by the exponent bits.

answer
B

Base

Starts at x and is repeatedly squared.

base *= base
E

Exponent

Is repeatedly divided by two until it reaches zero.

exponent /= 2

Practical Example — LC 50: Pow(x, n)

Question: Implement pow(x,n), which calculates x raised to the integer power n.

How to read it: The important signal is the potentially large exponent. Repeated multiplication would take O(n) time, so we need exponentiation by squaring.

Why this pattern fits: Every step halves the exponent while the base is squared, reducing the number of operations from linear to logarithmic.

Example Input: x = 2.0, n = 10

Example Output: 1024.0

Short Dry Run: Start with answer = 1 and base = 2. Since 10 is even, square the base to 4 and halve the exponent to 5. Since 5 is odd, multiply answer by 4, square the base to 16, and halve the exponent to 2. Square again to 256 and halve to 1. Multiply answer by 256, giving 1024.

Java — Fast Exponentiation
class Solution {
    public double myPow(double x, int n) {
        long exponent = n;
        if (exponent < 0) {
            x = 1.0 / x;
            exponent = -exponent;
        }

        double answer = 1.0;
        double base = x;

        while (exponent > 0) {
            if ((exponent & 1) == 1) {
                answer *= base;
            }
            base *= base;
            exponent /= 2;
        }

        return answer;
    }
}
class Solution {
public:
    double myPow(double x, int n) {
        long long exponent = n;
        if (exponent < 0) {
            x = 1.0 / x;
            exponent = -exponent;
        }

        double answer = 1.0;
        double base = x;

        while (exponent > 0) {
            if (exponent & 1LL) {
                answer *= base;
            }
            base *= base;
            exponent /= 2;
        }

        return answer;
    }
};
class Solution:
    def myPow(self, x, n):
        if n < 0:
            x = 1 / x
            n = -n

        answer = 1.0
        base = x

        while n > 0:
            if n & 1:
                answer *= base
            base *= base
            n //= 2

        return answer

Why the Example Works

The exponent is processed in binary rather than one multiplication at a time. Each iteration squares the current base, which represents the next power of two, and halves the remaining exponent. When a bit is set, that power contributes to the final answer.

Templates

Template 1 — Prime Check

Prime Detection
boolean isPrime(int number) {
    if (number < 2) return false;
    for (int divisor = 2; divisor * divisor <= number; divisor++) {
        if (number % divisor == 0) return false;
    }
    return true;
}
bool isPrime(int number) {
    if (number < 2) return false;
    for (int divisor = 2; divisor * divisor <= number; divisor++) {
        if (number % divisor == 0) return false;
    }
    return true;
}
def is_prime(number):
    if number < 2:
        return False
    divisor = 2
    while divisor * divisor <= number:
        if number % divisor == 0:
            return False
        divisor += 1
    return True

Template 2 — Sieve of Eratosthenes

Count or Generate Primes
boolean[] isPrime = new boolean[n + 1];
Arrays.fill(isPrime, true);
if (n >= 0) isPrime[0] = false;
if (n >= 1) isPrime[1] = false;

for (int prime = 2; prime * prime <= n; prime++) {
    if (!isPrime[prime]) continue;
    for (int multiple = prime * prime; multiple <= n; multiple += prime) {
        isPrime[multiple] = false;
    }
}
vector<bool> isPrime(n + 1, true);
if (n >= 0) isPrime[0] = false;
if (n >= 1) isPrime[1] = false;

for (int prime = 2; prime * prime <= n; prime++) {
    if (!isPrime[prime]) continue;
    for (int multiple = prime * prime; multiple <= n; multiple += prime) {
        isPrime[multiple] = false;
    }
}
is_prime = [True] * (n + 1)
if n >= 0:
    is_prime[0] = False
if n >= 1:
    is_prime[1] = False

prime = 2
while prime * prime <= n:
    if is_prime[prime]:
        for multiple in range(prime * prime, n + 1, prime):
            is_prime[multiple] = False
    prime += 1

Template 3 — Power of a Fixed Base

Divisibility by a Base
boolean isPowerOfBase(int number, int base) {
    if (number < 1 || base < 2) return false;
    while (number % base == 0) {
        number /= base;
    }
    return number == 1;
}
bool isPowerOfBase(int number, int base) {
    if (number < 1 || base < 2) return false;
    while (number % base == 0) {
        number /= base;
    }
    return number == 1;
}
def is_power_of_base(number, base):
    if number < 1 or base < 2:
        return False
    while number % base == 0:
        number //= base
    return number == 1

Template 4 — Binary Exponentiation

Fast Power Template
double answer = 1.0;
while (exponent > 0) {
    if ((exponent & 1) == 1) {
        answer *= base;
    }
    base *= base;
    exponent /= 2;
}
double answer = 1.0;
while (exponent > 0) {
    if (exponent & 1LL) {
        answer *= base;
    }
    base *= base;
    exponent /= 2;
}
answer = 1.0
while exponent > 0:
    if exponent & 1:
        answer *= base
    base *= base
    exponent //= 2

Modular Arithmetic

When a problem asks for a result modulo m, reduce intermediate values modulo m to keep numbers manageable while preserving the final remainder.

(a × b) % m=((a % m) × (b % m)) % m

The same principle applies to fast exponentiation: after every multiplication or squaring step, the value can be reduced modulo m.

Problem Progression

204

LC 204

Learn prime generation and the Sieve of Eratosthenes for efficiently counting primes.

326

LC 326

Recognize divisibility structure when checking whether a number is a power of a fixed base.

50

LC 50

Learn binary exponentiation and reduce power computation from linear to logarithmic time.

Common Mistakes

  • Checking every divisor: For a single prime test, only divisors up to the square root are necessary.
  • Using repeated multiplication for large powers: Binary exponentiation reduces the number of operations to O(log n).
  • Using floating-point logarithms for exact integer checks: Floating-point precision can make divisibility decisions unreliable.
  • Forgetting negative exponents: In Pow(x,n), a negative exponent means taking the reciprocal before exponentiation.
  • Integer overflow: In modular multiplication or large powers, choose a sufficiently wide numeric type and reduce intermediate values when appropriate.
  • Starting the sieve incorrectly: Composite multiples of a prime can begin at prime² because smaller multiples were already handled by smaller factors.

Complexity

Prime Check

O(√n) for testing one number by trial division.

Sieve

O(n log log n) time and O(n) space for all primes up to n.

Power

O(log |n|) multiplications using binary exponentiation.

Fast Power Space

O(1) auxiliary space for the iterative version.

Real Pattern

When you see primes, divisibility, powers, huge exponents, remainders, or a mathematical operation that seems too expensive to simulate, think Prime & Modular Arithmetic.

The key question is: What mathematical property lets me replace repeated computation with factorization, divisibility, modulo, or binary decomposition?
